title: Best Neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: Where to Stay and Explore
dek: From leafy Palermo to cobblestoned San Telmo, a guide to the Buenos Aires barrios worth staying in, strolling through and eating your way across.
body:
Buenos Aires is less a single city than a patchwork of barrios, each with its own rhythm, architecture and idea of what time dinner should start (late — always late). Where you base yourself shapes the whole trip, so it pays to know the personalities before you book. Here is how the most visitor-friendly neighborhoods stack up, whether you want grand boulevards, weekend markets or a quiet street lined with jacarandas.

Palermo Soho and Palermo Hollywood

Palermo is the city’s largest barrio, and its two most famous pockets are where many first-timers land. Palermo Soho, centered around Plaza Serrano, is all low-slung houses turned into boutiques, cafés and design studios, with cobbled corners that fill up on weekend afternoons. Just across the train tracks, Palermo Hollywood earned its name from the TV and radio studios that once clustered here; today it is better known for its restaurants and bar scene.

Both areas are walkable, green and close to the Bosques de Palermo, the big parkland of lakes, rose gardens and jogging paths. The trade-off: nightlife noise on weekends, so ask for a room away from the street if you like to sleep.

Recoleta

If your version of Buenos Aires involves Parisian-style facades, wrought-iron balconies and a coffee taken very seriously, Recoleta is the answer. The neighborhood is anchored by the Recoleta Cemetery, a hauntingly beautiful city of marble mausoleums where Eva Perón is buried, and by the weekend artisan fair on the plazas nearby.

It is polished, residential and one of the calmer choices for a first stay, with the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes and the giant steel flower sculpture, Floralis Genérica, within easy reach. Expect a more elegant, slightly quieter evening scene than Palermo.

San Telmo

San Telmo is the city’s old soul — cobblestones, colonial-era houses, antique dealers and tango drifting out of doorways. Sunday is its big day, when the Feria de San Telmo stretches along Calle Defensa with antiques, crafts and street performers, and the neighborhood’s covered market is worth a wander any day of the week.

It suits travelers who prefer character over polish. Some blocks feel a little rough around the edges after dark, so stick to well-lit streets and take a car late at night.

Puerto Madero, La Boca and Belgrano

  • Puerto Madero — The redeveloped docklands along the river, with brick warehouses, glassy towers and the sleek Puente de la Mujer footbridge. It feels modern, orderly and a bit corporate; great for a sunset stroll and access to the Costanera Sur ecological reserve.
  • La Boca — The birthplace of tango lore and home of the Boca Juniors stadium, famous for the brightly painted houses of Caminito. Visit by day and stay within the main tourist streets; it is not an area to wander aimlessly or linger in after dark.
  • Belgrano — A leafy, residential barrio north of Palermo with a compact Barrio Chino (Chinatown) and a local, lived-in feel. A good pick for longer stays or travelers who want to see how porteños actually live.

Villa Crespo and Chacarita

Just west of Palermo, Villa Crespo has become a favorite for travelers who want Palermo’s energy without the crowds. It has deep roots as a working-class and Jewish neighborhood, a cluster of outlet shops, and an ever-growing lineup of neighborhood cafés and wine bars.

Neighboring Chacarita, known for its vast cemetery, has steadily drawn a creative crowd with small restaurants and cafés tucked into quiet streets. Both work well if you want to feel like a local and do not mind hopping in a taxi or on the subway to reach the headline sights.

Choosing Your Base

For a first visit, Palermo or Recoleta give you the easiest balance of safety, walkability and things to do. San Telmo rewards those chasing atmosphere, while Villa Crespo and Belgrano suit repeat visitors and slower trips. Whichever you choose, the subway (Subte) and plentiful taxis and ride apps make it easy to hop between barrios.

Ready to put it all together? Our 3-day Buenos Aires itinerary strings these neighborhoods into a relaxed plan, and the full Buenos Aires guide covers everything from tango to steak.

Quick Tips

  • Keep phones out of sight on busy streets and in crowded markets — petty theft is the main concern for visitors.
  • Weekends are when the fairs and markets come alive; plan San Telmo for Sunday.
  • Dinner rarely starts before 9 p.m., so an afternoon merienda of coffee and medialunas is your friend.

title: Day Trips from Bogotá: Salt Cathedral, Guatavita and More
dek: An underground cathedral, a sacred lagoon, a colonial town and a mountaintop view — the most rewarding escapes from Bogotá.
body:
Bogotá sits on a high Andean plateau, and the green countryside around it holds some of Colombia’s most intriguing sights — a cathedral carved underground, a lagoon tied to the legend of El Dorado, and colonial towns that feel frozen in time. Once you’ve covered the city with our Bogotá guide, these are the escapes worth your time.

Zipaquirá Salt Cathedral

About an hour or so north of the city, depending on traffic, the town of Zipaquirá is home to one of Colombia’s most unusual attractions: a church built deep inside a salt mine. You descend through dim tunnels lined with Stations of the Cross before reaching a vast underground nave, dramatically lit and carved directly into the rock.

The town itself is worth a wander, with a handsome main square and colonial architecture. You can reach Zipaquirá by car, organized tour or public bus, and a heritage tourist train has traditionally run on some weekends — check current schedules and ticket options before you go.

  • Bring a layer — it’s cool underground.
  • Wear good shoes; the tunnels involve plenty of walking on uneven ground.
  • Arrive early on weekends and holidays, when domestic visitors pour in.

Guatavita Lagoon

The Laguna de Guatavita is a round, emerald lake set in the hills northeast of Bogotá, and it was sacred to the Muisca people. Ceremonies here, in which offerings of gold were made to the waters, are widely linked to the origins of the El Dorado legend — a story that sent generations of treasure hunters chasing a golden city that never existed.

Visits are typically by guided walk along a trail that climbs to viewpoints over the lagoon; swimming isn’t allowed. Access rules and visiting days can change, so confirm current details in advance. Nearby, the town of Guatavita is itself a curiosity — it was rebuilt in a whitewashed colonial style after the original was flooded to create the Tominé reservoir.

Guatavita pairs nicely with Zipaquirá for a full day, especially with a driver or tour handling the logistics.

Villa de Leyva: Better as an Overnight

Villa de Leyva, in the neighboring department of Boyacá, is one of Colombia’s best-preserved colonial towns: whitewashed buildings, cobblestone lanes and a vast, stone-paved main square that ranks among the largest in the country. The surrounding high desert landscape adds fossil sites, blue natural pools and vineyards to the mix.

It’s roughly three to four hours from Bogotá each way, which makes a same-day round trip tiring. We recommend at least one night — you’ll get the town at its most magical in the early morning and after dark, when the day-trippers have gone.

Monserrate: An Easy Half-Day

You don’t need to leave the city for one of the region’s most striking views. Monserrate rises above La Candelaria to more than 3,100 meters, crowned by a white church and a pilgrimage site that draws faithful visitors year-round. The panorama of Bogotá stretching across the plateau is unforgettable on a clear morning.

Ride up by cable car or funicular, or hike the stairway trail if you’re well acclimatized — it’s steep and demanding at that altitude, and access to the trail can vary, so check current conditions. Go early for the clearest skies and the smallest crowds, and bring a jacket: it’s noticeably colder at the top.

Planning Tips

  • Start early. Leaving Bogotá before the morning rush saves a surprising amount of time.
  • Avoid Sunday evening returns when possible; traffic into the city can crawl after long weekends.
  • Pack for changeable weather — sun, rain and chill can all happen in one day.
  • Confirm tickets and access for each site on official channels, since schedules and booking systems change.

Which Trip to Choose

Short on time? Pair Zipaquirá and Guatavita in one well-planned day, and fit Monserrate into a morning in the city. If you can spare a night, Villa de Leyva is the most rewarding escape of all. Slot them around the city highlights with our 3-day Bogotá itinerary.

title: What to Eat in Bogotá: Classic Dishes and Drinks to Try
dek: Ajiaco, changua, chocolate with cheese and a market full of fruit you’ve never heard of — a delicious primer on Bogotá’s food.
body:
Bogotá’s cooking is built for a cool mountain city: hearty soups, warm drinks and comforting breakfasts that make sense when the afternoon drizzle rolls in. Add a spectacular produce market and some of the world’s most famous coffee, and you have a food city that rewards curious eaters. Here’s what to order — and pair it with our Bogotá guide for where to explore between meals.

Ajiaco: The Signature Soup

If you eat one dish in Bogotá, make it ajiaco santafereño. This thick chicken soup gets its body from several varieties of potato, including the small yellow papa criolla, which melts into the broth. Its distinctive flavor comes from guascas, an herb from the Andean region.

It arrives with a half ear of corn in the bowl and a set of sides — typically cream, capers, avocado and rice — that you add to taste. It’s a lunch dish, and a filling one. Plan your afternoon accordingly.

Changua and the Bogotá Breakfast

Changua is the city’s most talked-about breakfast: a gentle soup of milk and water with a poached egg, scallions and cilantro, served with day-old bread that softens in the broth. It sounds unusual and tastes like pure comfort, especially on a chilly morning.

Breakfast here also often features tamales — big, generous parcels wrapped in plantain leaves and stuffed with corn dough, meat, rice and vegetables. The Tolima style is especially popular in the capital. Pair one with hot chocolate for a very traditional start to the day.

Arepas, Everywhere

Colombia’s corn cakes come in many regional forms, and Bogotá sees most of them. Look for the sweet, golden arepa de choclo made from fresh corn and folded around soft white cheese, and for thicker, cheesy versions from nearby Boyacá. They’re sold everywhere from street carts to sit-down cafés, and they make an excellent snack between museums.

Paloquemao Market and Tropical Fruits

A morning at Paloquemao, the city’s sprawling central market, is one of the most memorable food experiences in Bogotá. The flower section is a riot of color, and the fruit stalls showcase produce that rarely makes it abroad. Go early, bring small bills and ask vendors to let you taste.

  • Lulo — tangy and citrusy, a favorite for fresh juice.
  • Uchuva — the goldenberry, small and sweet-tart in a papery husk.
  • Granadilla — crack the shell and slurp the sweet, seedy pulp.
  • Pitahaya — yellow dragon fruit, mild and refreshing.
  • Guanábana and maracuyá — soursop and passion fruit, both superb as juices.

Many stalls will also blend fresh juice on the spot. Ask for it en agua (with water) or en leche (with milk).

Chocolate con Queso and Other Warm Drinks

Yes, it’s real: chocolate santafereño is hot chocolate served with a slice of soft, mild cheese that you drop into the cup, let melt, then fish out with a spoon. It’s traditionally paired with bread or almojábanas (cheesy bread rolls) and is a pillar of onces, the city’s afternoon snack break.

Aguapanela — unrefined cane sugar dissolved in water — is another staple, served hot on cold days, often with a squeeze of lime, or cold as a refreshment. On chilly nights, look for canelazo, a warming mix of aguapanela, cinnamon and aguardiente.

Colombian Coffee, from Tinto to Specialty

Order a tinto and you’ll get a small cup of black coffee — the everyday drink sold from thermoses on street corners. For the other end of the spectrum, Bogotá has a thriving specialty scene where baristas talk growing regions, processing methods and tasting notes, and pour-overs showcase beans from across the country. Trying both is part of the fun.

Tips for Eating Well in Bogotá

  • Make lunch your main meal. Many locals do, and set-lunch menus offer soup, a main and a drink.
  • Embrace onces. A mid-afternoon chocolate and pastry is the perfect pick-me-up.
  • Visit markets in the morning, when produce is freshest and stalls are busiest.
  • Go easy at first. Heavy meals and altitude don’t always mix on day one.

Build a few of these into your days using our 3-day Bogotá itinerary — and leave room for a second bowl of ajiaco.

title: Where to Stay in Bogotá: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: Colonial lanes, leafy dining streets or polished north-side calm — how to pick the right Bogotá neighborhood for your trip.
body:
Bogotá is enormous — a high-altitude capital that sprawls along the foot of the eastern Andes — and where you sleep shapes your entire trip. The good news: each of its most visitor-friendly neighborhoods has a distinct personality, from cobblestoned history to tree-lined dining streets. Here’s how to choose, with the rest of the city covered in our Bogotá guide.

La Candelaria: History on Your Doorstep

The colonial heart of the city is where Bogotá began, and it still looks the part: steep streets, colorful single-story houses, churches, and some of the city’s most celebrated street art. Plaza de Bolívar, the Gold Museum and the Botero Museum are all within walking distance, and the Monserrate cable car and funicular sit just above.

It suits first-time visitors and budget travelers who want to walk to the major sights. The trade-off is that the area empties out after dark once offices and universities close. Stay on busier, well-lit streets in the evening and take a cab or ride app home after dinner rather than wandering.

Chapinero, Zona G and Quinta Camacho: The Food Lover’s Pick

Chapinero is a large, lively district north of the center, and it contains two of the city’s most appealing pockets. Zona G — the G is widely said to stand for “gourmet” — is a compact grid of restaurants, wine bars and cafés. Just next door, Quinta Camacho is known for its English-style brick houses, many now converted into boutiques, bakeries and small hotels.

This is a great middle ground: central enough to reach La Candelaria in a short ride, residential enough to feel like you’re living in the city rather than touring it. Chapinero Alto, further up toward the hills, is quieter and greener; the lower blocks near the main avenues are busier and grittier.

Zona T and Parque 93: Polished and Convenient

Head north and the city gets glossier. The Zona T (named for its T-shaped pedestrian streets) and the surrounding Zona Rosa are packed with shopping, restaurants and nightlife. A few blocks further, Parque 93 centers on a well-kept park ringed by cafés and upscale dining.

These areas work well for business travelers, first-timers who want an easy landing, and anyone planning big nights out. They tend to be pricier, and you’ll be farther from the historic center — plan on a ride of anywhere from about 20 minutes to well over half an hour, depending on Bogotá’s famously unpredictable traffic.

Usaquén: Small-Town Charm in the North

Usaquén was once a separate town before the city swallowed it, and its old core still has that feel — a leafy main square, a whitewashed church and low-rise streets lined with restaurants. On Sundays, a popular flea market spreads through the area with crafts, snacks and street performers.

It’s a relaxed, charming base, particularly for repeat visitors or those who prefer a village mood over urban buzz. Getting downtown takes time, so it’s best if you don’t mind a longer commute to the historic sights.

Common-Sense Safety Tips

Bogotá is a big city, and big-city habits go a long way. Colombians have a phrase for it: no dar papaya — roughly, don’t make yourself an easy target.

  • Get around by app or registered taxi, especially at night, rather than hailing cars off the street.
  • Keep your phone out of sight when you’re not using it, particularly on busy sidewalks and on public transit.
  • Carry what you need for the day and leave spare cards and your passport secured where you’re staying.
  • Ask your hosts which nearby streets they’d walk after dark — local advice is the most current advice there is.

None of this should stop you from enjoying the city. Most visits are entirely uneventful, and neighborhoods like Zona G and Usaquén are lovely for an evening stroll.

A Note on Altitude and Weather

At roughly 2,600 meters above sea level, Bogotá can leave you breathless for a day or two. Take the first afternoon slowly, drink plenty of water and go easy on alcohol. The climate is cool year-round, with sunny mornings that can turn to rain by afternoon, so a light waterproof layer is worth packing no matter which neighborhood you choose.

The Bottom Line

For sightseeing on foot, pick La Candelaria. For food and a local feel, choose Chapinero, Zona G or Quinta Camacho. For polish and nightlife, go with Zona T or Parque 93, and for a gentler, village-like pace, Usaquén delivers. Whichever you land on, our 3-day Bogotá itinerary will help you map out the rest.

title: Lydia Lavín in Mexico City: Contemporary Fashion Woven With Memory
dek: Meet Carla Fernández in Mexico City, where geometric pattern cutting, Indigenous textile knowledge and contemporary travel style come together with Luxe Jetter.
body:
In Mexico City, where Roma Norte turns every afternoon into a study in color, texture and confident personal style, Carla Fernández offers a different definition of luxury: clothing whose beauty begins with the hands and knowledge behind it.

A Mexico City House With a National Point of View

Carla Fernández is a Mexico City fashion house devoted to preserving and revitalizing the textile legacy of Mexico’s Indigenous and mestizo communities. The label works collaboratively with more than 175 weavers, embroiderers, woodcarvers, leatherworkers, cutwork specialists and dyers across 12 Mexican states, translating long-held techniques into distinctly contemporary dress. That makes a visit feel less like conventional shopping and more like entering a living design archive. The silhouettes are architectural, the colors assured and the textiles allowed to speak with their own rhythm.

The Square Root of Mexican Dress

The house calls its geometric pattern language la raíz cuadrada—the square root. Rather than forcing cloth into curved Western tailoring, many pieces begin with squares and rectangles, then gain volume through folds, pleats and seams. It is an approach rooted in Indigenous garment construction, where the integrity and narrative of a woven panel matter as much as the finished silhouette. Look closely for boxy jackets, generous dresses, sculptural coats and hand-worked accessories. The most memorable pieces balance ease with presence: they travel beautifully, layer intelligently and never disappear into a room.

What to Notice

  • Geometry: square and rectangular construction that creates movement without excess cutting.
  • Handwork: embroidery, weaving, leather cutwork and other techniques developed with artisan collaborators.
  • Texture: surfaces that reward a closer look and make even a simple travel outfit feel collected.
  • Longevity: strong silhouettes designed to live beyond a single season.

Visiting and Shopping in Mexico City

The brand’s official site lists its Mexico City home at Álvaro Obregón 200 in Colonia Roma. Because collections, experiences and opening arrangements can change, confirm directly before making a special journey. Give yourself time to understand the construction and ask about the community and technique connected to a piece. For more city style inspiration, continue with our designer-boutique stroll through São Paulo’s Jardins district.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Note

Build the look around one expressive Carla Fernández piece. Pair a geometric jacket with wide-leg cream trousers and flat leather sandals, or let an embroidered dress stand alone with sculptural earrings and a compact bag. The secret is restraint: allow the textile to be the destination.

Style every journey

Pack Mexico City With Luxe Jetter

If the experience does not load, visit the full Luxe Jetter page.

A More Meaningful Kind of Souvenir

Carla Fernández makes the case that fashion can be directional and deeply accountable at once. In Mexico City, a garment becomes more than something to wear home: it is an invitation to understand construction, collaboration and the cultural intelligence held inside cloth.

Start your search near Parque Central

Our Antigua first-timer guide recommends staying within a few blocks of Parque Central. The square, cathedral surroundings and colonial streets give you a useful reference point when comparing hotel locations.

Open the map for each property rather than relying on “central” in its description. Compare the actual route to the square, the Santa Catalina Arch and the cafés you want to visit. A slightly different address may suit you better if it simplifies the walks you expect to make every day.

Choose the room as carefully as the courtyard

Restored colonial houses, courtyards and fountains are part of Antigua’s hotel character. Look beyond the courtyard photograph to the room you are actually booking: its window, stairs, bathroom and position within the property.

  • Ask whether the room faces the street or an interior courtyard.
  • If quiet matters, ask about nearby bars, events and the property’s own common areas.
  • If steps are a concern, confirm access to the specific room rather than assuming the entire building is accessible.
  • Check recent room photographs and the cancellation terms for your dates.

Use the answers to compare the rooms available for your dates. A beautiful shared courtyard matters less if the room itself does not suit the way you travel.

Match your base to the shape of the trip

For a city-focused stay, prioritize easy walks and a comfortable place to return between outings. Pair the location search with our breakfast and coffee guide; finding a convenient first stop is more useful than crossing town before every day begins.

For a coffee-farm visit or guided volcano excursion, ask the operator about the actual pickup and return arrangements. Do not choose a hotel on the assumption that every excursion collects from every address. If an outing spans a night, confirm luggage storage with the accommodation before booking it.

Arrival and onward travel

Antigua is reached from Guatemala City’s international airport; our first-timer guide recommends arranging a transfer. Share the correct hotel address with the provider and confirm arrival arrangements with the property. Leave flexibility around airport traffic and your arrival time.

Comfortable shoes matter on the uneven cobblestones, and layers are useful for cool highland mornings and evenings. Build the rest of your stay with our three-day itinerary, then treat a move to Lake Atitlán as a separate travel leg rather than an afterthought on checkout day.

Give Old San Juan a full day, then choose the beach or the city’s creative quarter for your second. This suggested two-day plan keeps meals and neighborhood changes manageable, with room to adapt to the weather and your arrival time.

Day one: settle into Old San Juan

Begin with coffee and the colonial streets rather than a tight timetable. Use our Old San Juan coffee and lunch guide to choose a stop that fits where you begin.

Make El Morro or San Cristóbal your main historical visit. Both forts feature in our first-timer guide; with only two days, choosing one as your anchor leaves space to explore the surrounding streets without rushing. Check current visiting arrangements before you go.

Pause for a Puerto Rican lunch, then spend the afternoon on the lanes and views you missed. Keep dinner flexible if your arrival day was tiring. This is a suggested sequence, not a timed tour with guaranteed entry slots.

Day two: choose a beach-led or culture-led day

For beach time, choose Condado or Ocean Park. Keep the morning and lunch in the same general area rather than repeatedly crossing back to Old San Juan. Choose beach activities according to the conditions on the day and your comfort in the water.

For a creative-city day, choose Santurce. Our first-timer guide introduces its murals, galleries and La Placita’s lively evenings. Build the day around the specific places you want to see, and check their opening days before setting off.

You can combine a beach morning with Santurce later if you want a fuller day. Treat that as an option, not a requirement; leave time for the transfer and a proper meal.

Choose your base before booking the extras

Old San Juan, Condado and Ocean Park suit different trips. Stay in the old city if the first day is your priority; compare the beach neighborhoods if you want more of the trip by the sea.

For just two days, one base keeps packing and check-ins from eating into your time. If arrival or departure leaves only a half day, shorten the second day rather than compressing everything into a checklist.

With an extra day

El Yunque and the bioluminescent lagoon at Fajardo are possibilities covered in our San Juan first-timer guide. Give an excursion its own space in the itinerary. Compare its actual pickup, duration and return arrangements before booking, especially if you are flying that day.

The two-day city plan stands on its own. You do not need to add a rainforest trip or a late return to feel that you have seen San Juan.

Mercado Central: browse before sitting down

Mercado Central brings seafood, other food stalls and restaurants together in the historic center. Treat it as a place to compare a few options rather than an instruction to accept the first table offered.

Read the menu and ask how a seafood order is priced before committing. Choose a lunch that suits your appetite, then leave time to look around. The market is a useful food anchor for a center-focused day; it does not need to become a multi-course event.

Lastarria: choose between a meal and a sandwich stop

Bar Liguria in Lastarria is listed by Santiago’s municipal tourism office for traditional Chilean cooking. Its examples include pastel de choclo and slow-cooked meat dishes. Use the current menu to decide whether this is the substantial meal you want to build an evening around.

Fuente Lastarria offers another direction: Chilean sandwiches, including versions with beef and pork. Choose it as a different style of meal, rather than trying to fit both venues into one evening.

Link food to the neighborhood

Lastarria and Bellas Artes pair food with galleries and cultural stops. The municipal neighborhood guide connects the area with museums, Parque Forestal and the Gabriela Mistral cultural center.

Our suggestion: make the market your lunch option on a historic-center day, and keep Lastarria for another meal or an evening after nearby sightseeing. If you already have a large lunch planned, choose a simpler dinner. You can experience the city’s food without reserving every break.

Before you build the day

Check current service days, menus and the exact branch of any restaurant. Leave room in your plan for a queue or a change of mind. Discuss dietary needs directly with the venue, especially when a traditional dish’s short name does not describe every ingredient.

Use our three-day itinerary below to fit these food options around the city. For a winery excursion, plan that as its own outing rather than adding it to an already full market-and-museum day. This guide is based on linked tourism sources, not personal restaurant reviews.

Jet Set LatAM · The city edit

Let Bogotá’s food give your sightseeing a rhythm: a traditional meal in La Candelaria, a separate market visit and enough time to sit over something warm. Here is how to make those choices without turning lunch into another cross-city errand.

Start with ajiaco in La Candelaria

Ajiaco santafereño is a substantial chicken-and-potato soup. Bogotá’s city tourism guide names La Puerta Falsa as a place to try it, with corn, rice and avocado among the accompaniments it describes.

Use the restaurant as a candidate for your historic-center day. Look at the current menu before joining a queue, and leave yourself an alternative if the timing does not work. A famous address is less useful when it forces you to rush the meal or miss the museum you came to see.

Chocolate, tamales and a different kind of pause

Visit Bogotá’s La Candelaria food guide highlights tamales and hot chocolate with cheese alongside ajiaco and other traditional dishes. This gives you a second way to use the neighborhood: choose a lighter pause or a different meal rather than repeating the same lunch.

If you are curious about the chocolate-and-cheese combination, order it as its own experience. Ask what comes with it before adding more food. There is no need to fit every traditional dish into a single sitting.

Give Paloquemao its own morning

Paloquemao is a separate market outing, not an extra stop to squeeze between two fixed restaurant reservations. Browse first, then decide what you want to eat. Capital’s reporting on the market also documents its ajiaco tradition.

Ask stallholders about unfamiliar produce, quantities and prices before buying. If you want explanations of ingredients and cooking traditions, compare a guided market visit with exploring independently. Check what any tour actually includes; “food tour” does not automatically mean a full meal.

Two days, two food anchors

On your La Candelaria day, choose one traditional meal and keep the rest flexible around the museums and streets you want to explore. On another morning, make Paloquemao the main food stop, then continue with the city plan rather than returning across town for a second lunch.

For your wider route, use our linked three-day itinerary. Check opening days and current menus directly, and discuss dietary requirements with the kitchen. This is a researched planning guide, not a claim of firsthand restaurant visits.

Hartwood: choose it for the cooking approach

Hartwood describes a daily-changing menu and cooking over an open fire, wood-burning oven and grill. Ingredients are sourced through markets and farms in the Yucatán. The attraction is the approach to that day’s ingredients, rather than a promise that one photographed dish will be available.

Use the restaurant’s own reservation link and current information before organizing your evening. If you need a particular dietary accommodation, ask in advance; a changing menu is not a guarantee of a suitable substitute.

Cetli: compare the menu before choosing

Cetli publishes its location on the Tulum–Cobá road and a menu grounded in Mexican cooking. Listed examples include a poblano pepper with huitlacoche and red peanut mole, chicken with black mole, and chiles en nogada.

Its website also separates breakfast and dinner menus. Choose the service that suits your day, then reconfirm availability. Nuts, dairy and other ingredients appear in several dishes, so ask the kitchen directly about any allergy rather than relying on a short menu description.

Town, beach or ruins: choose the day before dinner

Start with our Tulum sights and cenotes guide. Decide which part of the destination you will spend most of the day in, then map your restaurant and accommodation. Do not assume that a restaurant described as “Tulum” sits beside your hotel.

Leave enough time to return, change and travel to dinner if needed. On a beach day, one planned evening meal can be enough structure. On a day with ruins and a cenote, keeping lunch flexible avoids chaining several fixed arrival times together.

A useful booking checklist

  • Confirm the restaurant’s exact pin and how you will return to your accommodation.
  • Check the current menu, opening day and reservation conditions on its own website.
  • Ask what is included before committing to a special menu.
  • Keep an alternative near your base in case your sightseeing day runs long.

This is a focused, researched choice between two styles of meal, not an exhaustive ranking or a personal dining review.

A food day that still leaves time for the city

Begin with breakfast near your accommodation, then choose your sightseeing area. Save a coffee stop for a genuine break, and make the dinner reservation after checking the journey from your final activity. These are separate options, not a tested walking circuit.

Our El Poblado versus Laureles guide helps connect the food plan to a sensible base. If your day takes you to Comuna 13, avoid filling the afternoon with distant meal reservations; leave time for the visit and the return journey.

title: Mountain Biking in Latin America: Where to Ride and How to Plan It
dek: Volcano descents, Andean singletrack and jungle trails: where to go mountain biking in Latin America and how to plan the ride.
body:
Latin America is built for riding downhill. Volcanoes, high passes and long valleys mean that a short shuttle up can buy you hours of descent, often through landscapes that change from glacier to jungle in a single afternoon. Mountain biking in Latin America works for strong intermediates on a guided day out as well as for riders planning a whole trip around the trails.

The Andes: Big Descents With a Guide

Bolivia’s Yungas Road, the so-called Death Road, is the region’s most famous ride: a long descent from high-altitude cold into humid cloud forest. Gravity Bolivia pioneered guided rides here and is known for its focus on safety, which matters on a narrow gravel road with steep drops.

In Ecuador, Dutchman Adventure, the evolution of the long-running Biking Dutchman, runs day rides down the slopes of Cotopaxi. You start near the snowline of one of the world’s highest active volcanoes and roll back down through high páramo grassland. Park access can change with volcanic activity, so confirm before booking.

Near Cusco, Amazonas Explorer offers mountain biking and e-biking in the Sacred Valley, with routes that link Inca sites, farming villages and big Andean views. It is a smart way to cover ground while you acclimatize before a trek.

Easy Thrills: Waterfalls and Lakeshores

Not every ride needs full suspension. Ecuador’s Ruta de las Cascadas runs downhill from Baños along a river gorge, passing a string of waterfalls before reaching the thundering Pailón del Diablo. Rent a bike in town, ride the paved road and take a bus or truck back up.

In Costa Rica, Bike Arenal runs guided rides around La Fortuna and Lake Arenal, from relaxed volcano-view routes to more technical terrain. Expect rolling hills, rainforest and a good chance of spotting wildlife along the way.

Both rides are good choices for groups with mixed abilities, since everyone can set their own pace and the scenery keeps the less experienced riders motivated. They also slot easily into a wider itinerary of hot springs, canyoning or volcano hikes nearby.

Patagonia and Mexico: Singletrack and Road Trips

Bariloche is Argentina’s mountain-bike capital. The Cerro Catedral bike park has circuits built for beginners and experts, and the surrounding lakes district adds long rides to places like Lago Gutiérrez and Colonia Suiza. The city tourism office keeps a useful rundown of routes.

For a true expedition, Chile’s Carretera Austral is a bucket-list bikepacking route through fjords, glaciers and temperate rainforest. Much of it is gravel, villages are far apart and the weather is famously moody, so it suits experienced, self-sufficient riders with time to spare.

On Mexico’s Pacific coast, Eco Ride leads mountain bike tours in the Sierra Madre foothills above Puerto Vallarta, with river crossings, jungle trails and ocean views on the way down. It is a welcome change of pace from beach days, and the cooler months are the most comfortable time to ride.

Choosing an Operator

On big descents, the company you ride with matters as much as the trail. Look for operators that publish clear safety briefings, maintain their own fleet of quality bikes with hydraulic disc brakes and send a support vehicle behind the group. Good guides adjust the pace to the slowest rider and stop at the right spots for photos and water.

Ask practical questions before you book: what size frames are available, whether full-face helmets and pads are included, how large the groups are and what happens if weather turns. Reputable outfitters answer without hesitation, and many will happily suggest an easier or harder version of a ride based on your experience.

If you prefer to ride independently, stick to well-traveled routes like the Ruta de las Cascadas or the Bariloche lakes circuits, carry a basic repair kit and let your hotel know your plans. Remote routes like the Carretera Austral reward preparation: plan resupply stops, carry layers for wind and rain and expect long gaps between services.

How to Plan a Riding Trip

  • Choose a guide for big descents: local operators know conditions, supply bikes and handle shuttles.
  • Bring your own essentials: a helmet you trust, gloves and padded shorts make rental bikes far more comfortable.
  • Respect altitude: ride lower routes first and save high Andean descents for later in the trip.
  • Expect weather swings: layers matter as much as suspension.

Linking rides into one itinerary is easier when you can see the whole map. Save routes and plan the journey in Rallii, and browse more ideas in our Scenic Journeys hub.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: drier months, roughly May to September in the Andes; November to March in Patagonia.
  • Getting around: most operators include transport to trailheads; arrange shuttles for one-way rides.
  • Where to base: Quito for Cotopaxi and Baños; Cusco for the Sacred Valley.
  • Booking tips: reserve guided rides a few days ahead and confirm bike sizing and safety gear in advance.

title: The Best Hikes in Latin America for Travelers (Not Just Mountaineers)
dek: Glacier lakes, Inca paths and wax-palm valleys: the best hikes in Latin America for fit travelers who are not mountaineers.
body:
You do not need ice axes or a summit résumé to hike some of the most beautiful terrain on earth. The best hikes in Latin America for travelers reward good shoes, decent fitness and a willingness to start early, not technical skill. These are the trails that deliver the big views without asking you to become a mountaineer first.

Peru: Inca Paths and Rainbow Ridges

The Inca Trail to Machu Picchu remains the region’s most famous trek for a reason: stone stairways, cloud forest and ruins that you can only reach on foot, ending at the Sun Gate. Permits are limited and must be booked through a licensed operator, so this is one to plan months in advance. Note that the trail closes each February for maintenance.

For a single, very high day, Vinicunca, better known as Rainbow Mountain, is a popular early-morning trip from Cusco. The striped mineral slopes are the reward, but the altitude is serious, so give yourself a few days to acclimatize first.

In the south, the Colca Canyon trek from Cabanaconde descends to the green Sangalle oasis on the canyon floor. It is a steep two-day outing that feels remote, with a decent chance of spotting Andean condors riding the thermals above.

Patagonia: Granite Towers and Glacier Lakes

The W Trek in Torres del Paine National Park strings together three valleys and the famous granite towers into a multi-day route with refugios and campsites along the way. Reservations for lodging are required, and park rules can change with the season, so check CONAF’s current guidance before you go.

Across the border, El Chaltén’s Laguna de los Tres trail ends at a glacial lake directly beneath Monte Fitz Roy. It is a long day with a punishing final climb, but you can start from town without a guide, and the payoff is one of the most photographed views in South America.

Ecuador and Colombia: Craters and Cloud Forest

Ecuador’s Quilotoa Loop links small Andean villages over several days and finishes, if you choose, at the rim of a turquoise crater lake. Guesthouses along the way make it easy to hike light, and the route can be shortened to a single stage.

In Colombia’s coffee region, the Valle de Cocora near Salento is gentle enough for most travelers. The loop climbs through cloud forest to hillsides dotted with towering wax palms, Colombia’s national tree, and it works as an easy day trip.

Costa Rica: A Summit Without Ropes

Cerro Chirripó is Costa Rica’s highest peak, and reaching it is a long, steady hike rather than a climb. Most hikers overnight at the base lodge and push for the summit before sunrise, when clear mornings can reveal both the Pacific and the Caribbean. Entry is reserved in advance through SINAC.

How Hard Are These Hikes, Really?

Difficulty varies more than the photos suggest. Cocora Valley and the shorter stages of the Quilotoa Loop suit anyone who walks regularly at home. Laguna de los Tres, the Colca Canyon and Rainbow Mountain are full, demanding days, mostly because of steep climbs or thin air. The Inca Trail, the W Trek and Chirripó require stamina over several days, though porters, refugios and base lodges take much of the load off your back.

A good rule of thumb: if you can comfortably hike five or six hours with a daypack at home, you can enjoy most of this list with some preparation. Train on hills or stairs for a few weeks beforehand, break in your boots and practice with the pack you plan to carry.

It also helps to think about the rhythm of a trip. Mixing a demanding hike with rest days, hot springs or a city stop keeps legs fresh and makes the big days more enjoyable. Altitude hikes in Peru, for example, slot neatly around time in Cusco and the Sacred Valley, while Patagonian treks pair well with a lazy day of lake views and lamb asado in town afterward.

Hiking Smart

  • Acclimatize: spend two or three days at altitude before big Andean hikes.
  • Book the bottlenecks: Inca Trail permits, Torres del Paine lodging and Chirripó entry sell out first.
  • Pack layers: Andean and Patagonian weather can swing from sun to sleet within an hour.
  • Go with a guide where it is required or the route is unfamiliar.

Planning several hikes in one trip is easier when you can see them together. Save routes and plan the journey in Rallii, and find more ideas in our Scenic Journeys hub.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: roughly May to September in the Andes; November to March for Patagonia.
  • Getting around: most trailheads are reached by tour transfer or local bus from a nearby town.
  • Where to base: Cusco for Peruvian treks; Patagonia towns like Puerto Natales and El Chaltén for the south.
  • Booking tips: secure permits and lodging first, then build the rest of the itinerary around them.

title: Latin America’s Most Scenic Train Journeys
dek: From Andean switchbacks to Patagonian steam, the scenic train journeys in Latin America worth planning a trip around.
body:
Latin America never built a great continental rail network, which is exactly why the trains that survive feel so special. Scenic train journeys in Latin America tend to be short, purposeful and wildly photogenic: a glass-roofed carriage sliding toward Machu Picchu, a narrow-gauge steam engine puffing across the Patagonian steppe, a canyon railway clinging to the Sierra Madre. Here are the routes worth building a trip around.

Peru: The Andes by Rail

Peru is the region’s rail superstar, and the PeruRail Vistadome is the classic introduction. The route runs from Cusco and the Sacred Valley down the Urubamba gorge to Machu Picchu, with panoramic windows on the sides and ceiling so you can watch the cloud forest close in around you. The upgraded Vistadome Observatory adds an open-air balcony car for those who want the wind in their hair.

For something slower and far more indulgent, the Belmond Andean Explorer is a sleeper train that crosses the high Altiplano between Cusco, Lake Titicaca and Arequipa. Expect long views of grassland, grazing alpacas and snowcapped peaks, plus the kind of dining car that makes you forget you are above 13,000 feet. It is a splurge, and booking well ahead is essential.

Ecuador: The Devil’s Nose

The Nariz del Diablo line near Alausí is one of the great engineering stories of the Andes: a zigzag descent carved into a near-vertical mountainside. After a long pause, the route was rehabilitated and reopened to visitors in 2026, now run by the local Alausí government. It is a short ride, so pair it with time in the central highlands rather than treating it as a day trip from Quito.

Argentina: Clouds, Steam and the End of the World

Argentina offers three very different rail moods. The Tren a las Nubes climbs from the Salta region into the high puna to the La Polvorilla viaduct, one of the most dramatic railway bridges on the continent. The air is thin, the colors are mineral-bright and the scale is hard to absorb.

Further south, La Trochita, the Old Patagonian Express, still steams out of Esquel on a narrow-gauge line through open steppe. It is part museum, part living railway and entirely charming. At the bottom of the map, the Tren del Fin del Mundo near Ushuaia follows the route of a former prison railway into Tierra del Fuego National Park, with forest, rivers and mountains framing every window.

Brazil and Mexico: Rainforest and Canyon

In southern Brazil, the Serra Verde Express runs from Curitiba down through the Serra do Mar to the colonial town of Morretes. The line threads tunnels and bridges through some of the best-preserved Atlantic rainforest in the country, and the ride ends with a long lunch in a riverside town.

Mexico has two very different headliners. The Chepe Express crosses the Copper Canyon, a system of gorges in the Sierra Tarahumara that rivals anything north of the border, with stops for canyon-rim viewpoints. In the southeast, the newer Tren Maya links the Yucatán Peninsula’s beaches, colonial cities and archaeological sites, making it easier to combine Mérida, the Riviera Maya and the jungle ruins of Palenque without endless highway driving.

What the Ride Is Really Like

Scenic trains in the region are rarely about speed. Even the shortest routes move slowly through mountain terrain, and that is the point: you get time to watch landscapes change from farmland to gorge to forest. Bring a light layer, since carriages in the Andes can be cool in the morning and warm by midday, and keep your camera within reach on the side facing the river or valley.

Altitude is the other thing to plan for. The Andean Explorer and Tren a las Nubes both reach elevations that can leave visitors breathless, so schedule them after a couple of days at height rather than straight off a long-haul flight. Drink water, go easy on dinner the night before and let the scenery do the work.

Finally, think of each train as an anchor rather than a standalone experience. The Serra Verde Express pairs naturally with a night in Morretes, the Chepe Express with canyon-rim hotels and hikes, and La Trochita with the lakes and forests of Los Alerces National Park nearby. Building a few days around the ride turns a pretty journey into a memorable trip.

How to Choose Your Route

  • Short on time: the Vistadome or Tren del Fin del Mundo fit neatly into a trip you are already taking.
  • Bucket-list splurge: the Belmond Andean Explorer or Chepe Express are worth planning around.
  • Rail nerds: La Trochita and the Devil’s Nose are about the engineering as much as the view.
  • Slow travel: the Tren Maya lets you hop between stops over a week or more.

Because many of these lines run on limited days or seasonal calendars, it helps to map the journey before you book flights. Save routes and plan the journey in Rallii, then browse more ideas in our Scenic Journeys hub.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: the Andes are driest roughly May to September; Patagonian lines are most comfortable in the southern summer.
  • Getting there: most departures start in a gateway city, so build in a night before and after.
  • Where to base: Cusco for Machu Picchu and the Andean Explorer; Arequipa for the southern end of the Altiplano route.
  • Booking tips: reserve directly with the operator where possible, book luxury trains months ahead and confirm departures shortly before travel, since schedules change by season.

title: What to Pack for Kids on a Latin America Trip (and How to Let Them Help)
dek: What to pack for kids on a Latin America trip, from sun gear to snacks and documents, plus easy ways to let children pack their own bag.
body:
Knowing what to pack for kids is half the battle of family travel, and Latin America adds its own twists: strong sun, warm beaches, cool mountain evenings and the occasional tropical downpour, sometimes all in one trip. The good news is that a smart, compact list covers almost everything. Even better, children can help build it.

Start with the Climate, Not the Calendar

Latin America spans beaches, rainforests and high-altitude cities, so check the weather for each stop rather than packing for the month. Caribbean coasts like Cartagena or the Riviera Maya are hot and humid year-round. Mexico City and Andean cities can be warm by day and chilly at night.

A simple rule: pack for the hottest stop, then add one warm layer per child for every cooler one. Laundry services are easy to find in most cities and resorts, so you rarely need more than a week of clothes, even on longer trips.

Clothes That Work Hard

  • Lightweight, breathable tops and shorts: cotton or quick-dry fabrics, about one outfit per day for up to a week, then plan to do laundry.
  • One long-sleeve layer and long pants: for evenings, mosquitoes, air-conditioned buses and churches or museums.
  • A light rain jacket: afternoon showers are common in many places during the wet season.
  • Swimsuits, two each: one can dry while the other is in use.
  • Comfortable walking shoes plus water shoes or sandals: cobblestones and rocky beaches are tough on little feet.
  • A sun hat they actually like: let them choose it, and it is more likely to stay on.

Sun, Bugs and Water

The tropical sun is stronger than many families expect. Pack a reef-friendly sunscreen suited to children, especially if you will swim near reefs or in protected areas, plus rash guards for long beach days.

Bring an insect repellent appropriate for your children’s ages and check with your pediatrician about what to use for babies. A refillable water bottle for each child keeps everyone hydrated and cuts down on plastic.

The Small Bag That Saves the Day

Keep a day bag ready with the things you will reach for constantly:

  • Snacks from home plus room for local fruit and crackers.
  • Wet wipes, hand sanitizer and a small pack of tissues, since some public restrooms run short.
  • A mini first-aid kit: bandages, any regular medicines, a thermometer and something for tummy troubles your pediatrician recommends.
  • A change of clothes for younger children.
  • A small toy, a coloring book or a downloaded show for waits and transfers.

Documents and Practical Bits

Every child needs a passport, and some countries ask for extra paperwork if one parent is traveling alone with children. Keep copies of passports and any consent letters both on paper and on your phone.

Check whether you need a travel car seat or a lightweight stroller. Old towns with cobblestones and stairs can make a carrier more useful than wheels for toddlers. A universal outlet adapter is handy, since plug types vary across the region.

Leave a little empty space in every suitcase. Kids collect things, from shells and postcards to a woven bracelet or a painted toy from a market, and a souvenir they chose themselves is the one they will keep.

How to Let Kids Help

Children who help pack tend to be more invested in the trip, and less likely to ask where their favorite shirt went. Try these ideas:

  • Give them their own bag: a small backpack they are fully in charge of, with a book, a toy, a water bottle and a notebook.
  • Make a picture checklist: younger kids can tick off drawings of a hat, swimsuit and toothbrush.
  • Let them choose within limits: three outfits from a pile you have preselected keeps everyone happy.
  • Practice with a game: in Little Jetter, the kids’ travel app from the team behind this site, children dress their traveler for the destination, pack a virtual bag and collect a stamp. It is a gentle way to talk about why you pack a hat for the beach and a sweater for chilly nights.

For more family planning, visit our Family Friendly hub, and for adults, our full packing list covers the rest of the suitcase.

Plan Your Visit

  • Best time to pack: start a list two weeks out and let kids add to it.
  • Getting around: a carrier for toddlers in old towns, a lightweight stroller for flat cities.
  • Where to base: a place with a washing machine lets you pack half as much.
  • Booking tips: check airline baggage rules for car seats and strollers, and confirm entry documents early. Browse every option in Destinations.

title: Your First Family Trip to Latin America: An Easy Planning Guide
dek: How to plan a first family trip to Latin America: choosing an easy destination, timing, documents, health basics and a pace that works for kids.
body:
A first family trip to Latin America can feel like a big leap, but the region rewards families: short flights from much of the US, warm welcomes for children and destinations built around beaches, boats and history you can touch. The planning is mostly about choosing well and keeping things simple. Here is how to do both.

Pick an Easy First Destination

For a first trip, choose a place with direct flights, a manageable time difference and a clear rhythm. Three styles work especially well:

  • Beach resort: Punta Cana or the Riviera Maya, where pools, calm water and kids’ clubs do much of the heavy lifting.
  • City plus beach: Cartagena, which pairs a walkable walled city with island day trips.
  • Something different: Panama, where ships, rainforest and a modern capital sit close together.

Whichever you choose, the most important factor is your own children. Toddlers want pools and naps. School-age kids want something to climb, spot or collect. Teens want a little independence and good food. A destination that offers a bit of each keeps the whole family happy, and saves the more ambitious trips for when everyone has a feel for traveling together.

Time It Well

School holidays are the obvious window, but they are also peak season. If you can travel slightly outside them, you will find calmer beaches and more room at popular sights. Check rainy seasons for your destination: many places have afternoon showers that are easy to plan around, while hurricane season in the Caribbean, roughly June through November, is worth weighing for beach trips.

Flight times matter more with children than almost anything else. A morning departure that lands by mid-afternoon means you can check in, swim and eat dinner at a normal hour, which sets a calm tone for the whole trip.

Documents and Health Basics

Every traveler, including babies, needs their own passport, and some countries want it valid for months beyond your trip. Check entry rules for each family member with official government sources well ahead, especially if only one parent is traveling with the children, since some countries ask for a notarized consent letter.

Book a pre-travel visit with your pediatrician or a travel clinic a few months out to talk through routine vaccines and anything destination-specific. Pack a small kit with any regular medicines, a thermometer, sunscreen and insect repellent suitable for children.

Choose a Kid-Friendly Pace

The golden rule: one big outing per day. Mornings are for sightseeing, afternoons are for pools, playgrounds and rest. In hot destinations, the midday sun is a reason to slow down, not push through.

Build days around places that make kids lean in. A few favorites:

  • Watching a ship rise through the locks at the Miraflores Visitor Center on the Panama Canal.
  • The colorful, hands-on Biomuseo in Panama City, all about how the isthmus changed life on Earth.
  • Climbing the tunnels of Castillo San Felipe de Barajas in Cartagena.
  • A full day at Xcaret Park on the Riviera Maya, with underground rivers, animals and a dedicated children’s area.
  • Touching, building and experimenting at Papalote Museo del Niño in Mexico City.

Stay in the Right Kind of Place

Space matters more than style with children. Look for family suites, apartments with a kitchenette or resorts with more than one pool. A washing machine is gold on longer trips. In cities, a central base that lets you walk back for a midday break is worth paying a little more for. Ask hotels ahead about cribs, connecting rooms and whether the pool is shaded or fenced.

Get Kids Invested Early

Children travel better when they feel part of the plan. Let them help choose an activity, find the destination on a map and learn a few words of Spanish or Portuguese.

Little Jetter, the kids’ travel app from the team behind this site, is a fun warm-up: little travelers dress a character for the destination, pack a bag and collect stamps. For Latin America it currently features Cartagena and Mexico City, which makes either an easy first pick.

For more ideas, browse our Family Friendly hub, where every guide is written with kids in mind.

Plan Your Visit

  • Best time: slightly outside school holidays if you can; check rainy and hurricane seasons for beach trips.
  • Getting around: pre-book airport transfers and bring or reserve car seats if your kids need them.
  • Where to base: resorts for little ones, central apartments or family suites for city trips.
  • Booking tips: confirm passports and entry rules early, book popular parks and tours ahead, and leave one free day in every itinerary.

title: Mexico City with Kids: A Four-Day Family Plan
dek: A four-day plan for Mexico City with kids: Chapultepec’s museums and castle, churros downtown, Coyoacán’s market and a boat day in Xochimilco.
body:
Mexico City with kids is easier than its size suggests. The city has one of the best children’s museums in the Americas, a castle on a hill, giant parks and colorful boats, and most of the highlights cluster in a few neighborhoods. This four-day plan keeps travel time short and leaves room for naps, snacks and the occasional meltdown.

Before You Go: Base and Rhythm

Base in Condesa or Roma if you can. Both have leafy streets, playgrounds, cafés that open early and a short ride to Chapultepec. Polanco is a quieter, polished alternative right next to the park. Whichever you choose, a place with a kitchenette helps with early breakfasts and picky eaters.

Plan one big thing per morning and keep afternoons loose. The altitude can tire everyone out the first day or two, so hydrate, slow down and save the most ambitious outing for later in the trip. Pack layers too: mornings and evenings can be cool even when afternoons are warm.

Day 1: Chapultepec’s Hands-On Side

Ease in at Papalote Museo del Niño in the second section of Bosque de Chapultepec. It is built for touching, climbing and experimenting, with a dedicated early-childhood area for the littlest visitors. Kids can stay from opening until closing, and many families do. It is closed on Mondays, so plan around that.

Spend the afternoon outdoors in the park. Lawns, paddleboats on the lake and street snacks make for an easy, low-stakes first day.

Day 2: A Real Castle and Giant Stone Heads

Start at the Castillo de Chapultepec, home to the National History Museum. The walk up the hill is part of the fun, and kids tend to love the royal rooms, the stained glass and the terrace views over the city. Go early, before the crowds and the midday sun.

After lunch, cross the park to the Museo Nacional de Antropología. Do not try to see it all. Head straight for the Mexica hall and the Sun Stone, then let the kids pick one more room. The courtyard’s giant umbrella fountain is a crowd-pleaser on its own. Plan a snack break between the two; the park’s vendors make it easy.

If you have animal lovers, the Zoológico de Chapultepec is also in the park and works well as a swap for either museum on a sunny day.

Day 3: Downtown and Churros

Head to the Centro Histórico in the morning to see the Zócalo and the Museo del Templo Mayor, where the ruins of the main Aztec temple sit right in the middle of the modern city. It is a powerful lesson in how cities grow on top of each other, and kids grasp it instantly.

Then walk to Churrería El Moro on Eje Central, the city’s classic churro shop. Hot churros with sugar and a cup of chocolate for dunking is a reward everyone can agree on.

Afternoon is for rest. Head back to your base, find a playground and let everyone recharge.

Day 4: Coyoacán and Xochimilco

Spend the morning in Coyoacán, a colonial neighborhood with plazas, balloon sellers and the Mercado de Coyoacán, famous for its tostadas and a bustling, kid-friendly lunch.

In the afternoon, continue south to Xochimilco and its canals. From Embarcadero Nuevo Nativitas, families can rent a trajinera, a painted flat-bottomed boat, and drift past mariachis, flower sellers and floating snack vendors. Agree on the length of the ride before you board, and bring sunscreen and hats.

Get the Kids Involved

Mexico City is one of the destinations in Little Jetter, the kids’ travel app made by the people behind this site. Before the trip, children can dress their traveler for the city, pack a bag and collect a Mexico City stamp, which gives them a head start on the real thing.

Once you arrive, let them choose the churro order, count the trajineras or pick the one museum room they want to see. Small choices go a long way. A simple notebook for ticket stubs, drawings and favorite words makes a souvenir that costs nothing.

Plan Your Visit

  • Best time: the dry months, roughly November through April, are easiest; summer brings afternoon rain, so plan outdoor time for mornings.
  • Getting around: app rides are the simplest option with kids; the city is large, so group activities by neighborhood.
  • Where to base: Condesa, Roma or Polanco for parks, walkability and quick access to Chapultepec.
  • Booking tips: check museum closing days, which are often Mondays, and arrive early on weekends when local families flock to the park.
  • More ideas: our Mexico City guide, the Family Friendly hub and all of our Destinations.

title: Cartagena with Kids: Where to Stay, What to Do and How to Get Them Excited
dek: Forts, gold, boats and popsicles: a practical guide to Cartagena with kids, from where to stay to getting little travelers excited before you fly.
body:
Cartagena with kids sounds like a stretch until you remember what the city actually is: a walled town with cannons, a castle with secret tunnels and boats heading out to turquoise islands. Children tend to treat it like a storybook they are allowed to walk around in. The trick is pacing the heat, picking the right base and letting them in on the adventure early.

Where to Stay with Kids

The walled city is gorgeous and walkable, but boutique hotels there often mean small rooms, steep stairs and plunge pools rather than real ones. Families with younger children usually do better with more space and a proper pool, then dip into the old town in the cooler hours.

Hotel Las Américas, out toward the airport on the beach side of the city, is a long-running resort with several pools, beach access and plenty of room to run. If your crew is older and happy with a smaller pool, an apartment or family suite in the walled city or Getsemaní puts you steps from dinner and an easy walk back to bed.

  • Toddlers and little ones: a resort with pools and shade beats charm every time.
  • School-age kids: a walled-city apartment lets everyone retreat midday for a nap or a swim.
  • Teens: Getsemaní’s murals and plazas feel independent without being far.

Forts, Walls and Cannons

Start with the city walls themselves. Walking a stretch of the ramparts at sunset, with cannons poking out over the sea, is free, breezy and exactly the kind of thing kids remember.

The Castillo San Felipe de Barajas is the headliner. Kids can climb ramps built to slow down invaders and duck into narrow tunnels that were designed to carry sound, so a whisper at one end travels to the other. Go first thing in the morning, bring water and hats, and consider a guide so the stories land.

Back inside the walls, the Museo Naval del Caribe fills in the pirate-and-ships side of the story with model vessels and maritime history. It is compact enough for short attention spans and makes a good rainy-hour or hot-hour stop.

Gold, Ships and Islands

The Museo del Oro Zenú, run by Colombia’s central bank on Plaza de Bolívar, is small, cool and genuinely dazzling for children: tiny golden animals, ornaments and pieces made by the Zenú people long before the Spanish arrived. It fits neatly into a morning wander and leaves time for the plaza’s shady benches afterward.

For a full day on the water, book a trip to the Rosario Islands and stop at the Oceanario Islas del Rosario, an aquarium and marine research center where kids can see local sea life up close. Choose a reputable operator, pack life jackets for little ones if you have them and plan an early night afterward.

Snacks That Save the Afternoon

Cartagena’s heat is real, and the fastest mood-fixer is something cold. La Paletteria makes paletas in bright fruit flavors that double as a reward for one more plaza. Street fruit cups, fresh juices and arepas also keep small travelers going between meals.

Dinner runs late here, so feed kids an early snack and treat the restaurant as a fun extra rather than the main event. Restaurants in the walled city are generally welcoming to children, and many have courtyard tables where small travelers can wiggle without bothering anyone.

Build in a midday break every day. Between roughly noon and mid-afternoon, a pool, an air-conditioned room or a nap does more for family morale than any sight in town.

How to Get Them Excited Before You Go

Kids get more out of a trip they helped imagine. A few weeks before you fly, show them photos of the castle and the colorful balconies, find Colombia on a map and teach a handful of Spanish words, like hola, gracias and paleta.

Cartagena is also one of the destinations in Little Jetter, the kids’ travel app from the team behind this site. Children can dress their traveler for the Caribbean heat, pack a bag and collect a Cartagena stamp, which makes the real arrival feel like the next level of the game.

Once you land, give each child a job: map holder, photographer, chief paleta taster. Ownership turns long walks into missions.

Plan Your Visit

  • Best time: December through April is drier; mornings and late afternoons are the sweet spot for sightseeing year-round.
  • Getting around: the walled city is walkable; use taxis or app rides for the castle and beach hotels.
  • Where to base: a pool-forward resort for little kids, the walled city or Getsemaní for older ones.
  • Booking tips: book island trips with reputable operators, consider a guide for the castle and reserve family rooms early for holidays.
  • More ideas: our Cartagena guide, the Family Friendly hub and every city in Destinations.

title: Where to Eat in Havana: The Best Paladares, Cafés and Cuban Classics Still Worth Booking
dek: Havana’s private restaurants and cafés have weathered hard years. These paladares and cafés show recent signs of life and are worth planning a day around.
body:
Eating well in Havana takes a little more planning than it used to. Power cuts and supply shortages mean menus shift and kitchens adapt, but the city’s privately run paladares and cafés remain the heart of its food scene, serving ropa vieja, fresh seafood and strong Cuban coffee in some unforgettable rooms.

Every place below shows recent reviews from 2025 or 2026. Even so, confirm before you go, since conditions on the island can change quickly.

Dining today: what to expect

  • Menus are shorter than they once were, and dishes sell out. Ask what is available that day.
  • Many places prefer cash, and some prices are friendlier in Cuban pesos. Ask before ordering.
  • Reserve dinner through your accommodation or by message, and reconfirm on the day.
  • Generators are common, but a blackout can still change plans. Keep a backup nearby.

A little flexibility goes a long way. If a kitchen is closed or the menu is thin, the next paladar is rarely more than a short walk or taxi ride away, and Havana’s hosts are usually happy to point you toward a neighbor.

Havana’s most famous paladar

La Guarida occupies the upper floors of a faded palace on Calle Concordia in Centro Habana, reached by a dramatic, crumbling staircase. The building appeared in the 1993 film Fresa y Chocolate, and the restaurant has fed a long list of famous guests since opening in the mid-1990s.

Come for the setting as much as the food, and finish with a drink on the rooftop bar. Reservations are essential.

Old-school charm in Centro Habana

San Cristóbal Paladar on Calle San Rafael is packed with antiques, photographs and curiosities, a room that feels like a family’s attic of Cuban history. Reviewers praise the seafood platters and attentive owner, though service can vary on busy nights.

Book ahead and check which days it opens. Paying in Cuban pesos is often the better deal here.

Cuban home cooking near the cathedral

Tucked into the Callejón del Chorro, steps from the Plaza de la Catedral, Doña Eutimia is a small paladar known for traditional Cuban dishes such as ropa vieja, empanadas and flan. It has a steady stream of recent reviews that praise the friendly service and homey feel.

Lunch is a good way to avoid the dinner rush. The tiny alley tables are lovely on a mild evening, too.

Cocktails and tacos on O’Reilly

On Calle O’Reilly in Old Havana, El del Frente is the sibling of a popular spot across the street and has its own following for creative cocktails, ceviche, tacos and seafood. The rooftop terrace is the place to be at sunset.

It also runs cocktail classes covering Cuban classics like the daiquiri and canchánchara. The entrance is easy to miss, so look for the narrow stairs.

Coffee and breakfast in Old Havana

Havana’s café culture is about lingering: a strong cafecito, a pastry, and a long look at the street. Three spots make it easy, each with a different personality.

El Café, on Calle Amargura, bakes sourdough in-house and grinds coffee to order, which makes it a favorite for breakfast and light lunches. Go early, because it closes in the afternoon.

Café Arcángel, on Calle Concordia in Centro Habana, is a quirky back-street café with vintage decor and sewing-machine tables. It is cash only, and reviewers have mixed views, but its charm still wins many over.

Café Bohemia has outdoor tables on Plaza Vieja and an interior patio. You pay for the view, but few places are better for a slow coffee while watching the square.

Late nights at Fábrica de Arte Cubano

For dinner with a side of culture, head to Vedado and Fábrica de Arte Cubano, a converted factory that combines galleries, concerts, dance, film and DJ sets with bars and food. Doors open late and the energy builds toward midnight.

Check the program before you go, since the lineup changes from week to week and some nights are busier than others. It is the best single place to see how young Havana spends its evenings.

Bring Cuban pesos and keep track of the consumption card you receive at the door, since losing it carries a fee.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: November to April brings drier, cooler weather.
  • Getting around: walk Old Havana; use taxis between Old Havana, Centro and Vedado.
  • Where to base: Old Havana for walkability, Vedado for evenings at Fábrica de Arte Cubano.
  • Booking tips: reserve dinners ahead and reconfirm on the day; cafés are walk-in.
  • Before you go: check your government’s current travel rules for Cuba, and see our destinations for more of the region.

title: Valparaíso Art Guide: The Best Galleries, Open-Air Murals and Artist Spaces on the Hills
dek: A walkable guide to Valparaíso’s art: a palace of Chilean painting, small galleries on Cerro Alegre, an open-air mural museum and Neruda’s house on the hill.
body:
In Valparaíso, art is less a destination than the texture of the city. Murals climb stairways, funiculars rattle past painted walls, and small galleries hide behind pastel facades on the hills above the port.

The best way to see it is on foot, one hill at a time, mixing a museum or two with long, unplanned wanders. Start with our Valparaíso guide for the basics, then use this one to build your art itinerary.

Start in a palace of Chilean painting

The Museo de Bellas Artes de Valparaíso, housed in the Palacio Baburizza on Paseo Yugoslavo, is the natural first stop. The 1916 building blends Art Nouveau and Art Deco touches, and the collection spans nineteenth- and twentieth-century Chilean masters alongside European painters.

Step out onto the terrace afterward. The view over the bay is one of the best on Cerro Alegre, and it sets you up perfectly for the galleries nearby.

Small galleries on Cerro Alegre

Cerro Alegre and neighboring Cerro Concepción hold most of the city’s commercial galleries, many in restored houses. Two are especially worth your time.

Bahía Utópica, on Almirante Montt, focuses on artists who live and work in Valparaíso, with paintings, sculpture, prints, photography and art books. The staff can arrange international shipping, which makes buying an original far more practical.

Rojo Galería, on Pasaje Miramar in an 1887 building, mixes contemporary painting with work by Chilean street artists and handmade design objects. It is a good bridge between the gallery world and the walls outside, and the smaller pieces make lovely souvenirs.

  • Galleries open and close on their own schedules, so check social channels before setting out.
  • Ask about prints and editions if originals are beyond your budget.
  • Pair your gallery loop with a ride on one of the historic funiculars.

Walk the open-air museum

Across the city on Cerro Bellavista, the Museo a Cielo Abierto has been a pioneering project since 1992: around twenty murals painted on houses and walls along the hill’s lanes, including works by artists such as Roberto Matta and Mario Carreño.

It is free and always open, though the weather has faded some murals and neighbors have worked to restore others. Walk it in daylight, take your time on the stairways, and remember that these are people’s homes.

Culture in a former prison

Parque Cultural de Valparaíso occupies the city’s old prison on Cerro Cárcel, now reimagined as gardens, exhibition halls and performance spaces. Its program changes constantly, with exhibitions, theater, concerts and seminars, and many events are free.

Even without a show, the grounds are a calm place to pause, and the former cell blocks offer a powerful backdrop to contemporary exhibitions on memory and community.

Neruda’s house above the bay

La Sebastiana, Pablo Neruda’s Valparaíso home, is now a house museum run by the Fundación Pablo Neruda. The poet filled it with curiosities and arranged the rooms around the view, so the visit feels like stepping into a very personal collage.

Combine it with the open-air murals on the same side of the city. Expect stairs and steep streets, and wear comfortable shoes.

See the street art with a guide

The murals and graffiti that cover the hills have stories that are easy to miss on your own. Tours 4 Tips runs pay-what-you-like walking tours, and its highlights route focuses on the colorful murals and the artists behind them.

A guided walk early in your stay helps you read the city, so later wanders feel less like spotting pretty walls and more like recognizing artists and styles.

A simple two-day art itinerary

  • Day one: the street art walking tour in the morning, Palacio Baburizza after lunch, then the galleries of Cerro Alegre and a sunset stroll along Paseo Atkinson on Cerro Concepción.
  • Day two: the Museo a Cielo Abierto and La Sebastiana in the morning, then Parque Cultural de Valparaíso in the afternoon to catch whatever exhibition is on.

Leave gaps in both days. Some of the best discoveries in Valparaíso are the unsigned murals and tiny studios you find by taking the stairway you did not plan to climb.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: spring and fall bring mild weather and thinner crowds; summer weekends are busy with visitors from Santiago.
  • Getting around: walk the hills, use the funiculars where they run, and take taxis between Cerro Alegre and Cerro Bellavista.
  • Where to base: Cerro Alegre or Cerro Concepción for galleries, cafés and views.
  • Booking tips: galleries are walk-in; reserve walking tours ahead in high season, and check La Sebastiana’s visiting days before going.
  • Find more trip ideas in our destinations section.
