title: Where to Shop in Arequipa: Alpaca, Artisan Textiles and Design Courtyards Beyond the Souvenir Stalls
dek: Skip the identical souvenir stalls. Here is where to find quality alpaca, working artisans and locally designed pieces in Arequipa’s sillar-stone courtyards.
body:
Arequipa is Peru’s alpaca capital, which is both a blessing and a challenge for shoppers. The same machine-knit sweaters fill stall after stall near the Plaza de Armas, but a short walk away, artisans weave, carve and embroider in restored colonial courtyards, and some of the country’s best fiber is spun just across the river.

This guide focuses on where to learn what quality looks like, where to meet makers, and where to buy pieces that will last. For the rest of the city, see our Arequipa guide.

Learn the fiber first

Before you buy anything, spend an hour at Mundo Alpaca in San Lázaro, a short walk from the center. Entry is free, and you can meet alpacas and llamas, watch weavers from Cusco communities work on backstrap looms, and see how fiber is sorted and processed.

The site also holds a pre-Columbian textile collection with pieces from cultures such as Paracas, Nasca and Wari, plus a museum of early twentieth-century textile machinery. It is run by the Michell group, and its on-site Sol Alpaca boutique is a useful benchmark for what fine baby alpaca should feel like.

  • Compare the hand of baby alpaca with regular alpaca; the difference is obvious once you touch both.
  • Ask about blends: many pieces mix alpaca with silk or cotton, which is not a flaw, just a different garment.
  • Watch the weaving demonstrations closely before shopping for handwoven pieces elsewhere.

Meet the makers at Fundo El Fierro

Next to the San Francisco church, Fundo El Fierro occupies a building first raised in 1804, with two stone patios that now house more than fifty artisans. Ceramics, textiles, jewelry and retablos are made and sold here, and the regional government uses the space for themed fairs and workshops.

This is the place to talk to the person who made what you are buying. Look for rugs, woven pieces and the embroidery traditions of the Colca Valley, and ask how long a piece took; the answers are often the best part of the visit.

Local design in a restored casona

Casona San José, on Calle San José near the plaza, reopened in 2023 after a multi-year restoration of its sillar-stone rooms. It now gathers small, locally run businesses, including a café, a cocktail bar and makers of leather and silver accessories, with space set aside for clothing, fine craft and jewelry.

It is a good reflection of what locals call a neo-Arequipeño style, where volcanic stone and colonial vaults meet clean contemporary design. Tenants change, so treat it as a browse rather than a checklist.

Polished alpaca around Santa Catalina

Opposite the monastery, the eighteenth-century Casona Santa Catalina holds a Kuna store, a well-established Peruvian brand that blends Andean references with clean, modern cuts in alpaca and vicuña. It is not a small maker, but the quality and finish are consistent, and the courtyard also hosts a regional restaurant.

Back toward the plaza, Patio del Ekeko on Calle Mercaderes gathers alpaca, silver jewelry and artisan goods over several floors, around a towering carved altarpiece depicting local customs. It is a convenient one-stop browse when time is short.

Take inspiration from the monastery

The Monasterio de Santa Catalina is not a shop, but it is the city’s best color lesson. Its streets of indigo, terracotta and white walls explain a great deal about the palettes you will see in local textiles and design. Visit before you shop and you may find yourself choosing differently.

How to shop smart

  • Quality alpaca feels soft and slightly cool, not squeaky; very low prices usually mean synthetic blends.
  • Handwoven pieces show small irregularities; perfectly uniform patterns usually point to machine work.
  • Ask before photographing artisans at work, and buy directly when you can.
  • Carry some cash for small workshops, though larger shops take cards.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: April to November is the dry season, with clear skies and cool evenings.
  • Getting around: everything here is walkable from the Plaza de Armas except Mundo Alpaca, which is a short walk or taxi across the center.
  • Where to base: the historic center, or San Lázaro for quieter streets.
  • Booking tips: shops are walk-in; consider a guided visit at the monastery, and check opening days for Fundo El Fierro fairs.
  • Plan your wider trip with our Latin America destinations.

title: Mérida Museums and Architecture: A Design Lover’s Guide to Paseo de Montejo, Maya Heritage and Yucatecan Style
dek: From henequen-era mansions on Paseo de Montejo to a museum shaped like a ceiba tree, here is how to see Mérida through its museums, buildings and design shops.
body:
Mérida wears its history in layers: a sixteenth-century Spanish facade here, a Belle Époque mansion built on henequen money there, and a new wave of designers turning old courtyard houses into galleries and concept stores. For travelers who plan trips around beautiful rooms and good museums, the Yucatán capital rewards a slow, well-routed few days.

Start with the big picture of Maya history, then walk the city chronologically, from the main plaza north along Paseo de Montejo, and save the afternoons for shopping where contemporary makers meet traditional craft. Our Mérida guide covers the rest of the city.

Start with the Maya world

The Gran Museo del Mundo Maya sits north of the center, and its facade, inspired by the sacred ceiba tree, is worth the ride on its own. Inside, the permanent galleries trace Maya life from cosmology to the present day, which gives useful context before you visit any archaeological site in the region.

Give it a full morning, and go early on weekends, when local families arrive. Taxis and ride-hailing apps make the trip simple from the historic center.

Colonial Mérida around the Plaza Grande

The city’s founding story is carved into the stone of Museo Casa Montejo, whose plateresque facade dates to the decades after Mérida was founded in 1542. Today it is run by Fomento Cultural Banamex, with furnished period rooms upstairs and rotating exhibitions that change the reason to return.

Across the square, the Palacio de Gobierno holds one of the city’s essential art experiences: the large murals by Yucatecan painter Fernando Castro Pacheco, which tell the region’s history in bold, sometimes unsettling scenes. Entry to the public areas is generally free, and the upstairs hall is the highlight.

  • Visit both on the same morning, since they face the same plaza.
  • Look up from the courtyard: the arcades frame the square beautifully in late-afternoon light.
  • On Sundays the plaza fills with vendors and music, which is lively but busy.

Henequen-era grandeur on Paseo de Montejo

Paseo de Montejo is Mérida’s grand boulevard, lined with the mansions built during the henequen boom of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Two are open to visitors and show very different sides of that era.

Palacio Cantón, built between 1904 and 1911 in a French-influenced style, now houses the Museo Regional de Antropología. The building is as much the draw as the exhibitions, with its sweeping staircase and ornate ceilings.

A short walk away, Casa Museo Montes Molina is a 1902 neoclassical house still furnished as it was, with Carrara marble floors, crystal chandeliers and European antiques. Guided tours in English and Spanish bring the family history to life, so check the tour schedule before you go.

Contemporary art in the historic center

Mérida’s contemporary art scene has been in flux, and the most reliable place to see it right now is the Colección MACAY display at the Museo de la Ciudad de Mérida on Calle 56. It brings together around ninety works by artists based in Yucatán, a compact survey of how painters and sculptors here have interpreted the peninsula.

Pair it with a wander through the nearby streets, where many galleries and design studios open into colonial courtyards. Exhibitions rotate, so a quick look at the museum’s social channels before your visit helps.

Where to shop for Yucatecan design

Casa T’HŌ, at the southern end of Paseo de Montejo, is a restored nineteenth-century mansion turned concept house. About ten small boutiques share the rooms, selling fashion, jewelry, perfume, linens, homeware and art, and there is a courtyard restaurant for a long lunch between purchases.

For craft with a design eye, Taller Maya on Parque Santa Ana pairs artisans from Maya communities with designers, so the pieces feel contemporary without losing their roots. Look for textiles, jewelry and home objects that make thoughtful gifts.

  • Best for gifts: Taller Maya.
  • Best for an afternoon: Casa T’HŌ, with lunch in the courtyard.
  • Packing tip: leave room in your bag; ceramics and textiles here are hard to resist.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: November to March brings the most comfortable temperatures; April and May are very hot.
  • Getting around: walk the historic center and Paseo de Montejo; use taxis or ride-hailing for the Gran Museo del Mundo Maya.
  • Where to base: the Centro or Santa Ana, close to the plaza and the Paseo.
  • Booking tips: check guided-tour times at Casa Museo Montes Molina, and most museums close one day a week, so confirm before you go.
  • More inspiration: browse all our Latin America destinations.

title: Three Days in Bocas del Toro: Beaches, Boat Trips and Island Time
dek: A relaxed three-day Bocas del Toro itinerary: starfish beaches, a marine park boat day, jungle trails and sunset dinners.
body:
Three days in Bocas del Toro is just enough to fall into island time without feeling rushed. This Bocas del Toro itinerary balances one big boat day with easy beach time on Isla Colón and a jungle-and-surf day on Bastimentos. Base yourself in or near Bocas Town and let the water taxis do the rest.

Day 1: Isla Colón by land

Spend your first morning getting oriented in Bocas Town, then head to the island’s northwestern tip. A bus or taxi takes you across Isla Colón to Boca del Drago, a calm beach with small, laid-back restaurants along the sand.

From there, a short coastal path leads to Starfish Beach (Playa Estrella), where cushion starfish rest in a few inches of clear water. Look, photograph, but never touch or lift them out of the water; they are fragile and fewer than they once were.

Back in town, have dinner over the water at El Ultimo Refugio, where the menu follows what is fresh.

Day 2: The big boat day

Book a full-day boat tour from Bocas Town; most combine several stops and include snorkeling. This is the day for the postcard shots.

  • Dolphin Bay: calm water where tour boats often spot bottlenose dolphins. Ask for an operator who keeps a respectful distance.
  • Zapatilla Cays: two small, palm-covered islands inside Isla Bastimentos National Marine Park, with white sand and snorkeling.
  • Green Acres Chocolate Farm: a swap for snorkel stops if you prefer rainforest walks and a cacao tasting. It is by reservation, so plan ahead.

End the day with a short hop to Isla Carenero for a sunset seafood dinner at Bibi’s on the Beach.

Day 3: Bastimentos beaches

Take a water taxi to Isla Bastimentos and give yourself a beach day with a little effort built in. Red Frog Beach is the easy option: a pretty stretch of sand reached by a short walk from the dock, usually calm enough for a swim outside the surf season.

For something wilder, hike to Wizard Beach, a dramatic, empty stretch about twenty minutes along a trail from Bastimentos town. It is gorgeous, but currents are strong, so treat it as a place to look and wade rather than swim.

Swap-ins and rainy-day ideas

  • Surf or turtles: ride out to Bluff Beach on Isla Colón for big waves and, in season, nesting sea turtles. Swim with caution.
  • Slow afternoon: rent a kayak or paddleboard and explore the calm bay off Bocas Town.
  • Rainy spell: island rain is often brief, so keep plans flexible and shuffle the boat day to the clearest forecast.

Island-time tips

Boats set the rhythm here. Start early on tour days, when the water tends to be calmer, and carry cash, reef-safe sunscreen and a dry bag.

Leave a little slack in the schedule. The best Bocas moments are often an unplanned swim or an extra hour on a dock.

When choosing a tour, ask what is included before you pay: which stops, how long at each, whether snorkel gear and lunch are part of the deal and whether marine park fees are extra. Smaller groups usually mean more time in the water and less time waiting for everyone to climb back aboard.

Respect the reef as much as the beaches. Avoid standing on coral, keep fins clear of the bottom and skip any operator that chases dolphins or lets guests handle starfish. The archipelago’s wildlife is the reason everyone is here, and it deserves a light touch.

  • Pack light: swimsuit, rash guard, hat, insect repellent and a light rain layer cover most days.
  • Footwear: sandals for town, sturdy shoes for the Bastimentos trails, which can be muddy after rain.
  • Phones: a waterproof pouch saves a lot of worry on choppy crossings.

If you have a fourth day, use it for nothing at all. A hammock, a book and a lazy lunch are a legitimate Bocas itinerary item.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: drier spells often come in late winter and around September and October; calm seas make the boat day better.
  • Getting around: water taxis leave from docks in Bocas Town; buses and taxis cover Isla Colón by road.
  • Where to base: Bocas Town or nearby Carenero keeps every day trip simple.
  • Booking tips: book boat tours a day or two ahead, reserve sunset dinners in high season and arrange farm visits in advance.

title: Bocas del Toro Food Guide: Caribbean Cooking, Seafood and Local Cafés
dek: Over-water seafood, coconut-scented Caribbean plates and island cafés: the Bocas del Toro restaurants worth a water taxi.
body:
Eating in Bocas del Toro comes with a view of the water almost by default, and often with the water directly underneath your table. The archipelago’s cooking leans Afro-Caribbean, built on coconut, plantain and whatever the boats brought in that morning. These are the Bocas del Toro restaurants worth planning around.

What to eat in Bocas

Start with the Caribbean basics. Coconut rice turns up beside almost everything, fried whole fish arrives with crisp patacones, and ceviche is a near-daily ritual.

  • Rondón: a rich coconut stew of seafood and root vegetables, the region’s signature comfort dish.
  • Patacones: twice-fried green plantain, the island answer to fries.
  • Patí: spiced, flaky meat turnovers sold as a quick snack.
  • Lobster and octopus: best enjoyed in season and from places that buy locally.

Over-water seafood

Bibi’s on the Beach on Isla Carenero is the classic first dinner. The kitchen serves Caribbean fusion with seafood sourced close to home, from ceviche to fried fish with plantains and coconut rice, and the deck faces the sunset over Bocas Town.

Back on Isla Colón, El Ultimo Refugio is a long-loved over-the-water spot with a menu that changes with what is fresh. Seared tuna and ceviche are the dishes regulars talk about, and the back deck makes a lovely early-evening perch.

Bocas Town favorites

The main town packs a lot of good cooking into a few walkable blocks, and many places are set on piers over the bay.

  • Café del Mar: a busy, reliable choice for Caribbean and Latin plates, good for a relaxed lunch or dinner.
  • La Buga Gastromarket: an over-water spot with an inventive, international menu and a popular happy hour.
  • Coco Fastronomy: casual and great value, known for the bapé, its house-specialty fried bread with a range of fillings.

Tables at the most popular spots fill quickly at sunset, so arrive early or book where you can.

Island cafés and plant-forward plates

Bocas has a strong healthy-eating streak, fueled by a mix of locals, long-stay travelers and fresh produce from the mainland. Leaf Eaters Cafe on Isla Carenero is a vegetarian and vegan lunch spot set over the water, with bowls, salads and sandwiches that make a short boat hop very worthwhile.

Opening days at small island cafés can shift with the season, so check before crossing.

A chocolate detour

Cacao has deep roots on this coast, and you can taste it at the source. Green Acres Chocolate Farm on Dolphin Bay offers guided walks through its cacao plantation and botanical gardens, finishing with a tasting. It is reachable only by boat, and visits are by reservation.

Pair it with a Dolphin Bay boat trip for a half day that covers wildlife, rainforest and dessert.

How to eat well on the islands

Bocas rewards a little strategy. Fresh fish is the star, so ask what came in that day rather than defaulting to the menu’s safest line. Lobster has a closed season in Panama, and the better kitchens simply take it off the menu when it is out of season, which is a good sign rather than a disappointment.

Lunch is often the best-value meal of the day. Small local fondas around Bocas Town serve set plates of rice, beans, salad and a choice of fish or chicken, and they are a fine way to eat like a resident between boat trips.

  • Go early for sunset: the best deck tables tend to go first, and golden hour is short in the tropics.
  • Mind the water taxi: dining on Carenero means a boat ride home, so agree on a pickup time before you sit down.
  • Carry some cash: card machines can be unreliable on smaller islands and at casual spots.
  • Pace yourself on rum: sunshine, swimming and happy hour are a famously strong combination.

Island kitchens also run on island time. Service can be unhurried, so order a fresh juice or a cold Panamanian beer, look at the water and consider the wait part of the experience.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: sunset is prime dining time year-round, so plan dinners from late afternoon.
  • Getting around: water taxis run between Bocas Town and Carenero; agree on a return pickup if you dine late.
  • Where to base: Bocas Town puts the most restaurants within walking distance.
  • Booking tips: reserve ahead for popular sunset spots in high season; cafés are generally walk-in; book farm tours in advance.
  • Find more in our Panama guides or explore the region on our destinations page.

title: Bocas del Toro for First-Timers: Which Island to Stay On?
dek: Isla Colón, Carenero, Solarte or Bastimentos? A clear guide to where to stay in Bocas del Toro on your first trip.
body:
Bocas del Toro is not one place but a scatter of islands on Panama’s Caribbean edge, and the island you sleep on quietly decides the shape of your trip. Choose well and every water taxi feels like a bonus; choose badly and you spend the week commuting. Here is how to figure out where to stay in Bocas del Toro, island by island.

First, how the archipelago works

Almost everything runs through Bocas Town on Isla Colón, the main island, where the airstrip, ferry dock and most restaurants live. The other islands are a short water taxi away, and boats are the local version of the subway: frequent by day, sparser after dark.

That gives you a simple trade-off. Stay in town for convenience and nightlife, or stay across the water for quiet, nature and a nightly boat ride to dinner.

Isla Colón: the convenient choice

Bocas Town is the easiest base for a first visit, especially for a short stay. You can walk to dinner, book tours at the dock and hop on a boat to anywhere without planning around a schedule.

Tropical Suites is a solid pick for comfort in the heart of it all. The oceanfront boutique hotel sits just far enough from the main strip to feel calm, and its suites have full kitchens, which helps on longer stays. Staff can arrange tours and water taxis for you.

If you want Isla Colón without the bustle, look to Bluff Beach on the island’s wild Atlantic side. The Hummingbird is an off-grid, adults-focused bed and breakfast with six suites, a guest pool and direct access to a beach where sea turtles nest. Expect fans instead of air conditioning and stars instead of nightlife.

Isla Carenero: steps from town, a world away

Carenero sits about a minute by boat from Bocas Town, close enough to see the lights and far enough to hear the waves instead. It is a smart middle ground for travelers who want quiet nights but easy access to restaurants.

Even if you base elsewhere, cross over for a sunset meal at Bibi’s on the Beach, an over-water spot known for Caribbean-style seafood. It is one of the best introductions to the island’s pace.

Isla Solarte: overwater calm

Solarte is a long, leafy island a few minutes from town, and it is where Bocas does its most photogenic version of quiet. Lodging here usually comes with kayaks, docks and the gentle sound of water under the floorboards.

  • Sol Bungalows: four overwater bungalows with glass floors, net hammocks, snorkel gear and a farm-to-table breakfast. Ideal for couples who want to wake up over the water.
  • Bambuda Lodge: a sustainability-minded lodge and hostel with a freshwater pool and a famous waterslide into the bay. Social, playful and great value for younger travelers.

Isla Bastimentos: jungle and wild beaches

Bastimentos is the archipelago’s wilder heart, with a national marine park, rainforest trails and beaches that feel properly remote. It is the right base if your idea of luxury is a howler monkey alarm clock.

Red Frog Beach Island Resort offers villas, a beach club and adventure extras like ziplining, all near the island’s best-known beach. For something more intimate, La Loma Jungle Lodge is a boat-access eco-lodge set on a working chocolate farm, with treetop and rainforest bungalows and meals served on site.

Which island is right for you?

  • Short trip or first visit: Isla Colón, in or near Bocas Town.
  • Couples and honeymooners: Solarte or Bastimentos for overwater or jungle romance.
  • Budget and social travelers: Bocas Town or a lively lodge on Solarte.
  • Surfers and turtle fans: Bluff Beach on Isla Colón.
  • Families: Isla Colón for convenience, or a resort with its own beach on Bastimentos.

A popular move is to split your stay: a few nights in town to explore, then a few nights across the water to switch off completely.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: drier windows tend to come in late winter and again around September and October, though showers are possible year-round.
  • Getting there: fly from Panama City to Bocas Town, or travel overland to Almirante and take the ferry or water taxi across.
  • Getting around: water taxis connect the islands from docks in Bocas Town; ask your hotel about evening pickups if you stay off Isla Colón.
  • Booking tips: small lodges have limited rooms, so reserve ahead for peak season and holidays.
  • More ideas for the country live in our Panama guides, and you can browse every region on our destinations page.

title: Two Days in Punta del Este: Beaches, Art and Local Design
dek: A two-day Punta del Este itinerary: the port and La Mano, Casapueblo at sunset, La Barra’s wave bridge, MACA and the José Ignacio lighthouse.
body:
Two days in Punta del Este is enough to see why the resort has more art per square mile than most capitals. Spend day one on the Península and the cliffs of Punta Ballena, then day two heading east through La Barra to José Ignacio. Pack a swimsuit for both.

Day One Morning: The Port and Playa Brava

Start at the port at the tip of the Península, where fishermen unload at the dock and sea lions wait below for scraps. It’s lively early, and it’s where boat tours leave for Isla de Lobos, home to one of the largest sea lion colonies in the region. Book a tour with an operator at the port when conditions are calm.

Then walk the Rambla over to Playa Brava and La Mano, Mario Irarrázabal’s giant fingers rising out of the sand. Yes, everyone takes the same photo. Take it anyway, early, before the tour buses arrive.

Day One Afternoon: Ralli and Casapueblo

After lunch, head inland to the leafy Beverly Hills neighborhood and the Museo Ralli, a calm, airy museum devoted to contemporary Latin American art, with sculpture in the gardens. It opens on a seasonal schedule, so check before you go.

Save the late afternoon for Casapueblo at Punta Ballena, the whitewashed, sprawling home and studio that artist Carlos Páez Vilaró built by hand over decades. The museum shows his paintings, ceramics and murals, and every evening the terraces host the Ceremonia del Sol, when a recording of Páez Vilaró reads a poem to the setting sun.

Arrive with time to wander before the crowd gathers for sunset, then drive back to the Península for dinner near the port.

Day Two Morning: La Barra and MACA

Drive east across the Puente Leonel Viera, the rollercoaster-shaped bridge over the Arroyo Maldonado that has become a symbol of La Barra. Take it slowly; it’s part of the fun.

Continue to Manantiales and the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo Atchugarry (MACA), a striking contemporary museum set within a sculpture park founded by Uruguayan sculptor Pablo Atchugarry. Rotating exhibitions bring international and Uruguayan artists, and the outdoor works alone justify a slow loop. The café makes an easy coffee stop.

  • Combine with a swim: Playa Bikini and the beaches of Manantiales are minutes away.
  • Allow time: two hours lets you see the galleries and the park without rushing.

On the way back west, La Barra’s main street is lined with galleries, surf shops and small concept stores selling Uruguayan leather, knitwear and homeware. It’s a good place to pick up something made locally rather than another souvenir magnet.

Day Two Afternoon: José Ignacio Design

José Ignacio is where Uruguay’s laid-back, design-literate beach style is most concentrated: low houses in wood and stone, linen and handmade ceramics, and almost no signage. Have a long lunch at Parador La Huella on Playa Brava, then walk off the grilled fish around the point.

Climb up to the Faro de José Ignacio, the 19th-century lighthouse at the center of the village, for views over both beaches. Finish the day at La Susana on Playa Mansa, where the bamboo pergolas face west for one of the best sunsets on the coast.

If you have the energy after dark, José Ignacio’s handful of restaurants stay busy late in summer, but the village goes quiet early the rest of the year. Plan on an early dinner off-season, or head back toward La Barra, where the bars and beach clubs keep going well past midnight in January.

Make It Your Own

  • Wine lovers: swap lunch in José Ignacio for a tasting and meal at Bodega Garzón inland.
  • Shoppers: browse the craft fair at Plaza Artigas on the Península; works on the plaza run through 2027, so stalls may be on the surrounding streets.
  • Beach purists: skip the museums on day two and spend the morning on the wild beaches near La Barra.

For the bigger picture, read our Uruguay guide.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: December to March for beach weather; November and late March are quieter and still pleasant.
  • Getting around: a rental car makes this itinerary easy; taxis work on the Península but are scarce farther east.
  • Where to base: the Península for night one, or anywhere between La Barra and José Ignacio for a slower pace.
  • Booking tips: check seasonal museum schedules, reserve lunch in José Ignacio in high season, and book Isla de Lobos tours in advance.
  • More itineraries live in our destinations section.

title: Punta del Este Food Guide: Seafood, Restaurants and Market Stops
dek: From the fishermen’s stalls at the port to José Ignacio’s beach parrillas and a Mallmann-led winery lunch: where to eat in Punta del Este.
body:
Eating well in Punta del Este comes down to three things: fish pulled from the Atlantic that morning, beef cooked over wood, and a table with a view of the water. The best restaurants spread from the port on the Península all the way to José Ignacio and the vineyards inland, so plan meals as part of the route.

Start at the Port

The working port at the tip of the Península is the best introduction to local seafood. Fishermen sell their catch at stalls along the dock, and the sea lions lounging just below the boats are a show of their own. Look, don’t feed: the animals are wild and the crowds can get close.

Even if you’re not cooking, a stroll here tells you what’s in season, and it’s the right warm-up for lunch at one of the restaurants overlooking the marina.

Península Classics

Lo de Tere has held its corner of the Rambla del Puerto for years, with a terrace facing the boats, Isla Gorriti and the Mansa bay. The kitchen calls its style “Punta del Este cuisine”: Atlantic fish and shellfish, fish from the eastern lagoons and top-quality Uruguayan beef, backed by a deep wine list.

It’s the Península’s special-occasion table and a natural choice for a sunset dinner. Ask for the terrace when you book.

Up in the Hills: Fasano

Near La Barra, the restaurant at Fasano Las Piedras sits on a rocky hilltop looking over the countryside and the Maldonado river. The menu leans Italian, with homemade pasta and a Brazilian accent from the Fasano family, served in a cabin-like room designed by Isay Weinfeld.

Grab a balcony seat if you can, and bring a layer; evenings up here turn cool even in summer.

José Ignacio: Long Lunches on the Sand

José Ignacio’s restaurants are the reason many people make the drive. Most are casual in look and serious in execution, and they’re busiest from late December through February.

  • Parador La Huella is the legend: a beach house on Playa Brava with a menu that changes daily, built around grilled octopus, sea bass ceviche, fresh fish and steaks, plus a famous dulce de leche volcano for dessert. It has appeared on Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants list.
  • Marismo sets its tables on the sand among the dunes, with drinks around a fire before dinner and Mediterranean-leaning plates from a wood-burning oven.
  • La Susana on Playa Mansa is the sunset spot, with bamboo pergolas, fresh local cooking and views from the lighthouse all the way back to Punta.

Reserve ahead for all three in high season, and expect lunch to roll on well into the afternoon.

A Winery Lunch Inland

Bodega Garzón sits in the rolling hills behind José Ignacio, and its restaurant is guided by Francis Mallmann’s love of open-fire cooking. Tasting menus pair regional dishes with the estate’s wines, served on terraces looking over the vineyards.

Reservations are required at least a day ahead, and service is built around lunch. Book a winery tour beforehand, and designate a driver for the country roads home.

What to Order

  • Corvina and brótola: local white fish, usually grilled simply with lemon and olive oil.
  • Chivito: Uruguay’s towering steak sandwich, best eaten at a casual parador after the beach.
  • Tannat: the country’s signature red, sturdy enough for a parrilla, plus fresh Albariño from the coastal vineyards for seafood.

Market Stops and Snacks

Beyond the port, the best grazing is informal. Bakeries and almacenes along the coast stock alfajores, dulce de leche and good Uruguayan cheese for beach picnics, and the craft fair in Plaza Artigas on the Península is a pleasant evening stroll, though works are underway on the plaza through 2027 and stalls have shifted to the surrounding streets.

For more on the country’s food and wine, see our Uruguay guide.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: December to March, when every restaurant is open. Many José Ignacio spots cut back to weekends or close entirely in winter.
  • Getting around: walk on the Península; drive or take a taxi to La Barra, José Ignacio and Garzón.
  • Where to base: the Península for port dinners, José Ignacio if beach lunches are the priority.
  • Booking tips: reserve ahead for dinner in January and February, book Bodega Garzón at least 24 hours in advance, and confirm seasonal opening before driving out.

title: Where to Stay in Punta del Este: Península, La Barra or José Ignacio?
dek: Península, La Barra or José Ignacio? How Punta del Este’s main bases compare, plus verified hotels from city-center boutique stays to dune retreats.
body:
Punta del Este is less a single town than a 40-kilometer ribbon of coast, and where you sleep shapes the whole trip. Stay on the Península and you can walk to dinner; head east to La Barra or José Ignacio and you trade convenience for dunes, design and long, quiet sunsets. Here’s how to choose.

The Península: Walkable and Lively

The original Punta del Este fills a narrow finger of land between two very different beaches: calm Playa Mansa on the bay side and surf-pounded Playa Brava facing the open Atlantic. Avenida Gorlero runs down the middle with shops and cafés, and the port at the tip is where fishing boats and yachts tie up side by side.

This is the best base if you don’t want to rent a car. Restaurants, the bus terminal and both beaches are within walking distance, and the area stays reasonably lively outside the January peak.

Hotel Florinda is a practical pick a few steps from Gorlero and Playa Brava, a boutique-leaning hotel with a pool, a garden and bikes for guests. Just north of the Península, between Brava and Mansa, AWA Boutique + Design Hotel adds a spa and heated pool to a contemporary design scheme, and the bistro means you don’t have to go far for dinner.

La Barra: Surf Town With Polish

Cross the famous wave-shaped bridge over the Maldonado stream and you’re in La Barra, about ten minutes east of the Península. The vibe shifts to surf shops, art galleries, wooded streets and beach bars, and it’s the area people mean when they talk about Punta’s summer nightlife.

Casa Flor Hotel Boutique is the quiet antidote: nine rooms in a residential corner of Montoya, a block from the beach, with white interiors, surf-inspired art, a pool and a sauna. It holds a MICHELIN Key and is aimed at adults and older kids.

A short drive inland, Fasano Las Piedras spreads across hundreds of hectares of hills, boulders and river frontage. Expect Isay Weinfeld architecture, a spa, horseback riding and a river club, plus a hilltop restaurant with views that justify the climb. It’s a resort you settle into rather than a base for bar-hopping.

José Ignacio: Barefoot Luxury

About 40 minutes from the Península, José Ignacio is a former fishing village wrapped around a lighthouse, with unpaved lanes, design-forward houses and beaches on both sides of the point. It’s the most exclusive and the most relaxed of the three, and it feels nearly private outside high season.

  • Playa Vik is the showpiece: a Carlos Ott building with a sweeping glass facade, a bronze door by Pablo Atchugarry and contemporary Uruguayan art throughout.
  • Bahía Vik, its sister on Playa Mansa, scatters bungalows through the dunes and feels more bohemian, with a spa and plenty of outdoor activities.
  • Posada Ayana is a smaller, family-run retreat with locally made ceramics and textiles, landscaped gardens and a James Turrell Skyspace on site.

You’ll want a car here. Taxis exist but are thin on the ground, and the best restaurants and beaches are spread along Ruta 10.

Punta Ballena: The Wild Card

West of the Península, the Punta Ballena headland is best known for Casapueblo, Carlos Páez Vilaró’s whitewashed, hand-built fantasy on the cliffs. Club Hotel Casapueblo occupies part of the complex, with suites and apartments facing the water, pools and front-row seats for the sunset.

It’s a good choice if you want sunsets and a sense of place without the La Barra scene, and it puts you closer to Montevideo for the drive in.

How to Choose

  • No car, first visit: the Península.
  • Beach days and nightlife: La Barra or Manantiales.
  • Design, food and quiet: José Ignacio.
  • Sunsets and art: Punta Ballena.

Splitting the stay works well, too: two nights on the Península for walking and eating, then a few nights east for slow beach days. For the wider picture, start with our Uruguay guide.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: December to March for full beach season; January is the busiest and books up first. November and late March are calmer and pleasant.
  • Getting around: the Península is walkable; for La Barra, José Ignacio and Punta Ballena, rent a car or plan on taxis and transfers.
  • Where to base: the Península for convenience, José Ignacio for a splurge, La Barra for the middle ground.
  • Booking tips: reserve months ahead for January and February, and confirm seasonal opening dates for smaller hotels outside summer.
  • Compare more coastal bases in our destinations section.

title: Salvador’s Art, Afro-Brazilian Culture and Local Craft: A Thoughtful Guide
dek: A respectful guide to Salvador’s Afro-Brazilian culture: museums, churches, blocos afro, Pierre Verger’s house and where to find local craft.
body:
Salvador is often called the most African city outside Africa, and its music, food, faith and visual art carry that heritage in plain sight. Experiencing Salvador’s Afro-Brazilian culture well means slowing down, listening, and spending where it supports the people who keep these traditions alive.

Start with the museums

The Museu Nacional da Cultura Afro-Brasileira, known as MUNCAB, occupies a historic building in the Centro Histórico and presents Afro-Brazilian art, history and contemporary voices with real ambition. Tickets are timed, so buying online ahead of time saves a wait.

Nearby on the Terreiro de Jesus, the Museu Afro-Brasileiro (MAFRO), run by the Federal University of Bahia, holds African objects and items tied to Candomblé. Its highlight is a set of 27 carved cedar panels by the artist Carybé depicting the orixás.

Between the two, give yourself time simply to walk Pelourinho. The neighborhood’s name recalls the whipping post that once stood here, and knowing that history changes how its bright facades and lively squares read. Many local guides now lead walks focused on Black history in the old town, which are an excellent way to begin.

Churches that tell the story

The blue facade of the Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Rosário dos Pretos rises over Largo do Pelourinho. It was built by and for Black brotherhoods during the colonial era, and it remains a powerful symbol of faith and community.

Its masses are known for incorporating Afro-Brazilian music and drumming. Visitors are welcome, but treat it as a service first: dress modestly, stay seated and keep cameras away during worship.

Photography, letters and homes

In the residential neighborhood of Engenho Velho de Brotas, the Fundação Pierre Verger preserves the house of the French photographer and ethnographer who documented Bahia and West Africa for decades. The rooms display his personal objects, photographs and documents, and entry is free on weekday mornings.

In Rio Vermelho, the Casa do Rio Vermelho was home to novelist Jorge Amado and writer Zélia Gattai, whose work celebrated Bahia’s Afro-Brazilian life. The renovated house and garden now operate as a memorial, with exhibits on the couple and the artists who filled their circle.

Music: the blocos afro

Salvador’s blocos afro turned percussion into a statement of pride. Olodum, based in Pelourinho, is famous for its samba-reggae, and its seasonal open rehearsals in the run-up to Carnaval draw crowds into the old town.

Ilê Aiyê, founded in the Liberdade neighborhood in 1974, was the first bloco afro, and its home base, the Senzala do Barro Preto, hosts rehearsals in the months before Carnaval. Check current schedules locally and go with a guide or a local friend if it is your first time.

Buying craft with care

Feira de São Joaquim is where many Candomblé practitioners buy ritual items, along with clay pots, baskets and straw goods. Browse respectfully, ask before photographing stalls and remember that some objects carry religious meaning.

For souvenirs, Mercado Modelo gathers hundreds of stalls selling carvings, instruments, lace and Bonfim ribbons. Quality varies, so look for pieces made in Bahia and ask vendors about their makers.

  • Prefer handmade percussion, woodwork and lace over mass-produced trinkets.
  • Bargain lightly; a fair price matters more than a deep discount.
  • Avoid buying ritual objects as decor unless you understand their use.

Visiting with respect

Candomblé is a living religion, not a performance, and its terreiros are places of worship. Some welcome respectful visitors at public ceremonies, but the best way in is through a knowledgeable guide or a personal invitation, never by simply turning up with a camera.

The same courtesy applies across the city. Ask before photographing people, especially baianas and musicians, and tip performers when you do. Choosing local guides, Black-owned restaurants and artisans who make their own work is the simplest way to make sure your visit gives something back.

Continue your Bahia trip on the coast with our Trancoso guide, or find more culture-led itineraries in Destinations.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: the months before Carnaval for rehearsals; November, Black Consciousness Month, for special programming.
  • Getting around: walk within Pelourinho; use taxis or ride-hailing for Brotas, Liberdade and Rio Vermelho.
  • Where to base: the Centro Histórico keeps the museums and churches within walking distance.
  • Booking tips: buy MUNCAB tickets online, book a local guide for markets and rehearsals, and check museum days before you go.

title: What to Eat in Salvador: Bahian Dishes, Markets and Restaurants
dek: What to eat in Salvador, Bahia: acarajé, moqueca and more, plus the markets, restaurants and ice cream shop worth planning around.
body:
Bahian cooking is Brazil’s most distinctive regional cuisine, built on West African techniques, Portuguese habits and the produce of the coast. If you are wondering what to eat in Salvador Bahia, start with the dendê palm oil, coconut milk and fresh seafood, then follow them from street stalls to some of the country’s most talked-about dining rooms.

The dishes to know

  • Acarajé — black-eyed pea fritters fried in dendê and split open for vatapá, caruru, shrimp and pepper sauce.
  • Moqueca baiana — a fish or shrimp stew simmered with coconut milk, dendê, tomato and cilantro, served bubbling in a clay pot.
  • Bobó de camarão — shrimp in a silky cassava cream.
  • Cocada — chewy coconut sweets sold all over the city.

Order acarajé “quente” if you like heat and “frio” if you do not; the pepper sauce is generous by default.

Two side dishes appear again and again. Vatapá is a creamy paste of bread or cassava, peanuts, cashews, coconut milk and dried shrimp, while caruru is okra cooked down with shrimp and dendê. Both turn up stuffed into acarajé and served alongside moqueca.

Look also for abará, a cousin of acarajé that is steamed in banana leaves rather than fried, and for xinxim de galinha, a chicken dish rich with peanuts and dried shrimp. Many of these recipes have roots in Candomblé offerings, which is part of why they carry such weight in Bahian culture.

Acarajé, where locals line up

Acarajé is sold by baianas in white dresses at stands across the city, and the craft is recognized as part of Brazil’s intangible heritage. In Rio Vermelho, Acarajé da Dinha is a long-running name, now carried on by the family, and evenings in its little square have a festive, neighborhood feel.

Expect a short wait at peak hours. It is part of the ritual, and the people-watching is excellent.

Markets for grazing and browsing

Feira de São Joaquim is the city’s great working market, a sprawl of produce, dried shrimp, dendê, clay pots, baskets and religious goods. Go in the morning with comfortable shoes and, ideally, a local guide who can explain what you are seeing.

For something easier, the Mercado do Rio Vermelho, known locally as Ceasinha, mixes market stalls with casual restaurants and is a good place for a long lunch. Downtown, Mercado Modelo is mainly about crafts, but its bay-side setting makes a pleasant pause between sights.

Restaurants worth booking

Casa de Tereza in Rio Vermelho is a warm, colorful room devoted to Bahian classics, and it is a good first stop for moqueca done properly. Reserve ahead for dinner, especially on weekends.

Origem, in Caminho das Árvores, is where contemporary Bahian cooking gets its most ambitious treatment, with tasting menus that reinterpret local ingredients. It operates by reservation only, so plan well in advance.

On the waterfront in Comércio, Amado pairs seafood-forward cooking with views across the Baía de Todos os Santos. Its octopus rice is a signature, and a sunset table is worth requesting when you book.

End a day near the water at Sorveteria da Ribeira, an ice cream shop beloved for flavors built on Brazilian fruits and regional ingredients. The original sits in Ribeira on the bay, with a newer branch in Barra.

A one-day eating route

  • Morning: Feira de São Joaquim for a look at dendê, dried shrimp and fresh produce.
  • Lunch: Amado on the waterfront, or a casual moqueca at the Ceasinha.
  • Late afternoon: ice cream at Sorveteria da Ribeira.
  • Evening: acarajé in Rio Vermelho, followed by dinner at Casa de Tereza or a booked tasting menu at Origem.

Eating well, practically

  • Dendê is rich; pace yourself on your first day.
  • Lunch is the main meal for many locals, and moqueca is easily shared by two.
  • Carry cash for street stalls, though many vendors accept Pix and cards.

Heading south after the city? Our Trancoso guide covers Bahia’s beach side, and Destinations has more food-focused trips.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: September to March for drier weather; festival periods bring special dishes and bigger crowds.
  • Getting around: taxis or ride-hailing between Rio Vermelho, Comércio and Caminho das Árvores.
  • Where to base: Rio Vermelho puts you closest to acarajé stands and casual restaurants.
  • Booking tips: reserve ahead for Origem, Casa de Tereza and sunset tables at Amado; markets and acarajé are walk-in.

title: Salvador for First-Timers: Where to Stay and How to Spend Three Days
dek: Where to stay in Salvador and how to spend three days between Pelourinho, the bay, Barra and Bonfim, with verified places for a first visit.
body:
Salvador was Brazil’s first capital, and it wears the title lightly: baroque churches, drumming in the squares and a bay that turns gold every evening. This Salvador Bahia travel guide keeps the first visit simple, with three good bases and a three-day plan that covers the essentials without rushing them.

Where to stay: the historic center or the seafront

Most first-timers are happiest in or near the Centro Histórico, where the major sights sit within walking distance. The trade-off is that the old town gets quiet late at night, so plan on taxis or ride-hailing after dark.

  • Hotel Fasano Salvador — a restored Art Deco building near Praça Castro Alves with bay views from the rooftop pool. Book well ahead for holidays and Carnaval.
  • Casa do Amarelindo — a small boutique hotel inside Pelourinho, ideal if you want to step straight out onto cobblestones.
  • Fera Palace Hotel — a grand 1930s building on Rua Chile, between the upper town and the elevator down to the bay.

If you would rather wake up near the water, Barra is the classic alternative: easier evenings, beach walks and quick rides into the historic center.

Day one: Pelourinho and the upper town

Start early at the Igreja e Convento de São Francisco, whose gilded interior is one of the most extravagant in Brazil, and the blue-and-white tile panels in the cloister deserve a slow look. From there, wander the sloping streets of Pelourinho, pausing in the Terreiro de Jesus square.

Pelourinho is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its pastel facades, steep lanes and small plazas are best explored without a rigid plan. Look out for capoeira circles, drummers and baianas in their white dresses, and keep a little cash on hand if you take a photo with a performer.

In the afternoon, ride the Elevador Lacerda, the Art Deco lift that links the upper and lower city in under a minute. The view across the Baía de Todos os Santos is the real reward, so go before sunset if you can.

Day two: the lower city and the shoreline

At the foot of the elevator, Mercado Modelo fills a former customs house with crafts, percussion instruments and souvenirs. Browse with patience and expect friendly bargaining at the stalls.

A short walk along the waterfront brings you to Amado, a seafood-forward restaurant with tables facing the Baía de Todos os Santos. It makes an easy, unhurried lunch, and its octopus rice is the dish most people come back for.

After lunch, take a taxi south along the coast. The drive itself is a good introduction to the city, with glimpses of the bay, old forts and the hillside neighborhoods that stack up above the water.

Head south to Barra for the Forte de Santo Antônio da Barra, home to the lighthouse and the Museu Náutico da Bahia. The fort sits right where the bay meets the Atlantic, and the lawn around it is Salvador’s favorite place to watch the sun go down.

Finish with a cone at Sorveteria da Ribeira, an institution famous for tropical fruit flavors. The Barra outpost is the easiest stop on this route.

Day three: Bonfim and Rio Vermelho

Spend the morning at the Basílica do Senhor do Bonfim on the Itapagipe peninsula. The church is a center of Bahian faith, and the colored ribbons tied to its railings are a tradition visitors are welcome to join. Vendors outside will happily tie a fita on your wrist; custom says you make three wishes and let it fall off on its own.

If you have time, linger on the peninsula, which feels far calmer and more residential than the historic center. It is a glimpse of everyday Salvador that many short visits miss.

For your final evening, take a car to Rio Vermelho, the bohemian seaside neighborhood where locals gather for acarajé, cold beer and live music. It is a relaxed way to see the city off-duty.

A few practical notes

Salvador rewards an unhurried pace. Keep valuables out of sight in crowded areas, use registered taxis or apps at night, and consider a licensed local guide for your first walk through the old town.

  • Dress lightly but respectfully for church visits.
  • Carry small bills for markets and street food.
  • Learn a few Portuguese phrases; English is less common outside hotels.

Planning a longer Bahia trip? Pair the city with the beaches of the south in our Trancoso guide, or browse more ideas in Destinations.

Plan your visit

  • Best time: September to March is warm and generally drier; Carnaval brings huge crowds and higher rates.
  • Getting around: walk within the historic center and use taxis or ride-hailing between neighborhoods.
  • Where to base: the Centro Histórico for sightseeing, Barra for a beachier, livelier evening scene.
  • Booking tips: reserve hotels early for holidays and festivals, and book a guide for your first day in Pelourinho.

title: Mozhdeh Matin in Lima: Peru’s Textile Memory Made Modern
dek: Discover Mozhdeh Matin in Lima: contemporary Peruvian textiles, artisan collaboration, studio guidance and a thoughtful Luxe Jetter styling edit.
body:
Lima reveals its most interesting fashion in quiet rooms: a studio door opened by appointment, an archive of swatches, a garment whose surface records weeks of conversation between designer and maker. At Mozhdeh Matin’s textile studio, the destination is not merely represented in cloth. It is present in every technique, material and relationship. Matin’s work brings Peruvian textile knowledge into a distinctly contemporary language of gentle silhouettes, unexpected texture and studied color. The result feels intimate and intellectually alive—clothing that rewards touch, attention and curiosity.

A Textile-Led Fashion Stroll Through Lima

Build the day around Barranco’s creative rhythm: galleries, gardens, restored architecture and the Pacific light that softens every surface. Then make time for a studio encounter rather than treating fashion as a quick retail stop. Mozhdeh Matin’s official site invites visitors in Lima to book an appointment to see the textile archive, browse unique pieces and learn about current projects. Continue exploring Peru’s modern craft conversation with our ESCVDO in Lima fashion feature. Both practices value inherited knowledge, yet each develops a singular balance of material experimentation, collaboration and contemporary form.

The Creator and the Studio

Mozhdeh Matin was born in Cajamarca to an Iranian family and studied fashion and visual art in Bolivia and Peru. Her Lima-based creative textile studio has operated since 2008, with preservation of traditional techniques, form and detail at the center of its practice. For more than fifteen years, she has traveled across Peru and co-created with artisans in different regions. The studio describes consultation, dialogue, long friendships and mutual respect as fundamental to the process—not an ornamental story added after the collection is finished. That approach expanded from the earlier Mozh Mozh label into the Mozhdeh Matin studio: a practice where womenswear, textile research, commissions, collaborative capsules and art projects can meet.

Techniques and Materials to Notice

Handloom Weaving from Huancavelica

The studio’s handloom textiles are made in Huancavelica with a family that has carried the craft across generations. Baby alpaca, wool and cotton—used alone or in blends—become garments with rich surfaces and an unmistakable sense of the hand.

Circle Crochet

Matin’s signature circle crochet is both graphic and soft. The studio works with small ateliers, many run by women in neighborhoods on Lima’s outskirts, where crochet can provide economic independence and a network of support. Look closely at how the circles join, shift scale and shape the body.

Knitwear and Material Experiment

Small-scale knitwear ranges from innovative cotton silhouettes to baby-alpaca pieces. Across the archive, techniques include crochet, loom weaving, macramé, manual and industrial machine work, intarsia and jacquard. The studio’s art projects also reveal a willingness to treat samples and remnants as a living material archive rather than waste.

Pieces Worth Seeking Out

A tactile dress is the clearest introduction: one that lets crochet or knit structure create movement without excessive embellishment. The Circle Midi Dress demonstrates how a repeated motif can become a complete silhouette. A skirt such as the Boro offers an easier travel piece, while a hand-loomed top or layer can bring Peruvian texture to neutral trousers already in the suitcase. Choose according to material and climate. Baby alpaca belongs beautifully to Lima’s cooler season and highland itineraries; cotton crochet offers more ease for transitional days. Because many pieces rely on handmade structure, study care instructions before packing and fold rather than hang when the weight of the textile could change its shape.

Planning a Studio Visit

The studio asks visitors to book in advance through its official website. Treat the appointment as a chance to learn, not simply to transact. Ask which region and technique shaped a piece, how the collaboration developed and what the textile requires over time. Current collections and available work can also be explored online. Availability may be limited by the realities of small-scale production. Confirm timing, international shipping, duties and returns directly before ordering, particularly when a trip or event creates a fixed deadline.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Edit

For Lima, pair a circular crochet dress with a long, clean coat and a sculptural flat. Let the texture remain visible beneath the outer layer. A hand-loomed top looks modern with wide ivory trousers, a slim leather belt and silver jewelry; a tactile skirt becomes effortless beside a fitted knit and low boot. The fashion-forward move is to avoid turning craft into costume. Mix one extraordinary textile with disciplined contemporary shapes. Keep the palette tonal, repeat a single accent color and allow negative space around the piece. The handwork becomes more powerful when the styling is quiet enough to reveal it.

Continue the fashion stroll

Open Luxe Jetter in Its Own Page ✦

Clothing as an Archive of Relationships

Mozhdeh Matin offers a richer definition of luxury: not speed or spectacle, but material intelligence and the continuity of knowledge. Her garments connect Cajamarca, Huancavelica, Lima and other regions through relationships built over time. In a city full of beautiful objects, these are pieces that ask us to notice how beauty was made—and whose hands carried it forward. The Best Rooftop Bars in Latin America’s Big Cities

Latin America knows how to create a moment — soft light, sweeping views, curated cocktails, and music that sets the mood without overwhelming it. Rooftop culture is strong here, especially in the region’s major cities, where evenings unfold high above the streets in warm, golden air.

Begin in Mexico City, where rooftops blend design and ambiance effortlessly. From Polanco to Roma Norte, terraces glow at sunset as the skyline shifts from blue to amber. With views stretching across Chapultepec Park and the city’s endless patchwork of neighborhoods, CDMX rooftops feel cinematic, polished, and endlessly romantic.

In Lima, cliffs meet the Pacific, creating dramatic oceanfront terraces. Rooftop lounges here are built for sunset — breezy, vibrant, and infused with coastal energy. Sip a pisco cocktail as the sky turns pink over the water, and the city lights shimmer against the coastline.

Travel north to Bogotá, where chilly mountain air gives rooftops a cozy elegance. Wrap yourself in a light jacket, settle into a candlelit lounge chair, and watch the city glow from above. Bogota’s high-altitude views are sweeping, modern, and unexpectedly serene.

Further south, Santiago’s rooftops offer the perfect blend of urban architecture and Andes majesty. Here, rooftop bars feel like suspended sanctuaries — elegant furniture, fireplaces, and panoramic views of the mountains. It’s a refined, peaceful version of city nightlife.

In Buenos Aires, rooftop culture is intimate and romantic. Think warm terrace lighting, classic cocktails, soft music, and views of historic domes. Evenings stretch long here, in that dreamy, timeless way only Buenos Aires can create.

Each rooftop offers a unique window into its city — a blend of atmosphere, beauty, and quiet luxury that stays with you long after your trip ends.

Cities With the Best Rooftops

Mexico City: Stylish, architectural, warm twilight energy.

Lima: Oceanfront sunsets and breezy terraces.

Bogotá: Cozy, candlelit, high-altitude views.

Santiago: Andes panoramas and modern luxury.

Buenos Aires: Romantic domes and soft-lit terraces.

What to Wear

City evening chic: silky dresses, linen suits, gold earrings, heeled sandals, and a light wrap for cooler climates. Effortless glamour.

Luxury Spa & Wellness Retreats Across Latin America

Latin America’s landscapes naturally invite restoration — misty mountains, tropical forests, mineral-rich hot springs, and coastlines shaped by gentle waves. It’s a region where wellness feels organic, connected to nature, and infused with a quiet kind of luxury that grounds you from the moment you arrive.

Begin in Mexico, where spa resorts blend modern design with ancestral healing traditions. Whether it’s a temazcal ceremony guided by local practitioners or a beachfront massage framed by the sound of the waves, wellness here feels deeply rooted in culture and place.

Head south to Costa Rica, where rainforest retreats sit above the canopy and offer open-air treatment rooms surrounded by birdsong. Yoga platforms overlook rivers, meals are farm-to-table, and days unfold slowly between nature walks, sauna rituals, and mineral baths. It’s one of the most peaceful places on earth for a full reset.

In Peru’s Sacred Valley, wellness takes on a spiritual dimension. Boutique lodges offer Andean energy rituals, sound baths, herbal steam sessions, and slow mornings wrapped in blankets overlooking the mountains. The air is crisp, the landscapes grounding, and the sense of calm profound.

Across the continent in Brazil, the coastline hides spa hotels with private villas, long stretches of beach, and candlelit treatment rooms surrounded by lush Atlantic Forest. It’s tropical wellness at its most elevated — warm, sensual, and deeply restorative.

Finally, in Argentina, luxury hot spring lodges and vineyard spas create a different kind of wellness experience. Think thermal pools framed by mountain ranges, aromatherapy infused with local herbs, and long afternoons spent resting under the soft Andean light.

These retreats remind you that wellness is more than treatments — it’s atmosphere, landscape, and the gift of time.

Top Spa & Wellness Destinations

Mexico: Cultural healing traditions + beachfront luxury.

Costa Rica: Rainforest retreats and nature-forward wellness.

Sacred Valley, Peru: Andean healing, rituals, and mountain calm.

Brazil: Tropical spa escapes with private villas and forest views.

Argentina: Hot springs, vineyards, and mountain-set spa lodges.

What to Wear

Soft loungewear, linen robes, airy dresses, slip sandals, light knits, and minimal jewelry. A palette of warm neutrals enhances the sense of calm.

Jet Set LATAM Quick Tips

Plan spa appointments early — boutique retreats book out Choose at least one local or ancestral treatment Use TripAdvisor for wellness resort comparisons and package deals Build in unstructured time — restorative travel thrives on slow pacing

body:
Cartagena

Getsemaní vs. Bocagrande

Where should you stay in Cartagena? Two neighborhoods, two completely different rhythms.

Cartagena is a city of dualities — colonial charm wrapped in Caribbean heat, modern skylines rising beside centuries-old walls, and neighborhoods that each tell a different story. Two of the most popular areas for travelers, Getsemaní and Bocagrande, sit just minutes apart yet offer completely different rhythms, aesthetics, and experiences.

Getsemaní

Bohemian, colorful, and culturally immersive — Cartagena’s creative soul, a neighborhood of murals, music, plazas, and local life. Once working-class, now filled with boutique hotels, indie cafés, and the city’s best nightlife.

Best For

Culture lovers, walkers, foodies, and travelers who want Cartagena’s “real” energy.

Worth Knowing

Can be noisy at night near Plaza de la Trinidad; not beachfront — you’ll need a taxi or boat for the sand.

Bocagrande

Cartagena’s sleek, Miami-esque district — a peninsula of high-rise hotels, shopping malls, and long beaches. Polished, convenient, and ideal for travelers who want comfort, ocean views, and modern amenities.

Best For

Beachfront-hotel travelers who want comfort and easy access to everything.

Worth Knowing

More resort than romance — less of the Walled City’s historic texture.

If you’re deciding where to base yourself: Getsemaní delivers authenticity, walkability, and Cartagena’s artistic pulse. Bocagrande delivers the beach at your door and hotel-tower comfort. Either is a five-to-ten-minute ride from the Walled City itself.

title: Cartagena Itinerary — Seven Days of Culture, Cuisine & Coastal Beauty
dek: As you know from our prior posts, we have been researching Cartagena in preparation for our adventure there. The city already feels like the beginning of a story we’ve been waiting to live. As a couple, we’re buzzing with excitement to wander its colorful streets, soak in the warm Caribbean air, and lose track of…
body:
As you know from our prior posts, we have been researching Cartagena in preparation for our adventure there. The city already feels like the beginning of a story we’ve been waiting to live. As a couple, we’re buzzing with excitement to wander its colorful streets, soak in the warm Caribbean air, and lose track of time between plazas, sunsets, and slow, romantic dinners by the sea.

After polishing and reworking our original itinerary, we are now ready to share our (possibly) final version with you. This version emphasizes walking routes from Getsemaní. It clusters activities by neighborhood (Getsemaní, Old Town/Centro, and nearby sites), prioritizes walking between sites, and weaves in cultural stops at logical points. Like before, meals are generally Pescatarian friendly, with lots of local flavors.

We hope this post provides you with the inspiration for your own journey to Cartagena.

A week in Cartagena, with the right things booked

Start with a neighborhood, leave space for long lunches, and give the sea a day of its own. This seven-day outline began as our pre-trip plan. Our photographs and daily dispatches from the trip show how it actually unfolded—including the island day we moved when we wanted a break from sightseeing.

First, choose the Cartagena you want to come home to

Getsemaní: choose it for street art, lively evenings, and the walking routes in this itinerary. Before booking, check recent room-specific noise reviews and ask whether your room faces the street. The Walled City: choose it when historic streets, boutiques, and dinner close to your hotel matter most. Bocagrande: choose it for a beachfront high-rise base; allow for transfers to the historic center instead of expecting the same walking routine.

Compare Getsemaní and Bocagrande before choosing. If a kitchen or extra space suits your trip, search vacation rentals on Vrbo. Enter Cartagena, Colombia, your dates, and your party size, then check the map against your chosen neighborhood. The link opens Vrbo’s general search, not a preselected property. Compare the full stay cost, cancellation terms, air-conditioning, and check-in arrangements.

Arrival: make the first evening easy

Once your stay is confirmed, ask the property for an airport pickup quote and meeting instructions. Confirm the total price, luggage allowance, and what happens if your flight is delayed. Keep arrival day flexible: Getsemaní, a first look through the Clock Tower, and dinner nearby are enough.

Days 1–3: walk the city, then choose one special dinner

Use the neighborhood routes below for Getsemaní, the historic center, museums, and artisan browsing. Keep your outdoor exploring to the cooler parts of the day and leave room for a midday pause. Choose the restaurant you care about most and reserve through its current official channel; check opening days and dietary options before fixing the rest of that day around it. A self-guided walk needs no tour purchase. If you prefer a guide, compare the meeting point, language, group size, and included admissions before paying.

Day 4—or whichever day needs a change of pace: the island decision

For a beach-club day: our trip eventually took us to Blue Apple Beach. Read our firsthand island-day report for the experience, then use Blue Apple’s official site to check day visits and reserve. Blue Apple is on Tierra Bomba; it is a different outing from Barú or the Rosario Islands. Confirm the return boat, meeting point, seating, food charges, cancellation terms, and any age restrictions for your chosen date.

For a Rosario Islands excursion: use the Rosario Islands listings already referenced in this itinerary to compare actual routes. Check whether snorkeling, lunch, port charges, hotel pickup, and return transport are included. Choose one island outing and keep a weather alternative in the city.

Days 5–7: leave room for the places you want to revisit

Keep San Diego’s boutiques, the Manga waterfront, and a Bocagrande visit flexible around the days below. Reserve only the experiences with fixed capacity. Revisit a favorite street, make time for a slow meal, and keep the final day light enough for your departure.

Pack for the route

Comfortable walking shoes, breathable clothes, sun protection, and a swim layer cover more of this week than a suitcase of occasion outfits. For the city-to-coast wardrobe, explore our existing Agua by Agua Bendita edit on ShopMy. Browse the Cartagena resortwear story for the context behind the edit.

Book in this order: accommodation → arrival transfer → your chosen island day → the dinner you most want. Leave the walks and shopping time open. Then adapt the trip outline to your pace and continue with the seven daily routes below.

Day 1 — Getsemaní Immersion & Old Town Introduction

Your Cartagena journey begins in the vibrant heart of Getsemaní, a neighborhood alive with color, music, and street art. After settling into your hotel, step outside and let the district introduce itself. Wander along Calle de la Sierpe, admire the murals splashed across the walls, and pause in Plaza de la Trinidad, where locals gather and the energy is unmistakably Caribbean.

For lunch, return to Getsemaní for a comforting, coastal meal at La Cocina de Pepina, a beloved spot serving traditional Colombian dishes with heart and heritage.

As the afternoon cools, walk toward the walled city. Enter through the clock tower at Plaza de los Coches, then drift through Calle Santo Domingo, Calle de la Factoria, and the sweet‑filled Portal de los Dulces. When the sun begins to sink, climb onto Las Murallas, the centuries‑old city walls, and follow them toward Baluarte de Santo Domingo for a golden‑hour panorama.

Finally follow the wall south to El Baluarte San Francisco Javier, a tapas bar with a terrace overlooking the water. You can dine there or end your evening back in Getsemaní with dinner at one of the local restaurants.

Day 1 Google Map Walking Route

This route is optimized for smooth neighborhood flow and includes the individual stops mentioned in this itinerary.

Open Walking Route in Google Maps

Day 2 — Old Town’s History, Museums & Evening Charm

Begin your morning with breakfast at Café Stepping Stone, a social‑impact café in Getsemaní known for excellent coffee and wholesome plates. From there, take a short taxi or a longer walk to Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the imposing hilltop fortress that once guarded the city. Arrive early to avoid the heat and crowds, and explore its tunnels, battlements, and sweeping views.

Return to the walled city for a cluster of museums all within a few minutes of one another. Start at the Palace of the Inquisition on Plaza de Bolívar, then cross the square to the Gold Museum (Museo del Oro Zenú) for a compact but fascinating look at indigenous craftsmanship. Continue toward the waterfront to the Naval Museum of the Caribbean, which offers engaging exhibits on maritime history. If time allows, pass by the elegant Teatro Adolfo Mejía, a jewel of Cartagena’s cultural scene.

Lunch awaits at La Cevichería in Getsemaní, a lively, walk‑in‑only ceviche bar made famous by Anthony Bourdain.

Spend the afternoon strolling through Old Town’s boutiques, emerald shops, art galleries, and handicraft stores. As evening settles, relax in Plaza Santo Domingo, home to Botero’s famous sculpture “La Gorda Gertrudis.” Street performers, musicians, and warm lamplight make this plaza especially atmospheric.

Dinner tonight is at La Vitrola (reservations required), one of the city’s most iconic restaurants, known for its Cuban‑inspired ambiance and refined Caribbean dishes.

Day 2 Google Map Walking Route

This route is optimized for smooth neighborhood flow and includes the individual stops mentioned in this itinerary.

Open Walking Route in Google Maps

Find Guided Experiences

Day 3 — Panoramic Views, Artisan Shopping & Coastal Sunset

Start your day at Época Espresso Bar, a Getsemaní favorite for specialty coffee and inventive breakfasts. Afterward, take a taxi to Convento de la Popa, perched high above the city. The monastery’s courtyard and chapel are serene, but the real highlight is the panoramic view stretching from the bay to the Caribbean Sea. Always take a taxi both ways — the hill is not walkable.

Back in the walled city, stop for lunch at Casa del Tunel Restaurante Bar, a breezy, open-air inner patio in Getsemaníat.

Afterwards, spend the afternoon exploring Las Bóvedas, a series of colonial vaults now filled with artisan shops selling mochilas, jewelry, hammocks, and handicrafts. From there, stroll past the elegant Teatro Adolfo Mejía, any remaining museums or through Parque del Centenario, a leafy space connecting Getsemaní and Old Town.

Dinner is at Carmen (reservations required), one of Cartagena’s most celebrated restaurants. Reservations are essential, and the experience is worth every bit of planning.

Day 3 Google Map Walking Route

Day 4 — Island or Beach Adventure

Today is your escape to Cartagena’s turquoise waters. Choose the experience that best matches your mood:

Option A — Rosario Islands

Depart early from Muelle de la Bodeguita for a full‑day boat trip to the Rosarios. The ride takes 45–60 minutes, delivering you to white‑sand beaches and crystalline water ideal for snorkeling. Enjoy a fresh seafood lunch, swim, sunbathe, or visit the Oceanario for a marine‑life encounter. You can find links to guided tours here.

Option B — Playa Blanca (Barú)

A shorter boat ride brings you to Playa Blanca, known for its powdery sand and bright aquamarine water. It’s beautiful but can be crowded, with jet skis and vendors adding to the bustle. Some Google reviews mention that the beach has a gasoline smell and can be a bit dirty. Still, it’s a classic Cartagena beach experience.

Option C — Isla de Tierra Bomba

Just 10–15 minutes by boat, Tierra Bomba offers a range of beach clubs — from the lively Amare to the upscale Makani and the serene Marlin. It’s a convenient, relaxing alternative to the Rosarios. However, some Google Reviews mention that the public beach (Playa del Punta Arena) is crowded and a bit dirty, so it may be best to look for a Private Club Experience.

In the late afternoon, return to Cartagena rest at your hotel, and enjoy dinner at Donjuán, a refined seafood restaurant in Old Town (reservations recommended).

  • Top Beach Clubs & Beaches
  • Blue Apple Beach House: Known for its fun vibe, activities (scuba diving, horse riding, dance lessons), and good food. It’s located on the quieter far side of the island. [botegena.com]
  • Makani Beach Club: The most upscale option, offering luxury amenities and a chic atmosphere. [botegena.com]
  • Amare Beach Club: Popular for its party atmosphere, especially on weekends, with DJs and a lively crowd. [botegena.com]
  • Marlin Beach Club: Known for tranquility and privacy, ideal for relaxation. [botegena.com]
  • Palmarito Beach Club: Great for both day and night, with a welcoming, laid-back atmosphere. [botegena.com]
  • Namaste Beach Club (Punta Arena): Offers a nice setup and is recommended for wellness and relaxation. [lacarta.co]
  • Public Beaches
  • Playa de Punta Arena: The most popular public beach, with calm waters and several beach shacks serving fresh fish. It’s less crowded than city beaches, especially on weekdays. [cartagenae…plorer.com]
Day 5 — Local Markets & San Diego’s Quiet Elegance

Begin with breakfast at Mila Rooftop, then head to Bazurto Market with a guide (see safety tips below). This sprawling, energetic market is a window into daily life in Cartagena — full of tropical fruits, fish stalls, spices, and local vendors. A guide ensures both safety and context (Bazurto sits in a purely commercial, industrial zone of Cartagena, and it is not advisable to go there without a guide).

Afterward, taxi back to Las Bóvedas for any additional artisan shopping, then continue into the charming San Diego neighborhood. The San Diego stretch of Las Murallas offers some of the best views in the city. Along the way, stop at Casa de Rafael Núñez (if not visited earlier), a beautiful wooden balcony Republican era home and the former home of Colombia’s 19th‑century president. Its airy verandas and quiet gardens offer a gentle first glimpse into Cartagena’s layered history.

Spend the afternoon exploring Plaza de San Diego, browsing boutiques like St. Dom, Beatriz Camacho , and Casa Chiqui, and enjoying a quiet coffee at Café de las Novias.

Return to Getsemaní for a relaxed evening — a sunset walk on the walls, drinks at a favorite spot. Perhaps sunset drinks and dinner at Mirador Gastro Bar if you haven’t yet experienced it or at Alquimico.

Day 6 — Manga Waterfront Loop & Local Life

Ease into the morning with breakfast of your choice, then walk or take a short taxi to Manga, a leafy residential peninsula with a breezy waterfront promenade.

Stroll the Paseo Peatonal de Manga, watching boats drift across the bay. Continue toward the Club de Pesca marina area for postcard‑worthy views of the Bocagrande skyline. Pause in Parque de la Marina, a shaded local park perfect for a quiet moment.

If you enjoy architecture, pass by Casa Roman, a striking historic mansion.

Return toward Old Town in the afternoon, stopping at Gelateria Paradiso for a refreshing treat. Spend the rest of the day revisiting favorite plazas or boutiques.

In the evening, enjoy rooftop drinks at Townhouse, followed by dinner at a restaurant you haven’t yet tried. Perhaps Celeste, a trendy and high-demand spot (reservations required 1 month in advance) in Centro or Carta Ajena Restaurante, a highly rated spot.

Day 7 — Bocagrande Peninsula & Farewell to the City

For your final day, take a taxi to Castillo Grande, the upscale southern tip of Bocagrande. Walk the peaceful beachfront promenade, relax on Playa Castillo Grande, and enjoy the calm, residential vibe.

Continue north along the peninsula to explore Plaza Bocagrande Mall and the boutiques along Carrera 3. Stop for coffee at Juan Valdez Orígenes, which offers excellent brews and bay views.

Return to the walled city for last‑minute photos, shopping, or a final stroll through Getsemaní. End your Cartagena journey with a farewell dinner and one last sunset on Las Murallas, savoring the warm breeze and the glow of the city you’ve now come to know intimately. As the day cools, return to the clock tower for sunset drinks and dinner at Mirador Gastro Bar or at the rooftop bar Townhouse.

Day 7 Google Map Walking Route

This route is optimized for smooth neighborhood flow and includes the individual stops mentioned in this itinerary.

Open Walking Route in Google Maps

Important Tips

  • High Caution Recommended
  • Bazurto Market: Always visit with a guide.Not advisable to wander alone; keep valuables hidden; avoid large cameras.
  • Convento de la Popa (La Popa Hill): The hilltop road is isolated; never walk — taxi both ways. Don’t linger outside the monastery area.
  • Playa Blanca (Barú): Crowded beach; aggressive vendors; pickpocketing possible. Keep belongings close; avoid leaving bags unattended.
  • Public beaches on Tierra Bomba (especially Playa de Punta Arena): Crowded areas can attract opportunistic theft. Stick to beach clubs if possible.
  • Moderate Caution
  • Parque del Centenario: Safe during the day; avoid at night.Stay on main paths; keep phone secure.
  • Muelle de la Bodeguita (boat departure area): Busy, chaotic; watch for bag snatching. Ignore unofficial tour sellers.
  • Generally Safe With Normal Precautions
  • Getsemaní (daytime); nighttime in Getsemaní is lively and safe on main streets, but avoid quiet side streets after midnight.
  • Old Town / Walled City
  • Las Murallas (City Walls)
  • Museums, plazas, and main walking routes

  • Reservations Required:
  • Carmen (Old Town) — explicitly stated in itinerary
  • La Vitrola (Old Town) — one of Cartagena’s hardest reservations; always required
  • Reservations Recommended:
