title: Caraíva: A Guide to Bahia’s Car-Free Village
dek: Sandy lanes, a canoe crossing and forró under the stars: everything you need to know about visiting Caraíva from Trancoso.
body:
If Trancoso feels relaxed, Caraíva feels like it has opted out of the modern world entirely. This small village on Bahia’s southern coast has no cars, sand in place of pavement and a riverside setting that slows everyone down within minutes. It’s a place to switch off — and a memorable counterpoint to Trancoso’s polish.

Getting There: The Canoe Crossing

Caraíva lies south of Trancoso, reached by roads that include long unpaved stretches. The drive usually takes roughly an hour and a half to two hours, depending on conditions, and heavy rain can make the dirt roads slow going. Transfers and local buses are available, as well as private drivers.

If you’re flying in, the nearest airport is Porto Seguro. From there, many travelers stop in Trancoso or Arraial d’Ajuda first, then continue south; going straight to Caraíva is possible but makes for a long travel day, so time your arrival for daylight if you can.

The road ends at the bank of the Caraíva River. Vehicles stay behind, and you cross to the village by canoe — a short, scenic ride that sets the tone for everything that follows. With luggage, pack light, because from here you’ll be walking on sand.

Sandy Lanes and Village Life

Caraíva’s streets are simply sand, lined with colorful, low-slung houses, small pousadas, restaurants and shops. The absence of cars gives the village a rare quiet, broken mostly by conversation, music and the odd horse-drawn cart.

  • Footwear — flip-flops or bare feet are the local standard.
  • Luggage — rolling suitcases struggle in sand; a backpack or duffel is far easier.
  • Pace — this is a place for doing very little, very well.

As evening falls, the whole village seems to drift toward the riverbank and the music. It’s the kind of place where plans dissolve pleasantly.

Where the River Meets the Sea

Caraíva’s setting is its greatest luxury. The village sits where the Caraíva River flows into the Atlantic, so you can choose between the calm, fresh water of the river and the waves of the open ocean — sometimes within a few steps of each other.

Many visitors rent a tube or kayak for a lazy drift on the river, then stroll to the beach for a swim. Sunsets over the river are a daily event worth pausing for.

Forró Nights

Caraíva is known for forró, the lively partner dance and music style from Brazil’s Northeast. On many evenings — especially in high season — music drifts out of local venues, and dancers of all levels fill the floor. It’s joyful, informal and welcoming, even if you’ve never danced it before.

Don’t worry about technique; the basic step is easy to pick up, and locals are often happy to show visitors how it’s done.

Eating and Drinking

Food in Caraíva is simple and satisfying, built around the day’s catch. Expect grilled fish, shrimp, moqueca in the Bahian style — rich with coconut milk and dendê — and plenty of tropical fruit. Beachside kiosks serve cold beer, fresh coconuts and caipirinhas, while the village lanes hold a handful of relaxed restaurants that come alive after sunset. Bring an appetite and a flexible sense of time.

Nearby: Pataxó Community and Beyond

South of the village lies Barra Velha, a village of the Pataxó Indigenous people, in the wider region around Monte Pascoal National Park. Some visitors arrange cultural visits, and you may see Pataxó crafts sold in the area.

If you visit, go with respect: follow local guidance, ask before taking photographs and consider arranging your visit through community-endorsed channels. To the north, Praia do Espelho is within reach, and many travelers combine the two in one trip.

Practical Tips for Caraíva

  • Stay the night — a day trip is possible, but Caraíva’s charm really comes out in the evenings.
  • Carry some cash — card and internet connections can be patchy.
  • Bring a flashlight — lanes can be dark at night.
  • Pack insect repellent — especially for evenings near the river.
  • Check road conditions — particularly after heavy rain.

For how Caraíva fits into a stay on this coast, see our Trancoso guide and our 3-day Trancoso itinerary.

title: What to Eat in the Dominican Republic: Dishes and Drinks to Try
dek: From la bandera and mangú to pescado con coco and mamajuana — a flavorful guide to Dominican food beyond the resort buffet.
body:
Beyond the resort buffet lies one of the Caribbean’s most satisfying cuisines. Dominican food is hearty, home-style and full of flavor, shaped by Taíno, Spanish and African influences and built around rice, beans, plantains and slow-cooked meats. Here’s what to order — and for the rest of your trip, head to our Punta Cana guide.

La Bandera Dominicana

The national lunch is called la bandera — “the flag” — and it’s the backbone of the Dominican midday meal. The classic plate brings together white rice, stewed red beans (habichuelas) and a stewed meat, most often chicken (pollo guisado) or beef. It usually comes with a simple salad and often a side of fried plantains.

Lunch is traditionally the main meal of the day, so this is the time to find it at its best in local eateries. Don’t skip the concón — the crispy, golden layer of rice from the bottom of the pot, which many Dominicans consider the best part. It’s a small detail that says a lot about Dominican home cooking: nothing goes to waste, and the humblest bits are often the most prized.

Mangú and the Dominican Breakfast

Mangú is mashed green plantain, boiled and whipped with butter or oil until smooth, then topped with tangy, quick-pickled red onions. It’s the heart of the classic breakfast known as los tres golpes — “the three hits” — which adds fried salami, fried cheese and eggs.

It’s filling, comforting and utterly Dominican. Try it at least once, ideally before a long beach day.

Sancocho and Other Comfort Foods

Sancocho is a thick, deeply flavorful stew made with several kinds of meat, root vegetables such as yuca and yautía, plantain and corn. It’s the dish of celebrations, family gatherings and rainy days, often served with white rice and slices of avocado.

  • Tostones — green plantain slices fried, smashed and fried again until crisp. Salt them well; they’re irresistible.
  • Chicharrón — crispy fried pork, a favorite snack and side.
  • Yaniqueques — crunchy fried dough, a classic beach snack.
  • Locrio — a Dominican rice dish cooked with meat or seafood, similar in spirit to a paella.

Seafood by the Sea

With coastline on all sides, it’s no surprise that fish and seafood feature heavily. Look for whole fried fish served with tostones, grilled lobster and shrimp in garlic sauce. A standout is pescado con coco, fish simmered in a rich, fragrant coconut sauce with herbs and peppers — a specialty closely associated with the Samaná Peninsula.

Something Sweet

Habichuelas con dulce is one of the island’s most distinctive desserts: a sweet, creamy blend of red beans, coconut milk, sugar, spices, sweet potato and raisins, often served with small cookies. It’s closely tied to Lent and Easter, so you’re most likely to find it then.

Also look for dulce de leche and coconut sweets, and fresh tropical fruit — mango, pineapple, papaya and chinola (passion fruit), which also makes a superb juice. Morir soñando, a creamy mix of orange juice and milk, is a beloved cold drink.

Mamajuana, Rum and Presidente

The Dominican Republic has a lively drinking culture, and three drinks come up again and again:

  • Mamajuana — a bottle packed with bark, herbs and roots, steeped with rum, red wine and honey. It’s sweet and potent, and it’s often playfully credited with all sorts of benefits.
  • Rum — the country produces excellent aged rums, perfect for sipping neat or over ice.
  • Presidente — the iconic local beer, served famously ice-cold, often in bottles frosted from the fridge.

Eating Beyond the Resort

  • Look for comedores, small local eateries that serve homestyle set lunches.
  • Visit a colmado, the neighborhood corner store that often doubles as a social hub.
  • Eat lunch as your big meal, like the locals do.
  • Drink bottled or purified water, which is what most visitors and many locals choose.

Work a few local meals into your plans with our 4-day Punta Cana itinerary, and save room for a second helping of tostones.

title: Saona Island: A Day Trip Guide from Punta Cana
dek: Palm-lined beaches, a shallow natural pool and a protected national park — how to plan a memorable, responsible Saona Island day.
body:
If you picture the Caribbean as palm trees leaning over empty white sand and impossibly clear water, Saona Island is that picture. It’s the most popular excursion from Punta Cana, and with a little planning, it can be a highlight of your trip rather than just another crowded boat tour. For more on the region, see our Punta Cana guide.

About Saona Island

Saona is the largest of the islands off the Dominican Republic’s coast, lying just off the southeastern tip of the country. It’s protected as part of Parque Nacional del Este — officially renamed Cotubanamá National Park, though many still use the old name. The park covers coastal forest, mangroves, lagoons, reefs and beaches, and it’s an important habitat for birds, marine life and nesting sea turtles.

Development on the island is minimal, and there’s a small fishing village, Mano Juan, whose painted wooden houses give a glimpse of island life far from the resorts.

Getting There

Most Saona trips depart from the fishing town of Bayahíbe on the south coast, roughly an hour or so by road from the Punta Cana area. Tours typically include hotel pickup and transfers, so the full day often runs from early morning until late afternoon.

A typical day follows a familiar rhythm: a boat ride along the coast, a stop at the natural pool, then several hours on one of Saona’s beaches with a buffet-style lunch — often grilled chicken or fish, rice and salads — and drinks served under the palms. Some itineraries add a snorkeling stop on a reef or a visit to Mano Juan. Itineraries vary, so read the details closely before booking, especially if snorkeling or village time matters to you.

Catamaran or Speedboat?

Most tours combine the two — speedboat one way, catamaran the other — but it’s worth knowing what each offers.

  • Catamaran — slower, smoother and social, usually with music, shade and drinks on board. Great for groups and anyone prone to seasickness.
  • Speedboat — faster and more exhilarating, with more time on the island, but bumpier and with less shade.
  • Private or small-group boats — pricier, but offer more flexibility and a quieter experience.

The Natural Pool

A highlight for many visitors is the natural pool, a shallow sandbar in the middle of the sea where the water is just waist-deep and startlingly clear. Boats anchor here so you can wade, swim and float in the turquoise water.

The area is known for starfish. Admire them, but don’t lift them out of the water or handle them — it can harm them, and it’s widely discouraged for good reason. Keep a respectful distance from all marine life.

What to Bring

  • Reef-friendly sunscreen, a hat and sunglasses — there’s intense sun on the water.
  • Swimwear, a towel and a change of clothes.
  • A dry bag or waterproof pouch for your phone and valuables.
  • Water shoes, handy in the natural pool and on some landings.
  • Cash in small bills for tips, extras and souvenirs.
  • Motion-sickness remedies if you’re sensitive to boat rides.

Choosing a Responsible Operator

Saona’s popularity puts real pressure on a fragile protected area, so the operator you choose matters. Look for:

  • Licensed operators with clear safety practices and life jackets for everyone on board.
  • Reasonable group sizes — smaller groups mean less impact and a better day.
  • Wildlife-friendly practices, such as not handling starfish or feeding marine life.
  • Clarity on what’s included, such as transfers, meals, drinks and national park fees.

Park entry requirements and fees can change, so check current details with your operator before you book.

Making the Most of Your Day

Go with realistic expectations: popular beaches can be busy at midday, and the drive to Bayahíbe adds time. Walking a little way down the beach often reveals quieter stretches of sand. Pair it with a slower day afterward, and plan the rest of your stay with our 4-day Punta Cana itinerary.

title: What to Eat in Puerto Vallarta: Seafood, Street Tacos and Raicilla
dek: Pescado zarandeado, aguachile, smoked marlin, beach fish on a stick and raicilla — how to eat well in Puerto Vallarta.
body:
In Puerto Vallarta, the ocean sets the menu. Fresh fish, shrimp and octopus turn up everywhere from beach shacks to rooftop dining rooms, while the city’s taco stands keep things casual after dark. Here’s what to seek out, to pair with our Puerto Vallarta guide.

Pescado Zarandeado

The signature dish of this stretch of coast is pescado zarandeado. A whole fish — often snapper — is butterflied, brushed with a chile-based marinade and grilled over wood or charcoal in a hinged basket, giving it smoky, slightly charred edges and tender flesh.

It hails from neighboring Nayarit and is typically served family-style with tortillas, salsa, onion, cucumber and lime so you can build your own tacos. Order it to share — and expect a leisurely lunch. Because it’s cooked to order, a whole fish can take a while, which is all the excuse you need for a cold beer and a ceviche while you wait.

Aguachile, Ceviche and Cocteles

  • Aguachile — raw shrimp “cooked” in lime juice with fiery chile, cucumber and red onion. Green versions are made with serrano chile and cilantro; darker versions are smokier. Bright, cold and addictive.
  • Ceviche — fish or shrimp cured in citrus, piled onto crisp tostadas with tomato, onion and cilantro.
  • Cóctel de camarón — a Mexican-style shrimp cocktail served in a tall glass with a tangy tomato base and avocado.
  • Smoked marlin — shredded and smoky, served on tostadas or in tacos, quesadillas and empanadas.

Seafood spots tend to be busiest at lunch, when the catch is freshest and the vibe most relaxed.

On the Beach: Fish on a Stick and Friends

On beaches like Playa Los Muertos, look for pescado en vara — fish grilled on a stick over an open fire and sold straight from the grill. Beach vendors also walk by with fresh fruit, coconuts, grilled shrimp skewers and sweets.

As with any food bought on the beach, trust your instincts: go for items that are freshly grilled and hot.

Street Tacos and Late-Night Eats

After sunset, the city’s taco stands light up. Look for tacos de adobada or al pastor sliced from a spit, tacos de birria (a Jalisco specialty) and fish or shrimp tacos. Smoked-marlin tacos and seafood tacos are a local favorite, too.

Neighborhood stands in the Zona Romántica and Centro are easy to find — the busiest, with a crowd of locals, are usually the best bet. Many stands only open in the evening, and the classic order is several small tacos at once, topped at the counter with salsas, onion, cilantro and lime. Don’t skip the grilled onions and roasted chiles if they’re on offer.

Sweets and Refreshments

  • Coco frío — a chilled coconut, opened with a machete and served with a straw.
  • Fruit cups — mango, jicama, cucumber and more with chile and lime.
  • Churros and paletas — sweet snacks for a Malecón stroll.
  • Pie in Yelapa — the boat-access village is known for homemade pie sold on the beach.

What to Drink: Raicilla and Tequila

Raicilla is the local spirit — an agave distillate made in the mountains and along the coast of Jalisco. Once a rustic, homemade drink, it now appears on many bar menus. Expect anything from bright and fruity to funky and earthy. Sip it slowly. Ask the bartender for a comparison: raicillas from the coast and from the mountains can taste strikingly different.

Being in Jalisco, you’ll find tequila everywhere, too, along with ice-cold beer, micheladas and fresh agua fresca. Try tuba, a traditional drink made from coconut palm sap, if you see it on the street — it’s often topped with chopped fruit and nuts.

Tips for Eating Well

  • Choose busy seafood spots with high turnover.
  • Carry cash for street stands and beach vendors.
  • Ask about spice levels — aguachile can be fierce.
  • Stick to bottled or purified water.

title: Best Time to Visit Punta Cana: A Season-by-Season Guide
dek: Dry season sunshine, shoulder-month value and hurricane-season caveats — how to pick the right time for your Punta Cana trip.
body:
Punta Cana is warm and sunny for most of the year, which makes it one of the Caribbean’s most reliable beach escapes. Still, the season you choose affects everything from crowds and prices to rain, humidity and the state of the sea. Here’s how the calendar breaks down — and for everything else, see our Punta Cana guide.

The Short Answer

For the most dependable weather, we recommend the dry season, from roughly December through April. If you’re after better value and don’t mind a little more rain, the shoulder months of May and November can be a sweet spot. The heart of hurricane season, from about August to October, carries the most weather risk.

Dry Season: December to April

This is Punta Cana’s high season, and for good reason. Expect plenty of sunshine, lower humidity, cooling trade winds and calm, inviting water — ideal conditions for beach days, catamaran trips and snorkeling.

The flip side is demand. Winter holidays, spring break and Easter week (Semana Santa, an important holiday period in the Dominican Republic) bring the biggest crowds and the highest rates. Book flights and accommodation well ahead for these dates.

  • Best for: guaranteed-feeling sunshine and escaping a northern winter.
  • Bonus: from roughly January to March, humpback whales gather in Samaná Bay in the northeast — a long but memorable excursion from Punta Cana.
  • Watch out for: peak pricing and busier beaches and excursions.

Shoulder Months: May and November

These transitional months often offer a pleasing balance. Temperatures are warm, crowds thin out and prices generally soften. May marks the start of the wetter period, while November is the tail end of hurricane season, so there’s a bit more uncertainty — but many days are still bright and beautiful.

If you have flexibility and like a little breathing room on the beach, this is a smart window to consider. Just keep an eye on local holiday dates, which can bring bursts of domestic travelers to the coast even outside high season.

Hurricane Season: June to November

The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 to November 30, with activity typically peaking from around August through October. That doesn’t mean storms are constant — many weeks pass with nothing more than hot, humid weather and short, heavy afternoon showers that clear quickly.

Still, it’s wise to plan with care during these months:

  • Buy travel insurance that covers weather disruptions.
  • Book flexible flights and accommodation where you can.
  • Monitor official forecasts in the days before and during your trip.
  • Expect heat and humidity — summer is the hottest, stickiest time of year.

The reward for accepting some risk? Lower prices, fewer crowds and a more relaxed pace on the sand.

A Note on Sargassum

Sargassum is a floating brown seaweed that periodically washes onto Caribbean beaches, including along the Dominican Republic’s east coast. It’s natural, but large amounts can make the water murky and the shoreline less appealing.

Arrivals vary widely from year to year, month to month and even beach to beach, and warmer months tend to see more of it. Because conditions change quickly, check recent reports close to your travel dates rather than relying on any fixed seasonal rule. Some beaches are more sheltered or more actively cleaned, and boat trips to places like Saona Island can offer a clear-water alternative on a weedy day.

Weather at a Glance

Punta Cana is warm year-round, with daytime temperatures commonly in the high 20s to low 30s Celsius (low 80s to around 90°F). The sea is pleasant for swimming in every month. What changes most through the year is rainfall, humidity and the chance of tropical storms, rather than the temperature itself.

Plan Your Trip

If certainty matters most, go between December and April. If value and elbow room are your priorities, look at May or November — or even summer, with good insurance and flexible plans. Whenever you land, our 4-day Punta Cana itinerary will help you make the most of it.

title: Day Trips from Puerto Vallarta: Beach Towns, Islands and Mountain Villages
dek: Sayulita, Yelapa by boat, the Marietas Islands, Los Arcos, San Sebastián del Oeste and whale season — the best day trips from Puerto Vallarta.
body:
Puerto Vallarta is a great base for exploring the Bahía de Banderas and beyond. In a single day, you can surf in a bohemian beach town, take a boat to a road-free village, snorkel protected islands or climb into the mountains. Here are the most rewarding escapes, to pair with our Puerto Vallarta guide.

Sayulita and San Pancho

About an hour north, depending on traffic, Sayulita is a colorful surf town with a lively plaza, beginner-friendly waves and a buzzy, bohemian feel. Rent a board, take a surf lesson or simply people-watch from the beach.

Just beyond, San Pancho (San Francisco) is calmer and more laid-back, with a long beach and a slower pace. Visiting both in one day makes an easy, relaxed outing. Buses run up the coast from Puerto Vallarta, or you can hire a driver for more flexibility. Along the way, the coastal towns of Bucerías and La Cruz de Huanacaxtle make pleasant stops for a stroll or a seafood lunch.

Yelapa by Boat

South of the city, Yelapa is a small village tucked into a cove, reached mainly by boat. Water taxis run from Playa Los Muertos pier and from Boca de Tomatlán, farther down the coast. The ride along the jungle-backed shoreline is half the fun.

Once there, hike to the waterfall, swim, eat grilled fish on the beach and try a slice of the village’s famous homemade pie. Along the way, beaches like Las Ánimas and Quimixto offer further stops. Check the time of the last boat back before you settle in, and pack light — landings can be wet.

Marietas Islands

Off the tip of Punta Mita, the Islas Marietas are a protected national park, known for seabirds such as blue-footed boobies, clear water for snorkeling and dramatic rock formations. Tours depart from Puerto Vallarta and Punta Mita.

The famous Hidden Beach (Playa del Amor) hides inside a crater-like opening in the rock, open to the sky. Access has been restricted and permit-limited to protect the environment, and it has been closed at times, so check current rules and choose a licensed operator. Even without the beach, the islands are well worth the trip.

Los Arcos

Closer to the city, off Mismaloya, Los Arcos are a group of granite rock formations with natural arches rising out of the sea. The area is protected and popular for snorkeling, diving and kayaking. It’s often combined with a boat tour to the southern beaches — a great half-day option.

San Sebastián del Oeste

Up in the Sierra Madre, roughly an hour and a half to two hours from the city, San Sebastián del Oeste is a former mining town with cobblestone streets, whitewashed buildings and cool mountain air. It’s known for coffee, raicilla and a tranquil plaza anchored by a historic church. It has been named one of Mexico’s Pueblos Mágicos, and it’s an easy place to spend a slow afternoon with a cup of local coffee.

The winding road is part of the experience. Bring a light layer — it can be noticeably cooler up here than on the coast.

Whale Season

Roughly December through March, humpback whales arrive in the Bahía de Banderas to breed and give birth. Boat tours go out to spot them breaching and tail-slapping, and sometimes you can see them from shore.

Choose operators that follow responsible whale-watching guidelines and keep a respectful distance. Mornings often offer calmer water, and a light jacket helps on the ride back.

Planning Your Day Trips

  • Check conditions — boat trips depend on weather and sea conditions.
  • Protect the reef — use reef-safe sunscreen and avoid touching marine life.
  • Confirm the rules — park permits, access and fees change, so verify before booking.
  • Build in time — travel times are approximate and traffic in the bay can be slow.

Pick one or two of these escapes and weave them into our three-day Puerto Vallarta itinerary for a trip that balances beach, sea and sierra.

title: Where to Stay in Puerto Vallarta: Neighborhoods and Beach Towns Compared
dek: Zona Romántica, the Malecón, Marina Vallarta, Punta Mita or Sayulita? How to pick the right Puerto Vallarta base for your trip.
body:
Puerto Vallarta curls around the Bahía de Banderas, one of the largest bays in Mexico, with jungle-covered mountains tumbling to the water. Where you stay can mean cobblestones and taco stands, a sleek marina, or a hushed luxury peninsula. Here’s how the options stack up, to pair with our Puerto Vallarta guide.

Zona Romántica: Old Town Energy

South of the Río Cuale, the Zona Romántica — also called Old Town — is the city’s most characterful base. Cobblestone streets are packed with cafés, galleries, taco stands and bars, and everything leads down to Playa Los Muertos and its striking pier. It’s also the heart of Vallarta’s famously welcoming LGBTQ+ scene.

It’s lively, walkable and social, with water taxis from the pier to the southern beaches. Hillside streets can be steep, and nights can be noisy near the bars, so choose your block wisely. Stays here range from small guesthouses to beachfront towers, so there’s something for most budgets.

Centro and the Malecón

Just north of the river, Centro is anchored by the Malecón, a seaside promenade lined with bronze sculptures, street performers and sunset crowds. Above it rises the crown-topped Church of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the city’s most recognizable landmark.

Centro puts you close to the action, with easy walks to Old Town. Beaches here are narrower and rockier than elsewhere, so it suits travelers more focused on atmosphere than sunbathing.

Hotel Zone and Marina Vallarta

The Hotel Zone stretches north of Centro along a wide, sandy beach lined with large resorts. It’s convenient and practical for families and beach-first travelers, with shopping and supermarkets nearby.

Farther north, near the airport, Marina Vallarta is a planned development of condos, hotels and golf courses wrapped around a yacht marina. It’s calm, tidy and ideal for boaters and longer stays — though you’ll likely taxi into town for nightlife and street food.

Conchas Chinas: Hillside Views

Just south of Los Muertos, Conchas Chinas climbs the hillside with villas, boutique stays and condos overlooking small rocky coves. The views across the bay are superb, and it’s a short ride or a walk into the Zona Romántica.

The catch: steep streets and stairs. It’s best for couples and travelers who value privacy and a view over walkability. Many rentals come with plunge pools or terraces — perfect for whale-spotting in winter.

Nuevo Vallarta and Punta Mita

Across the Ameca River, in the neighboring state of Nayarit, Nuevo Vallarta is home to long, flat beaches and many large all-inclusive resorts. It’s popular with families who want to settle in and stay put. The trade-off is distance: getting into Vallarta’s Old Town takes a while, especially at busy times, so it works best if the resort is the main event.

At the bay’s northern tip, Punta Mita is the luxury end of the spectrum, with high-end resorts, golf, private residences and surf breaks nearby. It feels a world away from the city — which is exactly the point — but plan on longer drives for day trips.

Sayulita: Surf-Town Alternative

About an hour north of Puerto Vallarta, depending on traffic, Sayulita is a bohemian surf town with a lively plaza, beginner-friendly waves, colorful streets and a youthful energy. It can get crowded, especially on weekends and in high season.

For something mellower, neighboring San Pancho (San Francisco) offers a quieter beach village vibe. Along the coast between, towns like Bucerías offer a middle ground between city and village.

Quick Picks

  • First visit, walkable fun — Zona Romántica
  • Sunsets and landmarks — Centro and the Malecón
  • Family resort stay — Hotel Zone or Nuevo Vallarta
  • Calm and marina-side — Marina Vallarta
  • Views and privacy — Conchas Chinas
  • Top-tier luxury — Punta Mita
  • Surf and bohemian vibes — Sayulita or San Pancho

High season runs roughly through the winter months, so book early if you’re traveling then. Once you’ve chosen your base, plan your days with our three-day Puerto Vallarta itinerary.

title: Boquete: A Guide to Panama’s Coffee Highlands
dek: Cool mountain air, cloud-forest trails, Volcán Barú and world-famous geisha coffee — why Boquete belongs on your Panama trip.
body:
After the heat of Panama City, Boquete feels like a deep breath. This small mountain town in the western province of Chiriquí sits in a green valley beneath Volcán Barú, surrounded by cloud forest, rushing rivers and some of the most celebrated coffee farms on earth. It’s a place for slow mornings, long hikes and very good cups — and a natural addition to the itinerary in our Panama guide.

Getting There and Getting Oriented

Boquete lies in western Panama, not far from the Costa Rican border. Most travelers arrive via the city of David, the regional hub, which has an airport with domestic flights from Panama City; from there it’s a drive of roughly 45 minutes to an hour uphill. Making the whole journey by road from the capital is possible but long — plan on most of a day.

The town itself is compact and easy to navigate, with a central plaza, a riverside setting and roads fanning out into the surrounding hills, where many farms and lodges are located.

A Cool Mountain Climate

At roughly 1,200 meters above sea level, Boquete is noticeably cooler than the coast — warm days, fresh evenings, and air that smells like damp earth and flowers. A signature feature is the bajareque, a fine, misty drizzle that drifts through the valley and is often lit up by rainbows.

Broadly, the drier months run from about December to April, while the rest of the year brings more frequent rain, often in the afternoon. Whenever you visit, pack a light rain jacket and a warm layer for the evenings.

Hiking and the Great Outdoors

Boquete is a trailhead town. Well-loved options include forest walks to waterfalls, river trails and birding hikes where lucky visitors spot the resplendent quetzal, whose iridescent green plumage draws birders from around the world. The Sendero Los Quetzales, a scenic route through Volcán Barú National Park, is a highlight when open — trail access can close after heavy weather, so check current conditions.

Beyond hiking, the area offers river rafting, zip-lining and hot springs in the lowlands nearby. Hiring a local guide is worthwhile for anything beyond the most popular trails.

Climbing Volcán Barú

Volcán Barú is Panama’s highest point, and on a clear morning, the summit offers the rare chance to glimpse both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. The most popular approach is a long, steep overnight hike timed to reach the top at sunrise.

  • It’s a serious climb — long, rocky and at altitude. Train accordingly.
  • Bring real cold-weather gear; temperatures at the summit can drop close to freezing.
  • Go with a guide or experienced company, and check current park rules and conditions before setting out.
  • Manage expectations: clouds often roll in, and a two-ocean view is never guaranteed.

Coffee Farms and Geisha Coffee

The volcanic soil, altitude and misty climate around Boquete create exceptional growing conditions, and the region is known for high-quality specialty coffee. Its most famous export is geisha (also spelled gesha), a variety with roots in Ethiopia that rose to international fame after Panamanian farms began winning competitions and auctions in the 2000s. Geisha is prized for its delicate, floral profile, with notes often described as jasmine, citrus, bergamot and tea.

Many farms welcome visitors for tours that cover the whole journey from cherry to cup: planting, harvesting, processing, drying, roasting and, finally, a guided tasting. It’s a fascinating look at why exceptional coffee commands such high prices. Tours and schedules vary by farm and season, so book ahead.

Planning Your Visit

  • Stay at least two or three nights — Boquete rewards an unhurried pace.
  • Start hikes early, before afternoon clouds and rain move in.
  • Bring layers and waterproof shoes, whatever the season.
  • Taste widely: try geisha alongside other varieties to understand the difference.

Combine a stay in the highlands with the canal, the capital and the islands using our 5-day Panama itinerary as a starting point.

title: Torres del Paine: A First-Timer’s Guide
dek: W Trek or day trips? Refugios or campsites? What first-time visitors need to know to plan a trip to Chile’s Torres del Paine National Park.
body:
Torres del Paine is the kind of place that looks retouched even in person: granite spires, blue-white glaciers, lakes in impossible shades of turquoise and wind strong enough to rearrange your plans. It is also one of the most popular national parks in South America, which means planning ahead is not optional. Here is what first-timers need to know.

Where Is It, and Where to Base Yourself

The park sits in Chilean Patagonia, a few hours’ drive from the town of Puerto Natales, which is the main base for visitors. Natales is where you will find most accommodation, gear rental shops, supermarkets and bus connections into the park. Many travelers also arrive overland from El Calafate in Argentina, a journey that involves a border crossing, so carry your passport and check current entry requirements.

There is also accommodation inside and near the park, from refugios and campsites to more upscale lodges, which saves time on long travel days.

W Trek vs Day Visits

The big decision is whether to hike multi-day or explore on day trips.

  • The W Trek — The park’s most famous route, usually done over about four to five days. It links three highlights: the base of the Torres, the French Valley and Grey Glacier. You sleep in refugios or campsites along the way.
  • The O Circuit — A longer loop that includes the W plus the remote back side of the park, typically taking a week or more. Best for experienced hikers.
  • Day visits — Staying in Puerto Natales or a lodge and doing day hikes or scenic drives. You can still see major viewpoints, lakes and waterfalls, and the hike to the base of the Torres is possible as a long, demanding day.

If you have limited time or prefer a real bed, day visits are a perfectly good way to experience the park.

Book Refugios and Campsites Well Ahead

This is the part first-timers most often underestimate. Overnight stays on the trails must be reserved in advance, and you generally cannot just turn up and camp. Refugios and campsites are run by different operators depending on location, and spaces for the peak summer months can sell out many months ahead.

Plan your route first, then book each night in sequence so your itinerary fits together. Keep your confirmations handy, as rangers may ask to see them.

If your first-choice nights are gone, stay flexible: reversing the direction of the W, adjusting your dates, or basing yourself in a lodge and doing day hikes can often rescue a trip that seemed fully booked.

Park Entry and Rules

Torres del Paine is managed by CONAF, Chile’s national forest service. Entry tickets, registration processes and trail regulations change from season to season, so always check current official CONAF information before your trip. A few principles tend to stay constant:

  • Stick to marked trails and follow any direction-of-travel rules.
  • Camp and cook only in designated areas.
  • Fires are strictly prohibited — the park has suffered devastating wildfires in the past.
  • Pack out all of your trash.

Weather: Expect All Four Seasons

Patagonian weather is famously unpredictable, and it is common to get sun, rain, sleet and gale-force wind in a single day. Summer (roughly December to February) brings long days and the most reliable access, but also the strongest winds and biggest crowds. Spring and autumn are quieter and can be beautiful, with fewer services in operation.

Pack a proper waterproof shell and warm layers, and build flexibility into your plans. Viewpoints like the Torres can be hidden in cloud, so an extra day gives you a second chance.

Practical Wrap-Up

  • Decide early between the W Trek and day visits.
  • Book refugios, campsites and park entry well in advance.
  • Use Puerto Natales as your base for supplies and transport.
  • Check current CONAF rules and weather before setting out.

title: El Calafate: A Guide to Argentina’s Glacier Town
dek: Perito Moreno walkways, ice trekking, glacier cruises and flamingos on the lake: everything to know about visiting El Calafate.
body:
El Calafate is a small town with a very big neighbor. Set on the shore of the milky-turquoise Lago Argentino, it is the gateway to Los Glaciares National Park and the famous Perito Moreno Glacier. Come for the ice, stay for the lake views, the slow evenings and the sense of being somewhere wonderfully remote.

Perito Moreno Glacier: The Walkways

The main event lies roughly an hour and a half’s drive from town. The Perito Moreno Glacier is a vast tongue of ice that flows down from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field and ends in a towering wall facing a peninsula of land. That geography makes it one of the most accessible glaciers on Earth.

A network of walkways and viewing platforms zigzags down the hillside opposite the ice, with routes of different lengths and levels of difficulty. Give yourself several hours here. The glacier is famously active, and the thunderous crack of ice calving into the lake is something you will hear long before you see it. Be patient — the waiting is half the fun.

Boat Trips to the Glacier Face

For a different perspective, short boat trips cruise along the lake right up toward the face of the glacier. From the water, the scale becomes almost absurd: sheer ice cliffs dozens of meters high, cut with deep blue crevasses. These trips are relatively short and pair easily with a visit to the walkways on the same day.

Ice Trekking on the Glacier

If you want to actually stand on the ice, guided ice trekking excursions let you cross the lake by boat and strap on crampons to walk across the glacier’s surface. Expect ridges, meltwater streams and pools of improbable blue.

Shorter treks suit most reasonably fit travelers, while longer options go deeper onto the glacier for those with more stamina. Age and fitness restrictions often apply, and places are limited, so book ahead and check current requirements.

Upsala and Spegazzini Glacier Cruises

Perito Moreno may be the star, but Lago Argentino is fed by other giants too. Full-day and half-day cruises head into the lake’s northern arms toward the Upsala Glacier, one of the largest in the park, and the steep, dramatic Spegazzini Glacier. Along the way you will often pass drifting icebergs in shades from bright white to electric blue.

These cruises are a good choice if you want to see more of the park without hiking. Lake conditions can affect routes, so keep an open mind about exactly which glaciers you will get close to.

In Town: Laguna Nimez and the Glaciarium

  • Laguna Nimez — A nature reserve on the edge of town with an easy walking trail around wetlands and ponds. It is a peaceful spot for birdwatching, and you may see flamingos, black-necked swans and a range of waterfowl.
  • Glaciarium — An interpretive center dedicated to glaciers and ice, just outside town. Its exhibits explain how glaciers form, move and change — useful context before or after visiting Perito Moreno — and it is a good option on a windy or rainy afternoon.

The town itself is compact and easy to walk, with a main street of shops, cafés and outdoor gear stores. Try dishes made with Patagonian lamb and anything flavored with calafate, the local berry that gives the town its name. Legend says that anyone who eats it will return to Patagonia.

Practical Wrap-Up

  • When to go — The main season runs roughly from spring through early autumn, when days are long and excursions run most frequently. Winter is quieter and colder, with some trips reduced.
  • How long to stay — Two to three days lets you see Perito Moreno and take a cruise without rushing.
  • Book ahead — Ice treks and cruises can sell out in peak season.
  • Park fees — Los Glaciares charges an entry fee; check current official information on rates and payment methods.
  • Dress in layers — Wind is constant and weather changes fast, even on sunny days.

El Calafate is a natural anchor for a wider journey; see how it fits with Torres del Paine in our 7-day Patagonia itinerary, or explore the full Patagonia guide.

title: What to Pack for Patagonia: A Practical Layering Guide
dek: Wind, rain, sun and ice in a single afternoon: here is the layering system and gear that keeps you comfortable in Patagonia.
body:
Patagonia has a reputation for weather with a sense of humor. A clear blue morning can turn into sideways rain by lunch and back to dazzling sunshine by afternoon, all with a wind that seems to have somewhere urgent to be. Packing well is not about bringing more — it is about bringing the right layers.

Master the Layering System

Rather than one heavy coat, think in three layers you can add or remove as conditions change:

  • Base layer — A moisture-wicking top (merino wool or synthetic) that keeps sweat off your skin. Avoid cotton, which stays wet and cold.
  • Mid layer — A fleece or light insulated jacket for warmth. A packable down or synthetic puffy is excellent for cold mornings and viewpoints.
  • Outer layer — A windproof and waterproof shell to protect everything underneath.

Bring a couple of base layers so you can rotate them, and hiking pants that dry quickly. Thermal leggings are useful for chilly evenings or shoulder-season trips.

The beauty of this system is flexibility. Start a hike bundled up, peel off the mid layer as you warm up on a climb, then zip everything back on at a windy viewpoint. It is far more comfortable than sweating under one bulky coat, and it packs down much smaller.

Your Shell Is Everything

If you invest in one piece of gear, make it a good waterproof, windproof jacket with a hood that stays put in strong gusts. Waterproof overpants are also worth packing, especially if you plan to hike for several days or take boat trips near glaciers, where spray and rain are common.

Look for a shell that is breathable and roomy enough to fit over your mid layer. In Patagonia, you will be wearing it constantly.

Footwear

Sturdy, broken-in hiking boots with good ankle support and a waterproof membrane are ideal for trails that can be rocky, muddy or wet. Do not bring brand-new boots — blisters can ruin a trek fast.

  • Wool or synthetic hiking socks, with a spare pair or two.
  • Comfortable sneakers or sandals for towns and evenings.
  • Gaiters if you expect muddy trails or snow.

Accessories That Make a Big Difference

  • Gloves — A light pair for hiking and a warmer pair for cold, windy viewpoints and glacier boat trips.
  • Buff or neck gaiter — Blocks wind, keeps your neck warm and doubles as a headband or face cover.
  • Warm hat — A beanie for cold mornings, plus a cap or brimmed hat for sun.
  • Sunglasses — Essential for glare off ice, snow and lakes. Choose a pair with good UV protection.
  • Sunscreen and lip balm — The sun can be strong at these latitudes, and wind makes it easy to underestimate. Use high SPF and reapply.

Day Pack and Dry Bags

A comfortable day pack of around 20 to 30 liters holds your layers, water, snacks and camera on hikes and excursions. Look for one with a hip belt and a rain cover, or line it with a pack liner.

Dry bags are small but mighty. Use them to keep electronics, documents and spare clothes dry on boat trips and rainy trails. A few in different sizes also help keep your pack organized.

Other Useful Extras

  • Trekking poles for steep descents and windy ridges.
  • A reusable water bottle.
  • A headlamp for early starts and refugio nights.
  • A small first-aid kit, blister plasters and any personal medications.
  • A power bank, since charging can be limited on trails.
  • Plug adapters for both Argentina and Chile if you are crossing the border.

Practical Wrap-Up

Pack in layers, prioritize a quality shell and boots, and never underestimate the wind or the sun. Aim for versatile pieces in colors that mix and match, so a small wardrobe covers hiking days, boat trips and relaxed dinners in town. If you are short on gear, Puerto Natales and El Calafate both have outdoor shops and rental options, though choice and availability vary.

title: Cachaça and Food in Paraty: What to Taste and Where It Comes From
dek: Historic alambiques, cachaça tastings, fresh seafood and azul marinho: a guide to eating and drinking your way through Paraty.
body:
In Paraty, the flavors are as rooted in history as the cobblestones. The surrounding hills have produced cachaça for centuries, and the bay supplies seafood that shapes the local table. Come thirsty, and curious.

Paraty’s Cachaça Heritage

Cachaça — the Brazilian spirit distilled from fresh sugarcane juice — has deep roots in Paraty. During the colonial era, the region’s cachaça became so renowned that the town’s name was once used as a synonym for the spirit itself.

Today, a number of traditional distilleries, known as alambiques, still operate in the green hills just outside town. Many are small, family-run operations using copper pot stills, and several welcome visitors.

Visiting an Alambique

A visit usually includes a look at how cane is crushed, fermented and distilled, followed by a tasting. It’s a lovely half-day outing, often combined with a swim at one of the nearby rivers or waterfalls.

  • Getting there — most alambiques are a short drive from the historic center; tours, taxis or a rental car all work.
  • Designated driver — if you’re driving, plan for someone to skip the tasting.
  • Check ahead — visiting arrangements vary, so confirm current details before you go.

How to Taste Cachaça

Good cachaça is meant to be sipped, not just mixed. You’ll encounter two broad styles:

  • Unaged (branca or prata) — clear, bright and grassy, showing the character of the sugarcane.
  • Aged — rested in wooden barrels, which add color, softness and notes of spice, vanilla or dried fruit. Brazil uses many native woods alongside oak, so flavors can be quite distinctive.

Sip slowly, at room temperature, and compare a few side by side. You’ll also find flavored cachaças and liqueurs, sometimes infused with fruits, herbs or spices. And yes, a well-made caipirinha with local cachaça is part of the education.

Beyond the caipirinha, local bars and restaurants often feature cachaça in creative cocktails, and some producers make blends that nod to the region’s history, such as spiced or herb-infused styles. Ask what’s local — bartenders in Paraty tend to be proud of what comes from the surrounding hills, and happy to point you toward something you won’t find at home.

Seafood and Caiçara Cooking

Paraty’s food is shaped by caiçara culture — the traditional communities of Brazil’s southeastern coast, whose lives have long revolved around fishing and the forest. Expect fresh fish, shrimp, squid and mussels served simply, whether grilled, fried or stewed.

At beach kiosks, a plate of fried fish with rice, salad and fries is a classic lunch. In town, menus lean on seafood too, often paired with Brazilian staples like farofa and pirão, a thick gravy made with fish stock and manioc flour.

Moqueca and Azul Marinho

Moqueca is a fragrant seafood stew cooked in a clay pot with tomatoes, onions, peppers and cilantro. You may find the Bahian version, enriched with coconut milk and dendê (palm oil), as well as lighter styles.

The dish to seek out, though, is Paraty’s own azul marinho. This local specialty is a stew of fish cooked with green bananas. As it simmers, the unripe bananas react with the pan and take on a distinctive bluish tint — hence the name, which means “navy blue.” It’s traditionally served with pirão and rice, and it’s a genuine taste of caiçara cooking.

Sweets and Small Pleasures

Keep an eye out for traditional Brazilian sweets like cocada (coconut candy) and doce de banana, often sold from carts around the historic center. In the evenings, the old town fills with diners on candlelit streets — part of Paraty’s easy charm. Sidewalk carts selling crepes and sweets are part of the after-dinner stroll, too.

Practical Tips

  • Pace the tastings — cachaça is strong, typically around 40% alcohol.
  • Buy locally — a bottle from a small producer makes a great souvenir; check your home country’s customs allowances.
  • Eat where the fish is fresh — beach kiosks near fishing communities are often a good bet.

For how to fit an alambique visit into your stay, see our 3-day Paraty itinerary and our Paraty guide.

title: Best Time to Visit Paraty: Weather, Tides and Festivals
dek: Rainy summers, drier winters, FLIP and high tides in the historic center: how to choose the right time for a Paraty trip.
body:
Paraty is a year-round destination, but its moods shift with the seasons. Summer brings beach days and heavy rain, winter offers clearer skies and cooler evenings, and a handful of events and holidays fill the town almost overnight. Here’s how to choose your moment.

Summer: Hot, Green and Rainy (December–March)

Summer is peak season along Brazil’s Costa Verde. Days are hot and humid, the sea is warm and the forest is at its most lush. It’s also typically the rainiest period, with frequent downpours — often heavy afternoon storms, though some days see more persistent rain.

That rain can cancel boat trips or make forest trails muddy and slippery. The upside: waterfalls are at their fullest. Expect crowds and higher prices over Christmas, New Year’s and Carnival, when domestic travelers flock to the coast.

Autumn: A Sweet Spot (April–May)

As summer fades, rain usually becomes less frequent and crowds thin out. The water stays pleasantly warm and the weather is often ideal for exploring both the town and the bay. For many travelers, this is one of the most rewarding times to visit.

Outside of Easter and holiday weekends, you’ll also find it easier to book boat trips at short notice and to wander the historic center without the summer bustle — a real bonus in a town this small.

Winter: Drier and Cooler (June–August)

Winter tends to be the driest season in Paraty, with more clear, sunny days and comfortable temperatures for walking and hiking. Evenings can be cool, and the sea is noticeably colder — refreshing rather than tropical.

It’s a great season for hiking to remote beaches like Praia do Sono, visiting alambiques and wandering the historic center. Just note that cold fronts can occasionally bring gray, rainy spells.

Spring: Warming Up (September–November)

Spring brings rising temperatures and gradually longer beach days. The sea is still on the cool side early in the season, and rain begins to pick up again as summer approaches, but crowds are generally modest outside of holiday weekends.

It’s a good choice if you want a mix of town time and coastal outings without peak-season prices. Weather can be changeable from day to day, so keep your boat trip flexible and have a rainy-day plan — an alambique visit or a long lunch in the historic center works nicely.

FLIP and Other Busy Times

Paraty is home to FLIP, the International Literary Festival of Paraty, one of Brazil’s most important literary events. It usually takes place mid-year, but dates vary, so check the current schedule before you plan.

During FLIP, the town fills with authors, readers and events, and accommodation books up well in advance. The same goes for major holidays and long weekends, when visitors from Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo drive down the coast for a quick escape. If you want to experience these events, reserve early; if you’d rather have a quiet town, avoid them.

High Tides in the Historic Center

One of Paraty’s quirks is that the sea sometimes enters the town. During especially high tides, water flows into some streets of the historic center, briefly flooding the cobblestones. The town’s colonial layout has long been associated with this tidal washing of the streets.

  • When it happens — the highest tides tend to occur around the full and new moons.
  • What to expect — some lower streets become shallow, reflective pools for a few hours before the water recedes.
  • How to plan — check a local tide table and wear sandals; the cobblestones are uneven and slippery.

It’s a beautiful sight, especially at dusk, and a reminder of how closely the town is tied to the sea.

So When Should You Go?

  • For beaches and boat days — late summer into autumn, when water is warm and crowds ease.
  • For hiking and sightseeing — winter, when conditions are typically drier.
  • For culture — FLIP, if you book early.
  • Always pack — a light rain jacket, sturdy sandals and insect repellent.

title: Paraty Beaches and Islands: A Guide to the Bay and Beyond
dek: Trindade’s natural pools, remote Praia do Sono, schooner days on the bay and the Saco do Mamanguá: how to explore Paraty’s coast.
body:
Paraty’s cobblestones get the postcards, but the real magic lies just offshore. The town sits on a bay dotted with green islands, backed by mountains draped in Atlantic Forest, with beaches that range from easygoing to wonderfully remote. Here’s how to see the best of the coast.

Trindade and the Cachadaço Natural Pool

About 30 kilometers south of Paraty, the village of Trindade has a laid-back, slightly bohemian feel and a string of beaches framed by giant granite boulders. It’s easy to reach by car or local bus, making it one of the most popular outings from town.

The star attraction is the Piscina Natural do Cachadaço, a natural pool formed where huge rocks shelter a pocket of calm, clear seawater from the open ocean. It’s ideal for floating and snorkeling. You can reach it via a forest trail from Praia do Cachadaço or by a short boat ride from Trindade.

Trindade’s other beaches deserve time too: Praia do Cepilho draws surfers, Praia do Meio offers calmer water beside the path to the pool, and the village itself has a relaxed scene of kiosks and casual bars.

  • Go early — the pool is small and gets busy by midday, especially on weekends and holidays.
  • Watch the sea — conditions vary, and rough swells can make the pool unsafe; follow local guidance.
  • Wear good shoes — the trail can be slippery, particularly after rain.

Praia do Sono: Worth the Walk

Praia do Sono is a long, golden beach with a small fishing community and very few crowds by comparison. There’s no road access: most people hike roughly an hour or so along a forest trail from Laranjeiras, or take a boat when conditions allow.

That effort is the point. The reward is a wide, wild beach backed by forest, with simple kiosks serving fish and cold drinks. Strong hikers can continue along the trail to even more secluded beaches like Antigos and Antiguinhos.

Paraty-Mirim: A Quiet Escape

About 20 kilometers from Paraty’s historic center, Paraty-Mirim is a calm, sheltered beach with gentle water and a small, historic whitewashed chapel near the sand. It’s a pleasant spot for a lazy swim and a seafood lunch.

It’s also the jumping-off point for boat trips into the Saco do Mamanguá, which makes it a convenient first stop on a longer day.

Schooner Trips Around the Bay

A day on a schooner is a Paraty rite of passage. Large, colorful wooden boats — along with smaller private boats — leave from the town pier and cruise between islands and beaches, stopping for swimming and snorkeling in the bay’s calm, green water.

  • Big schooners — sociable and affordable, but often lively with music and big groups.
  • Private boat hire — more flexible, quieter and ideal for couples or small groups.
  • What to bring — reef-safe sunscreen, a hat, water and snorkel gear if you have it.

Look for trips that visit islands and quieter coves rather than rushing through as many stops as possible.

Saco do Mamanguá: The Fjord-Like Inlet

The Saco do Mamanguá is a long, narrow inlet reaching roughly eight kilometers inland, flanked by steep, forested mountains and fringed by mangroves. It’s often described as Brazil’s only fjord — geologically it isn’t a true glacial fjord, but the look is undeniably dramatic.

Visit by boat from Paraty or Paraty-Mirim, and consider kayaking or stand-up paddleboarding in its still waters. The more adventurous can hike the Pão de Açúcar do Mamanguá, a steep climb to a peak with sweeping views over the inlet. Small caiçara fishing communities live along its shores, so be respectful.

Tips for Exploring Paraty’s Coast

  • Check the weather — rain and wind can cancel boat trips; build in a spare day.
  • Bring cash — some remote kiosks and boat operators may not take cards.
  • Leave no trace — many beaches sit within protected areas; carry out what you bring in.
  • Confirm current rules — access and boat regulations can change, so check before you go.

title: Visiting the Panama Canal: Locks, Boat Trips and Gatún Lake
dek: How to see the Panama Canal up close — from the Miraflores and Agua Clara visitor centers to partial transits and Gatún Lake.
body:
Few engineering projects have reshaped the world quite like the Panama Canal. Opened in 1914, it cuts across the isthmus to link the Atlantic and Pacific, and watching enormous ships rise and fall through its locks is a genuine thrill. Here’s how to see it for yourself, with more on the capital in our Panama guide.

How the Canal Works, in Brief

The canal runs roughly 80 kilometers (about 50 miles) between Panama City on the Pacific side and Colón on the Caribbean side. Rather than cutting down to sea level, it uses a system of locks to lift ships up to Gatún Lake, an artificial lake created by damming the Chagres River, then lower them back down on the other side.

In 2016, an expansion added a new, larger set of locks to accommodate much bigger ships — the so-called Neopanamax vessels. Today you can see both the original locks and the newer ones.

The history is just as dramatic. A French effort in the 1880s collapsed amid disease and engineering setbacks before the United States completed the project. Control passed fully to Panama at the end of 1999, and the canal remains a deep source of national pride.

Miraflores Locks Visitor Center

The easiest and most popular way to see the canal is from the Miraflores Locks, on the Pacific side just outside Panama City. The visitor center has viewing terraces overlooking the locks, along with exhibits on the canal’s history, construction and ecology, plus a film about its story.

The main event is watching a ship ease into a lock chamber as it fills or drains, with small locomotives guiding it along the walls. Ship traffic follows operational needs rather than a tourist timetable, so transits aren’t guaranteed at any given hour. Check current visitor information and, if you can, ask on arrival when vessels are expected.

Agua Clara Visitor Center on the Atlantic Side

On the Caribbean side near Colón, the Agua Clara Visitor Center overlooks the expanded locks, where the giant Neopanamax ships make their way through. It also offers sweeping views over Gatún Lake and surrounding forest.

It’s farther from the capital — plan on a longer drive — but it’s a rewarding outing if you want to see the canal’s newest chapter or combine your visit with other sights along the Atlantic coast.

Partial Transit Boat Trips

For the most immersive experience, join a partial transit — a boat trip through part of the canal, usually including one or more sets of locks. You’ll feel the water rise and fall beneath you, pass under the Bridge of the Americas or Centennial Bridge, and share lock chambers with cargo ships many times your size.

Partial transits generally take a good part of a day, and full transits of the entire canal are offered less frequently. Departures depend on canal operations and can change at short notice, so book ahead and confirm details with your operator.

Exploring Gatún Lake

Gatún Lake is more than a shipping channel. Its flooded valleys created a maze of forested islands, now rich with wildlife. Boat tours on the lake often spot monkeys, sloths, birds and crocodiles, all with the surreal backdrop of massive ships gliding past.

The lake also surrounds Barro Colorado Island, home to a long-running tropical research station. Access to the island is restricted and generally requires advance arrangement, so check current rules if it interests you.

Tips for Your Visit

  • Check before you go. Visitor center hours, ticketing and ship schedules can change.
  • Bring sun protection. The viewing platforms and boat decks can be very sunny and hot.
  • Combine sights. Miraflores pairs easily with a day in Panama City; Agua Clara pairs well with the Caribbean coast.
  • Be patient. Canal viewing rewards those who wait for a ship to pass.

Whether you spend an hour at Miraflores or a full day on the water, the canal is a must on any trip to Panama. Fit it into your plans with our 5-day Panama itinerary.

title: Guna Yala (San Blas) Islands: What to Know Before You Go
dek: Postcard islands in an Indigenous autonomous territory — how to visit Guna Yala respectfully, what to expect and how to plan.
body:
Scattered along Panama’s Caribbean coast, the islands of Guna Yala look like a screensaver come to life: palm-fringed specks of white sand in water every shade of turquoise. But this isn’t a resort zone. It’s the homeland of the Guna people, and visiting well means understanding that first. For more on the country, see our Panama guide.

An Autonomous Guna Territory

Guna Yala — long known to outsiders as San Blas — is a comarca, a semi-autonomous Indigenous territory governed by the Guna people through their own traditional congresses and leaders. The Guna have maintained their language, governance and customs with remarkable determination, and tourism here operates on their terms.

The territory includes a long strip of mainland coast and hundreds of islands, only a fraction of which are inhabited. Some are home to dense villages; others hold little more than a few cabins, a kitchen and swaying palms. You’ll likely see molas, the intricate layered textile panels made by Guna women, which are a celebrated art form and a meaningful souvenir to buy directly from their makers.

Getting There

Most visitors travel by 4×4 from Panama City along a winding mountain road to the coast, a journey of roughly two and a half to three hours, followed by a boat ride to the islands. Transport is usually arranged as part of an island stay or tour package, often with an early-morning pickup.

Expect a checkpoint on the way into the territory, where you’ll need your passport and will pay entry fees. Requirements and fees are set by Guna authorities and can change, so confirm current details with your host before you travel.

The boat rides themselves can be bumpy, particularly when the wind picks up, and you may get splashed. Keep valuables and electronics in a waterproof bag, sit toward the back if you’re prone to seasickness, and don’t be surprised if schedules shift with the weather.

Day Trip or Overnight?

Day trips from Panama City are possible, but they involve a very early start and many hours in vehicles and boats for a relatively short time on the water. If you can, stay at least one night. You’ll see the islands at their most serene — at sunrise, after the day visitors have gone, and under a spectacular starry sky.

Multi-day sailing trips are another popular option, including routes that travel between Panama and the Colombian coast. If you consider one, research carefully and choose operators with strong safety standards.

What Island Stays Are Like

Accommodation is simple by design, and that’s part of the appeal. Think of it as rustic island living rather than hotel comfort.

  • Basic cabins, often with sand floors, and sometimes shared bathrooms.
  • Limited electricity, often from solar panels or generators, for a few hours a day.
  • Little or no Wi-Fi or mobile signal in many places.
  • Set meals, usually built around fresh fish, rice, plantains and coconut, with seafood depending on the season.

Respect the Local Rules

Visitors are guests in a community with its own rules, and following them is the heart of responsible travel here.

  • Ask before photographing people; some communities request a small fee for photos.
  • Expect small fees to visit or land on certain islands, set by the local community.
  • Don’t take coconuts — they are owned and are an important source of income.
  • Dress modestly when visiting inhabited villages, keeping swimwear for the beach.
  • Pack out your trash and avoid single-use plastics where possible.

What to Pack

Bring cash in small bills, since there are no ATMs on the islands and cards generally aren’t accepted. Add reef-friendly sunscreen, a hat, a dry bag for the boat rides, a headlamp, insect repellent and any medication you need, including something for motion sickness if the sea tends to bother you.

The Takeaway

Go for the beauty; stay for the perspective. Guna Yala offers a rare chance to experience a place where Indigenous autonomy shapes everything. Plan an overnight if you can, check current entry requirements, and fit it into your trip with our 5-day Panama itinerary.

title: Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal or Isabela: Which Galápagos Island to Base On
dek: Planning a land-based Galápagos trip? How Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal and Isabela compare for convenience, wildlife, beaches and atmosphere.
body:
A cruise is not the only way to see the Galápagos. Basing yourself on land — and taking day trips by boat — offers flexibility, stable ground at night and a feel for island life. The key decision is where to stay, and it usually comes down to three inhabited islands. Here is how they compare; our Galápagos guide has the bigger picture.

Santa Cruz: The Convenient Hub

Santa Cruz sits near the center of the archipelago, and its main town, Puerto Ayora, is the busiest in the islands. That central position makes it the easiest base for day trips to other islands, and the town has the widest range of places to stay and eat.

  • Charles Darwin Research Station — learn about conservation efforts and see giant tortoises.
  • Tortuga Bay — a long white-sand beach reached by a walking path, with a calmer cove for swimming.
  • The highlands — spot giant tortoises roaming in the wild and explore lava tunnels.
  • Las Grietas — a swimming spot set in a narrow volcanic fissure.

Most visitors fly into nearby Baltra and cross a short channel to reach Santa Cruz. The trade-off for all this convenience: Puerto Ayora feels more developed and busier than the other towns. Even so, it is easy to find quiet corners, and the evening waterfront has a pleasant, easygoing buzz.

San Cristóbal: Sea Lions and Easy Access

San Cristóbal is the provincial capital, and its town, Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, has a relaxed, lived-in feel. It also has an airport right by town, which makes arrival refreshingly simple.

The island’s signature sight is its sea lions, which lounge on benches, beaches and the waterfront promenade as though they own the place — because, in a sense, they do. You can reach several good beaches and snorkeling spots from town on foot or by short taxi ride.

  • Kicker Rock (León Dormido) — a dramatic offshore rock formation popular for snorkeling and diving tours.
  • Interpretation center — a good introduction to the islands’ natural and human history.
  • La Lobería — a coastal area known for sea lions and marine iguanas.
  • Frigatebird Hill — a scenic hike with views over the bay.

Isabela: Wild and Laid-Back

Isabela is the largest island in the archipelago, yet its small town, Puerto Villamil, is the most low-key of the three. Sandy streets, a long beach and a slower pace give it a castaway charm that many travelers fall for.

  • Sierra Negra volcano — a hike to the rim of one of the largest volcanic calderas in the islands.
  • Los Túneles — striking lava formations and arches, often combined with snorkeling.
  • Concha de Perla — a sheltered spot for snorkeling close to town.
  • Lagoons and a tortoise breeding center — look for flamingos along the way.

The catch is access. Isabela is farther from the other islands, and visitors typically arrive by inter-island boat, which can be a long, bumpy ride. Services and cash access are also more limited, so plan ahead.

Getting Between the Islands

Inter-island speedboats connect Santa Cruz with both San Cristóbal and Isabela, and the crossings take a couple of hours each way. Seas can be rough, so bring seasickness remedies if you need them. Small inter-island flights are another option on some routes. Schedules and services change, so confirm current options when planning.

Which Island Is Right for You?

  • Short trip or first visit — Santa Cruz, for convenience and day-trip options.
  • Easy arrival and a relaxed town — San Cristóbal.
  • Nature, quiet and a slower pace — Isabela.
  • A week or more — split your stay between two or even all three.

Final Tips

Many visitors find that combining islands gives the fullest picture of the archipelago, since each has its own landscapes and atmosphere. Book popular day tours in advance during busy periods, and check current national park rules and entry requirements before you go. For a ready-made plan, start with our five-day Galápagos itinerary.

title: What to Pack for the Galápagos: A Practical Packing List
dek: Reef-safe sunscreen, a rash guard, water shoes and a dry bag: a practical Galápagos packing list, plus the biosecurity rules to know before you fly.
body:
Packing for the Galápagos is less about outfits and more about sun, sea and respect for a fragile ecosystem. You will spend your days on boats, beaches and lava trails, often switching between them in a single afternoon. Here is what to bring — and what to leave at home — with more planning help in our Galápagos guide.

Sun Protection: Non-Negotiable

The equatorial sun is intense, even on overcast days, and reflection off water and pale sand amplifies it. Treat sun protection as essential equipment.

  • Reef-safe sunscreen — choose mineral-based formulas and apply generously; you will be swimming alongside sensitive marine life.
  • Rash guard — a long-sleeved swim shirt protects your back and shoulders while snorkeling and cuts down on sunscreen use.
  • Wide-brimmed hat — ideally one with a chin strap, because boat rides get breezy.
  • Polarized sunglasses — helpful for glare and for spotting wildlife in the water.
  • Lip balm with SPF — small, easy to forget, much appreciated.

Clothing: Light Layers for Every Season

Days are generally warm, but boat rides, the misty highlands and cooler-season evenings can feel surprisingly brisk. Think lightweight and quick-drying.

  • Breathable shirts and shorts — plus at least one pair of lightweight long pants.
  • A light fleece or sweater — for evenings, the highlands and windy crossings.
  • A packable rain jacket — useful for showers in the warm season and garúa mist in the cool one.
  • Two swimsuits — so one can dry while you wear the other.

Galápagos style is casual. Nobody will judge your hiking sandals at dinner.

Footwear: Wet and Dry Landings

Some landings mean stepping from a small boat directly into shallow surf, while others put you on rocky or uneven volcanic terrain. Plan accordingly.

  • Water shoes or sturdy sport sandals — for wet landings, tide pools and rocky beaches.
  • Comfortable walking shoes — closed-toe options are good for lava trails and highland hikes.
  • Flip-flops — for town and downtime.

On the Water

Boats are central to most Galápagos trips, whether you are cruising or hopping between islands from a land base. Crossings can be bumpy, especially when seas are rougher.

  • Seasickness remedies — whatever works for you, and take them before you board. Ask a doctor or pharmacist for advice if you are unsure.
  • Dry bag — keeps your phone, camera and a spare layer safe from spray.
  • Snorkel mask — gear is often provided by tours, but a mask that fits you well makes a big difference.
  • Wetsuit — often available to rent or included; especially worthwhile in the cooler months.

Biosecurity: What Not to Bring

The Galápagos ecosystem is uniquely vulnerable to introduced species, so the islands take biosecurity seriously. Luggage is inspected before you fly to the islands and again on arrival, and there are restrictions on bringing in organic items — typically things like fresh fruit and vegetables, seeds, plants, soil and live animals.

Rules are updated from time to time, so check current biosecurity regulations and park requirements before you pack. Before you leave home, clean mud and seeds off your shoes and outdoor gear. And the same principle works in reverse: do not take anything from the islands, including shells, sand, rocks or plants.

Useful Extras

  • Reusable water bottle — the islands have restrictions on single-use plastics.
  • Binoculars — lovely for birds and distant wildlife.
  • Camera with extra batteries and storage — you will take more photos than you expect.
  • Cash — ATMs and card acceptance can be limited, especially on smaller islands.
  • Personal medications and a small first-aid kit — pharmacies exist, but selection is limited.

The Short Version

Pack light, pack for sun and water, and pack respectfully. A rash guard, reef-safe sunscreen, a hat, water shoes, a warm layer and a dry bag will carry you through most days. Double-check the latest entry and biosecurity rules before departure, then follow our five-day Galápagos itinerary and enjoy the islands exactly as they are meant to be seen.

title: Best Time to Visit the Galápagos: A Season-by-Season Guide
dek: Warm, calm and green or cool, misty and full of marine life? How the Galápagos seasons compare, and how to choose the right time for your trip.
body:
Here is the headline: there is no bad time to visit the Galápagos. The islands sit right on the equator, wildlife is present all year and the animals are famously unbothered by people in every month. What changes is the ocean — its temperature, its mood and what it brings with it — and that is what should shape your timing. Our Galápagos guide covers the rest.

How the Galápagos Seasons Work

The archipelago has two broad seasons, driven largely by shifting ocean currents rather than by summer and winter in the usual sense. Roughly speaking, the warm, wet season runs from about December to May, and the cool, dry garúa season runs from about June to November. The transitions are gradual, and conditions vary from year to year — occasionally dramatically, during El Niño or La Niña events.

Warm and Wet Season (Roughly December to May)

This is the season of sunshine and short, sometimes heavy showers. Air and water temperatures are at their warmest, which makes snorkeling more comfortable for longer stretches. Seas also tend to be calmer, a real plus if you are prone to seasickness or planning inter-island boat rides.

  • Warmer water — many snorkelers find they can skip or lighten their wetsuit.
  • Calmer seas — generally smoother crossings and cruise conditions.
  • Greener islands — the rains bring color to the lowlands and highlands.
  • Nesting and breeding — this period is associated with sea turtle nesting and plenty of activity among land birds.

The trade-off is humidity and the chance of rain, though showers are often brief and followed by sun. It is also a popular time for families, since it overlaps with school holidays in many countries.

Cool and Dry Garúa Season (Roughly June to November)

When cooler currents take over, the islands shift into a different mood. Skies are often overcast, and a fine mist known as garúa settles over the highlands, keeping them green even as the lowlands turn drier. Water temperatures drop noticeably, and seas can be choppier, particularly in the later months.

So why go? Because cooler, nutrient-rich water fuels the food chain. This season is widely considered excellent for marine life, with abundant fish and very active seabirds and sea lions. Divers and serious snorkelers often favor these months — just plan on a wetsuit.

  • Richer marine life — plankton-rich water supports busy underwater scenes.
  • Cooler temperatures — comfortable for hiking, cooler for swimming.
  • Rougher seas — worth bearing in mind for boat days and cruises.

Wildlife Is a Year-Round Story

Particular breeding cycles, nesting periods and migrations do cluster in certain months, and some species are only present on specific islands at specific times. If there is a particular animal you are dreaming of, research its season and location before you book, and ask your cruise or tour operator directly — itineraries vary widely. Otherwise, rest easy: sea lions, marine iguanas, giant tortoises, frigatebirds and boobies are part of the scenery in any month.

Crowds and Booking Considerations

Beyond weather, demand shapes the experience. Holiday periods such as Christmas and New Year, Easter and the northern summer tend to be busier, and popular cruise departures can book up well ahead. If you are traveling in these windows, plan early. Shoulder months on either side of the seasons can offer a pleasant balance of conditions and availability.

Visitor rules, park fees and entry requirements are set by the authorities and can change, so check current official information before you travel.

So, When Should You Go?

  • Prioritize comfortable snorkeling and calm seas — aim for roughly December to May.
  • Prioritize marine life and diving — consider roughly June to November.
  • Prone to seasickness — lean toward the warm season, and consider a land-based trip.
  • Flexible — honestly, just go. The Galápagos rarely disappoints.

Whenever you land, pack for both sun and a bit of chill, and use our five-day Galápagos itinerary to make the most of your days on the islands.
