title: The Sacred Valley: A Guide to Písac, Ollantaytambo, Maras and More
dek: Inca terraces, salt pans, weaving villages and mountain views: a guide to the highlights of Peru’s Sacred Valley near Cusco.
body:
Stretching along the Urubamba River north of Cusco, the Sacred Valley was a fertile heartland of the Inca world, and it remains one of Peru’s most beautiful regions. Terraced hillsides, Andean villages and some of the country’s most impressive ruins sit beneath snow-dusted peaks. It is also lower than Cusco, which makes it a gentle place to start your trip.

Písac: Ruins and Market

At the eastern end of the valley, the town of Písac is known for two things. High above town, the Písac archaeological site spreads across a mountainside, with sweeping agricultural terraces, ceremonial structures and fine Inca stonework, all with dramatic views over the valley.

Down below, the town’s handicraft market fills the streets and plaza with textiles, ceramics, jewelry and produce. It is busiest on market days, so check the current schedule if you want to catch it at full swing.

Urubamba: The Valley’s Hub

Urubamba sits near the middle of the valley and works as a practical base. It is less of a sight in itself than a convenient, relaxed town with easy access to Maras, Moray and Ollantaytambo. Many travelers stay in or around Urubamba to explore the region at an unhurried pace, surrounded by countryside and mountain views.

Ollantaytambo: A Living Inca Town

At the western end of the valley, Ollantaytambo is a highlight. Its old quarter still follows an Inca street grid, with stone channels carrying water alongside the lanes. Above town, the massive terraces and temple complex, often referred to as a fortress, climb the hillside in steep steps, crowned by enormous carved stones.

Ollantaytambo is also the main train station for Machu Picchu, so it is a natural place to spend a night before or after your visit. Our 4-day Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary shows how the valley and Machu Picchu fit together.

Maras and Moray: Salt and Circles

These two sites sit close together on the high plateau above the valley and are usually visited as a pair.

  • Maras salt pans — the Salineras de Maras are a hillside of thousands of shallow terraced pools, fed by a naturally salty spring. Local families have harvested salt here since before the Incas, and the patchwork of white and tan pools is striking in person.
  • Moray — a set of concentric circular terraces sunk into the earth like an amphitheater. Many researchers believe the Incas may have used the different levels, each with its own microclimate, for agricultural experimentation.

Chinchero: Weaving Traditions

Chinchero, on the high road between Cusco and Urubamba, is known for its textile traditions. Local weaving cooperatives and demonstrations show how wool is cleaned with natural roots, dyed with plants and insects and woven on backstrap looms into intricate patterns. The town also has Inca terraces and a colonial church built on Inca foundations.

Note that Chinchero is actually higher than Cusco, at around 3,700 meters, so pace yourself if you are just arriving.

Planning Your Visit

You can see the highlights on a single full-day tour from Cusco, but it is a long, fast-paced day. With two or three nights in the valley, you can visit Písac in the morning light, linger in Ollantaytambo’s lanes after the day-trippers leave and add Maras and Moray without rushing. Staying overnight also makes the connection to Machu Picchu much smoother.

  • Getting around — many travelers use a private driver or a guided tour to string several sites together; local transport also connects the main towns.
  • Tickets — several sites, including Písac, Ollantaytambo, Moray and Chinchero, have typically been covered by Cusco’s tourist ticket (boleto turístico), while the Maras salt pans have a separate entry. Check current official information, as ticket systems change.
  • Timing — the dry season, roughly May to September, brings clearer skies; the rainy months bring green hillsides and fewer crowds.
  • Altitude — the valley floor sits at roughly 2,800 to 2,900 meters, lower than Cusco.

Practical Wrap-Up

Give the Sacred Valley at least one full day, and ideally two or more. Starting your trip here helps you acclimatize while seeing some of Peru’s most memorable landscapes. Bring layers, sun protection and cash for markets, and wear comfortable shoes for stairs and terraces. For more on the region, visit our Cusco guide.

title: Monteverde, Costa Rica: A Cloud Forest Guide
dek: Misty reserves, hanging bridges, night walks and a shot at spotting the quetzal: what to know before you visit Monteverde’s cloud forest.
body:
High in the mountains of northwestern Costa Rica, Monteverde feels like another world: moss-draped trees, drifting mist and a soundtrack of birdsong and dripping leaves. It is one of the country’s most celebrated nature destinations, and it rewards travelers who slow down. Here is what to know, with more ideas in our Costa Rica guide.

What Makes a Cloud Forest Special

A cloud forest is exactly what it sounds like: a forest where clouds regularly settle among the trees. Moisture carried by the trade winds condenses on the mountains, keeping everything damp and green. The result is extraordinary biodiversity, with orchids, bromeliads, ferns and mosses covering nearly every surface, and a huge variety of birds, insects and mammals.

The area around Monteverde also has an interesting human story: Quaker settlers arrived in the mid-20th century, established a dairy community and played a role in early conservation efforts here.

The Reserves

Several protected areas surround the small town of Santa Elena, and each has its own character.

  • Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Reserve — the best-known, with well-maintained trails through classic cloud forest and across the continental divide.
  • Santa Elena Cloud Forest Reserve — slightly higher and often quieter, with its own trail network.
  • Children’s Eternal Rainforest — a large private reserve with trails near its field station.
  • Smaller private reserves — many offer excellent birding, often with fewer visitors.

Entry requirements, hours and fees vary, so check current information before you go. Hiring a naturalist guide is highly recommended; they carry spotting scopes and have an uncanny ability to find animals you would walk right past.

Hanging Bridges and Canopy Views

Some of the most memorable views in Monteverde come from above. Several parks in the area offer networks of suspension bridges strung through the canopy, letting you walk at treetop level among epiphytes and birds. For something faster, the region is also known for its ziplines, some of which cross impressive valleys.

Night Walks

When the sun goes down, a different cast comes out. Guided night walks are one of Monteverde’s highlights, with flashlights revealing tarantulas, stick insects, frogs, sleeping birds and — with some luck — sloths, kinkajous or other nocturnal mammals. Walks typically last a couple of hours, and a good guide makes all the difference.

Looking for the Quetzal

For many visitors, the resplendent quetzal is the ultimate sighting. With iridescent green plumage and, in males, spectacularly long tail feathers, it is one of the most beautiful birds in the Americas. Sightings are never guaranteed, but chances are often better during the breeding season, commonly cited as roughly spring. Early mornings, patience and a knowledgeable guide improve your odds considerably.

Weather and Getting There

Monteverde is noticeably cooler than Costa Rica’s coasts, and it can be windy, misty and damp at almost any time of year. Bring layers, a waterproof jacket and sturdy shoes with good grip for muddy trails. Mornings are often the clearest time for wildlife and views, and evenings can be chilly enough for a sweater.

Part of Monteverde’s charm has always been its relative remoteness. The mountain roads leading up are winding, and some stretches have historically been unpaved, rough and slow — though conditions have changed over the years and vary by route. Check current road conditions, allow plenty of time and consider a vehicle with good clearance if you are driving yourself. Shared shuttles and private transfers are common alternatives.

Practical Tips

  • Stay at least two nights — enough for a reserve visit, a night walk and a canopy experience.
  • Book guides in advance — especially in the busy dry season.
  • Bring binoculars — they make a real difference in dense forest.
  • Keep expectations flexible — wildlife is wild, and mist is part of the magic.

Monteverde pairs beautifully with Arenal and the Pacific coast. See how it fits into a wider trip in our five-day Costa Rica itinerary.

title: Where to Stay in Arenal and La Fortuna: Town vs. Volcano Lodges
dek: Stay in walkable La Fortuna or out by the volcano? How to choose your base in Costa Rica’s Arenal area, from town hotels to hot springs resorts.
body:
Few places in Costa Rica pack in as much as Arenal: a perfectly conical volcano, rainforest trails, waterfalls, a sprawling lake and naturally heated hot springs. The town of La Fortuna is the gateway, but where you stay in the area shapes your trip more than you might expect. Here is how to choose, with more in our Costa Rica guide.

Understanding the Area

La Fortuna sits at the base of Arenal Volcano, in the northern lowlands. From town, the main road heads west toward the volcano and Lake Arenal, lined with lodges, hot springs resorts and attractions along the way. Arenal Volcano itself has been in a resting phase since around 2010, so visitors come for the scenery and nature rather than lava views. Its summit is often wrapped in clouds, which makes a clear morning feel like a gift.

Staying in La Fortuna Town

Staying in town puts everything within easy reach. La Fortuna is compact and walkable, with a central park, a church framed by the volcano, and plenty of restaurants, cafés, sodas (casual local eateries) and tour offices.

  • Pros — convenient, lots of dining choices, easy tour pickups and generally a wider range of budgets.
  • Cons — less nature on your doorstep, and volcano views can be partial or obstructed.

Town works well for travelers without a car, shorter stays and anyone who likes to wander out for dinner. It is also handy for early tour departures, since many operators pick up from town.

Staying on the Volcano Side

Head out along the road toward the volcano and the lake, and you will find lodges set in gardens and rainforest, many with direct volcano views from rooms or terraces. Waking up to birdsong and a mountain framed in your window is the big draw.

  • Pros — immersive nature, quieter nights, views and on-site wildlife spotting.
  • Cons — you will likely need a car, taxi or shuttle to get into town, and dining options nearby can be limited.

If you want the lodge experience, look at how far the property is from town and whether it offers meals or transport.

Hot Springs Resorts

Geothermal activity feeds a number of hot springs in the Arenal area, and several resorts are built around them, with multiple pools at different temperatures, landscaped grounds and spa facilities. Staying at one means you can soak after a day of hiking without going anywhere — a very appealing idea when an afternoon shower rolls in.

Many hot springs also sell day passes, so you do not need to stay at a resort to enjoy the water. Some travelers split their stay: a night or two in town, then a splurge night at a resort.

Other Options Nearby

For something quieter, consider the small community of El Castillo on the far side of the volcano, which offers lake and volcano views and a peaceful, rural feel. Lodges around Lake Arenal suit those who want scenery and space, though they are farther from the main attractions. The drive around the lake is scenic but winding, so allow extra time.

What to Consider Before You Book

  • Transportation — without a car, town is easiest; with one, the volcano side opens up.
  • Your must-dos — La Fortuna Waterfall, Arenal Volcano National Park trails, hanging bridges and the lake all sit a short drive apart.
  • Views — if a volcano-facing room matters, confirm it before booking.
  • Weather — rain is possible year-round, so a place with covered outdoor space is a bonus.
  • Length of stay — two or three nights lets you enjoy the area without rushing.

The Bottom Line

Choose La Fortuna town for convenience, walkability and choice; choose a volcano-side lodge for immersion and views; and consider a hot springs resort if soaking is high on your list. Any of them makes a great base. Arenal pairs naturally with Monteverde — see how the two fit together in our five-day Costa Rica itinerary.

title: Best Time to Visit Costa Rica: Dry Season vs. Green Season
dek: Dry season sunshine or green season lushness? How Costa Rica’s weather works on the Pacific and Caribbean sides, and how to pick your months.
body:
Costa Rica is a year-round destination, but it is not a one-climate country. Mountains, two coastlines and a web of microclimates mean the answer to “when should I go?” depends on where you are going — and what you are willing to trade for sunshine. Here is how the seasons actually work, with more in our Costa Rica guide.

The Two Seasons, Simply Put

Locals talk about two seasons rather than four. The dry season, often called summer, runs roughly from December to April on the Pacific side and in the Central Valley. The green season, sometimes called winter, runs roughly from May to November. Temperatures in the lowlands stay warm all year; it is rainfall that changes. Higher elevations, meanwhile, stay cooler throughout.

Dry Season (Roughly December to April)

This is peak travel season, and for good reason. The Pacific coast — especially the northwest province of Guanacaste — sees long stretches of sunshine, blue skies and easy beach days. Hiking trails are drier, roads are generally in better shape and outdoor plans are simpler to make.

  • Best for — beach time, reliable weather and first-time visitors who want fewer variables.
  • Keep in mind — it is the busiest period, especially around Christmas, New Year and Easter week, so book accommodation and rental cars early.
  • Landscape — parts of Guanacaste turn dry and golden by the end of the season.

Green Season (Roughly May to November)

Do not let the word “rainy” scare you off. In much of the country, green season days often start sunny, with clouds building into afternoon showers or downpours. Mornings are for adventures; afternoons are for hot springs, coffee and a good book.

The landscape is at its most lush, rivers run full and there are generally fewer crowds. Many travelers find it a rewarding time to visit. Rain tends to increase as the season goes on, with September and October typically the wettest months on the Pacific side, when some roads can be muddy and some businesses may close temporarily.

  • Best for — rainforests, waterfalls, wildlife and quieter trips.
  • Keep in mind — plan outdoor activities early in the day, and allow extra time for driving.

The Caribbean Side Plays by Different Rules

Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast — think Puerto Viejo, Cahuita and Tortuguero — does not follow the Pacific pattern. Rain can fall at any time of year, but September and October are often among the drier, sunnier months there, just when the Pacific side is at its wettest.

That makes the Caribbean a smart pivot if you are traveling in early autumn. It is also worth knowing that Tortuguero is famous for sea turtle nesting at certain times of year; if seeing turtles is a priority, research the nesting seasons and book with licensed local guides.

Microclimates and Mountains

Elevation changes everything. Cloud forest areas like Monteverde are cool, misty and breezy much of the year, and the Arenal area can see rain in any month. Meanwhile, the Central Valley around San José has a mild, spring-like climate. The south Pacific, including the Osa Peninsula, tends to be among the wettest regions overall. Pack layers wherever you go, and do not assume the weather in one region predicts the next.

Wildlife and Seasonal Highlights

Sloths, monkeys, toucans and frogs are around all year. Some experiences are seasonal, though — turtle nesting, whale watching along the Pacific and certain bird breeding periods cluster in specific months. If one of these is on your wish list, check timing for the exact region you plan to visit.

Choosing Your Dates

  • Sun-first beach trip — December to April on the Pacific side.
  • Lush landscapes and value — May to August, before the heaviest rains.
  • September or October — consider the Caribbean coast.
  • Holiday travel — book well ahead.

Whenever you go, bring a light rain jacket and a flexible attitude. Then map out your days with our five-day Costa Rica itinerary.

title: Bolo de Rolo in Recife: Pernambuco’s Most Beautiful Sweet Spiral
dek: Taste Recife’s bolo de rolo, the guava-filled spiral recognized as cultural heritage of Pernambuco, with bakery and travel guidance.
body:
Sweet Strolls · Recife, Brazil

Bolo de Rolo in Recife

Thin as ribbon, bright with guava and inseparable from the sweet history of Pernambuco.

At first glance, bolo de rolo looks like a perfect spiral drawn by hand. Cut closer and its true delicacy appears: layer after layer of very thin cake wrapped around guava paste, each turn precise, tender and fragrant.

Born in Pernambuco, the dessert evolved from the Portuguese colchão de noiva. Local bakers adapted the recipe to the ingredients and tastes of Brazil, replacing the traditional almond filling with guava. In 2008, bolo de rolo was recognized by state law as cultural and intangible heritage of Pernambuco.

A cake measured in patience

The beauty is not simply in the roll. Each fine sheet must be baked quickly, spread while supple and wrapped before the next layer joins it. The result should feel balanced: soft cake, concentrated fruit and a gentle sweetness that invites another slice. Recife’s dessert culture carries the imprint of centuries of sugar production, trade and reinvention. Bolo de rolo belongs to that history, but it also remains vividly present—served in cafés, given as a gift and packed for journeys home.
Classic guavaThe essential first taste. Look for many fine rings and a filling that is rich rather than sticky.
A café pairingOrder a thin slice with strong Brazilian coffee; bitterness sharpens the fruit.
The gift boxA whole roll travels better than a cream cake, though it should still be protected from heat.

How to taste it in Recife

Begin in the historic center or a traditional bakery and ask whether the cake is made in-house. Compare a classic slice before trying modern variations. Wrapped versions make an elegant edible souvenir, but check storage guidance and airline rules before packing.
Jet Set LatAM note: Build the tasting into a wider day of Recife architecture, music and waterfront light. For more Brazilian flavor and design, continue with our fashion stroll through São Paulo’s Jardins.

Practical sweetness

The traditional recipe contains wheat, eggs, butter and sugar; commercial versions may include additional allergens. Ask before ordering if you have dietary restrictions. Recife is warm and humid, so avoid leaving packaged cake in direct sun or a hot car.
Save the sweet moments

Take Let Them Eat to Recife

Keep the cakes, bakeries and beautiful little discoveries you never want to forget. Discover Let Them Eat on the App Store

The final slice

Bolo de rolo is both intricate and generous: a pastry of repetition, memory and regional pride. In Recife, its pink spiral is not merely pretty. It is Pernambuco, rolled into something you can taste.
Sources: Recife municipal tourism; Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco; Fundação Joaquim Nabuco. Details verified September 2026.

A small Antigua route with lasting appeal: learn about jade, choose handwoven textiles, and finish with coffee and chocolate.

Antigua’s shopping is most rewarding when you ask how a piece was made. This route gives that conversation three forms: jade, woven cloth and edible gifts. Start east of the center at Jade Maya, continue toward Calle del Arco, then finish farther northwest for coffee.

The map estimate is about 17 minutes of walking before any browsing. Allow two to three hours for the full outing. Cobblestones and uneven surfaces can slow the pace, so use shoes you would happily wear for more than a quick photograph.

Jade Maya — main showroom

4a Calle Oriente 34, Antigua Guatemala, Guatemala

title: Kuchen in Puerto Varas: Southern Chile’s Sweetest Afternoon Ritual
dek: Taste the kuchen tradition of Puerto Varas, where southern Chile’s German heritage meets local fruit, lakeside cafés and the perfect afternoon slice.
body:
Sweet Strolls · Los Lagos, Chile

Kuchen in Puerto Varas

A lakeside ritual of fruit, crumb and cream—where southern Chile’s immigrant history becomes the loveliest possible afternoon.

On a mist-softened afternoon in Puerto Varas, kuchen feels less like dessert than a way of understanding the south. A slice arrives beside coffee with the Osorno volcano beyond the lake: buttery pastry, seasonal fruit and a generous layer of custard or crumb.

The word and technique came with German settlers who shaped parts of southern Chile’s culinary landscape. Over generations, kuchen became distinctly local—made with the berries, apples, dairy and rhythms of Los Lagos, and woven into family tables, cafés and community celebrations.

A pastry with a southern Chilean accent

Chile’s food culture is a long conversation between Indigenous ingredients, Spanish traditions and later European arrivals. In the lake district, German baking joined local abundance. The result is not one fixed recipe but a family of cakes and tarts: apple kuchen layered neatly under custard, berry versions stained ruby, and crumb-topped slices whose edges are the first to disappear. Puerto Varas even celebrates Día del Kuchen, a regional gastronomy event associated with foods made by descendants of German settlers. That living heritage matters: kuchen is not a themed novelty, but a beloved part of how the region welcomes guests.
AppleClassic, fragrant and ideal with strong coffee. Look for a tender base and fruit that keeps a little bite.
BerryMurta, raspberry or mixed berries bring brightness to the richness of custard and butter.
StreuselA crumb-topped version offers the best contrast: crisp, soft and gently spiced.

How to plan the sweetest afternoon

Begin with a walk along Puerto Varas’s waterfront, then settle into a café before the late-afternoon rush. Ask what was baked that morning; the freshest seasonal version is usually the right choice. Share two slices if you can—one fruit-forward and one creamy—then continue north toward Frutillar, the lake town known for its calm shoreline and Teatro del Lago.
Jet Set LatAM note: Weather shifts quickly around Lago Llanquihue, so bring a light waterproof layer even for a café day. Build a longer southern itinerary with our Patagonia seasons and weather guide.

What to order—and what to notice

A good slice should taste balanced rather than simply sweet. Notice the dairy, the freshness of the fruit and whether the pastry holds together without becoming heavy. Coffee is the traditional companion, though black tea makes a graceful alternative. Travelers with allergies should ask directly about wheat, eggs, dairy and nuts; recipes vary widely. Café hours and daily selections can also change seasonally, especially outside the busiest summer months.
Save the sweet moments

Take Let Them Eat along

Use Let Them Eat to remember the pastries, cakes and little neighborhood discoveries worth returning for. Discover Let Them Eat on the App Store

The final crumb

Kuchen belongs to the pleasure of traveling slowly: looking out at the lake, warming your hands around a cup and choosing a second slice because the rain has started again. In Puerto Varas, history is not locked behind glass. It is baked fresh, cut generously and served in the afternoon.
Sources: Memoria Chilena on Chilean culinary history and German settlement; SERNATUR Los Lagos regional guide; Chile Travel guidance for Puerto Varas and Frutillar. Verified September 2026.

title: Where to Stay in Punta Cana: Bávaro vs. Cap Cana vs. Uvero Alto
dek: Bávaro for energy, Cap Cana for polish, Uvero Alto for quiet — how to choose your Punta Cana base.
body:
“Punta Cana” covers a long stretch of the Dominican Republic’s eastern coast, and where you stay along it shapes the whole trip — from how busy your beach is to how far you are from dinner.

Bávaro: for energy and choice

Bávaro has the biggest concentration of resorts, the longest walkable beach and the most beach bars, water sports and restaurants. It suits first-timers, groups and anyone who likes a bit of life around them. See our Bávaro beach guide for more.

Cap Cana: for polish

South of the airport, Cap Cana is a gated resort community with a marina, championship golf and some of the area’s most refined hotels and villas. Its signature beach, Juanillo, is calm and beautiful. Expect higher prices and a quieter, more exclusive feel.

Uvero Alto: for quiet

North of Bávaro, Uvero Alto has wilder, emptier beaches and more secluded resorts, several of them adults-focused. The water can be rougher and you will be farther from restaurants outside your hotel — which, for many, is the point.

How to choose

Want to walk the beach and try different bars? Bávaro. Celebrating, golfing or traveling with a bigger budget? Cap Cana. Honeymoon or total switch-off? Uvero Alto. All three are within reach of Punta Cana International, though Uvero Alto is the longest transfer. Compare Punta Cana hotels ↗, then plan your days with our 4-day Punta Cana itinerary.

title: When to Visit Patagonia: A Season-by-Season Guide
dek: Long summer days, empty autumn trails or snowy winter silence — how to choose your season in Patagonia.
body:
Patagonia’s weather is famously changeable in any month, but the seasons still shape almost everything — from which trails are open to how far ahead you need to book a lodge in Torres del Paine.

Summer (December to February)

This is peak season. Days are long — the light lasts well into the evening — trails and boat trips run at full schedule, and temperatures are at their mildest. It is also the windiest and busiest time, with the highest prices. Book lodging, especially inside Torres del Paine, many months ahead.

Spring and autumn (October–November and March–April)

The shoulder seasons are the sweet spot for many travelers: fewer people, lower rates and, in autumn, beech forests turning red and gold around El Chaltén. Expect cooler days and a higher chance of rain or early snow, and check that the services you need are still operating late in the season.

Winter (May to September)

Much of the region slows down. Some lodges and trails close and days are short, but El Calafate stays open for Perito Moreno Glacier, and the landscapes are quiet and snowy. It suits flexible travelers who care more about solitude than long hikes.

Whatever the month

Pack for all four seasons in one day: a windproof shell, warm layers, gloves and sunglasses. Leave buffer days in your plan for weather, especially for long hikes like Laguna de los Tres. Our 7-day Patagonia itinerary builds these in, and the Patagonia guide covers where to stay in El Calafate, El Chaltén and Torres del Paine.

title: El Chaltén Trekking Guide: Patagonia’s Most Beautiful Day on Foot
dek: Plan an unforgettable day of trekking in El Chaltén, from Laguna de los Tres to gentler Patagonia trails, with seasonal safety guidance and a Rallii Rail scenic-route companion.
body:
Wild Routes · Argentine Patagonia

El Chaltén, One Extraordinary Day on Foot

Granite peaks, turquoise water and a trail that begins at the edge of town: this is Patagonia at walking pace.

El Chaltén is the rare mountain town where the adventure begins before the taxi arrives. Trails leave directly from the village and climb into the northern sector of Los Glaciares National Park, drawing the eye toward Fitz Roy—Chaltén—and the serrated drama of Cerro Torre. Argentina recognizes the village as its National Trekking Capital, but the mood feels more intimate than the title suggests: boots at breakfast, weather maps over coffee and a horizon that keeps changing.

The signature day is Laguna de los Tres, a demanding 25-kilometer round trip that national tourism guidance classifies as medium-to-high difficulty. The reward is the closest natural viewpoint toward the Fitz Roy massif, with the lagoon held beneath sheer granite. It is a full day, not a casual scenic walk, and the final ascent asks for patience even from strong hikers.

Choose the trail that fits the day

Laguna de los Tres

Allow roughly eight to nine hours for the 25-kilometer route. Start early, carry layers and save energy for the steep final approach.

Laguna Torre

A lower-gradient alternative of about 18–19 kilometers round trip, following the Fitz Roy River valley toward views of Cerro Torre.

Laguna Capri

A shorter taste of the Fitz Roy trail with rewarding mountain views—ideal when time, conditions or energy rule out the full ascent.
Shorter options near town include Mirador de los Cóndores y de las Águilas and Chorrillo del Salto. Choosing the smaller trail is not a consolation prize. Patagonia rewards attentiveness more than mileage, and wind, visibility and trail conditions should shape the plan.
Jet Set LatAM note: Build two versions of the day before you arrive: a full-route ambition and a beautiful lower-risk alternative. The most elegant itinerary is the one that adapts without drama.

When to go—and what September means

Los Glaciares National Park recommends September through April for visiting, with the broadest trekking season generally unfolding across the Southern Hemisphere’s spring and summer. September is transitional: longer light begins to return, but cold, snow, ice and mud can remain. National park guidance warns that winter conditions may make trails extremely complex and calls for poles and crampons during the May-to-September period. Never rely on an old trail report. Check current conditions with the park and the El Chaltén visitor center shortly before departure. Remote zones may require registration; established campgrounds including De Agostini, Capri and Poincenot require reservations. Walk only on open marked trails, leave your route with someone, and plan to return before dark.

What to pack for a polished, practical day

Begin with broken-in hiking shoes, moisture-managing base layers, an insulating midlayer and a genuinely waterproof shell. Add gloves, a warm hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and a small headlamp. Carry water and enough food for the day: park guidance notes that there are no shops on the trails. Trekking poles are useful for the descent, and traction equipment belongs in the plan whenever current conditions require it. Keep the palette simple—moss, stone, navy, deep berry—so every layer works together. A compact crossbody can stay in town; on the trail, use a fitted daypack with space for discarded layers. For broader seasonal planning, pair this story with the Jet Set LatAM Patagonia weather guide and our Chile-side Patagonia lodge story.

Arriving by the scenic route

El Chaltén sits about 220 kilometers from El Calafate, reached by road through open Patagonian steppe. Build an extra day around the journey rather than treating it as dead time. Rallii Rail can help frame the larger itinerary around scenic transport and memorable overland segments—even where the final connection is by coach—so the route becomes part of the story rather than a gap between pins on a map.
Take the scenic route

Plan the journey with Rallii Rail

Save the rail journeys and overland connections that turn a Patagonian adventure into a beautifully paced itinerary. Discover Rallii Rail on the App Store

The mountain sets the pace

El Chaltén makes ambition feel cinematic, but its real luxury is attention: watching cloud move across granite, hearing meltwater below the trail and knowing when to continue—or turn back. Build the day around conditions, not ego, and Patagonia gives you something better than a conquered route: a landscape experienced fully and carried home vividly.

title: Chepe Express: A Stylish Rail Journey Through Mexico’s Copper Canyon
dek: Ride Mexico’s Chepe Express through Copper Canyon with an elegant stopover plan, current 2026 timing, packing advice and Rallii Rail inspiration.
body:
Rail Adventures · Northern Mexico

Chepe Express Through Copper Canyon

A slow, cinematic journey from Pacific palms to high-country pine, with canyon views unfolding beyond the window.

The Chepe Express does not simply transport you across northern Mexico; it changes the scale of the journey. Leaving Los Mochis, the landscape rises from warm Sinaloan lowlands toward the folds of the Sierra Madre Occidental, where bridges, tunnels and immense canyon walls turn the window into a moving cinema.

The route links Los Mochis, El Fuerte, Bahuichivo, Divisadero and Creel. A full journey takes roughly nine hours and forty minutes, but the most rewarding itinerary makes room for stopovers—allowing the train to become the spine of a deeper Copper Canyon escape.

The elegant three-stop itinerary

El FuerteBegin with colonial streets, shaded courtyards and an unhurried evening before boarding eastbound.
DivisaderoPause for the most dramatic canyon viewpoints and time outdoors at altitude.
CreelFinish among pine forest, rock formations and a mountain-town rhythm that invites an extra night.
Stopovers must be included correctly in your ticket, so decide the shape of your journey before purchase. The official operator recommends booking early—often one to three months ahead—and arriving at the station an hour before departure.

When to go and how the train runs

For 2026, the published timetable lists Los Mochis to Creel departures on Monday, Thursday and Saturday, with return services Tuesday, Friday and Sunday. In May, June, August and September, the train operates only Thursday through Sunday. Schedules can change, so recheck the official Chepe Express site before committing to hotels or flights. Spring brings warmer lowlands; summer can mean rain and greener canyon scenery; autumn is crisp and luminous; winter nights at elevation can be genuinely cold. Pack for temperature swings rather than one forecast.
Practical note: There are no sleeper cars. The operator allows two checked pieces up to 25 kg each plus carry-on, but bicycles and motorcycles are not accepted. Onboard connectivity can be limited and Wi-Fi is not provided, so download confirmations and maps in advance and carry some cash.

Safety, comfort and accessibility

Choose daylight transfers, use established lodging or tour operators for excursions, and ask locally about trail and road conditions. Canyon viewpoints involve uneven ground and significant drops; comfortable closed-toe shoes are more useful than delicate footwear. Travelers with mobility needs should contact the railway and hotels before booking to confirm boarding assistance, room access and transfer arrangements at each stop. For the carriage, wear soft layers, a light scarf and shoes you can walk in. Keep water, medication, a portable charger and sun protection in your day bag rather than checked luggage. First Class includes access to enhanced onboard spaces such as the bar and terrace, but availability varies by service.

The Chepe Express is a reminder that arrival is only one kind of pleasure. Here, distance becomes the story: desert softening into foothills, pine appearing at the glass, and Copper Canyon revealing itself curve by curve.

title: Gabriela Hearst in Uruguay: The Quiet Power of Honest Luxury
dek: From Gabriela Hearst’s Paysandú ranch roots to Manos del Uruguay, discover honest luxury, timeless travel style and a destination wardrobe built with Luxe Jetter.
body:
Fashion Strolls · Uruguay

Gabriela Hearst in Uruguay

From the quiet strength of a Paysandú ranch to modern wardrobes built to last, this is honest luxury with an unmistakably Uruguayan soul.

In Uruguay, luxury rarely needs to announce itself. It lives in a beautifully made saddle, a wool knit that improves with age, a coat cut precisely enough to become part of a life. Gabriela Hearst grew up with that vocabulary on her family’s Santa Isabel ranch in Paysandú, surrounded by horses, cattle and sheep. The lesson was simple and enduring: the most valuable things are made carefully, used fully and kept.

That philosophy became the foundation of her namesake label, launched in 2015 after more than a decade working in New York. Hearst describes the house through timelessness, uncompromising quality and sustainability—an approach that connects the practical intelligence of Uruguay’s countryside with the exacting polish of an international fashion wardrobe.

Where Uruguay meets New York

Hearst’s clothes carry two landscapes at once. From Uruguay comes respect for noble materials, utility and the long view; from New York comes pace, architecture and a need for pieces that perform. Tailored coats, strong suiting, tactile knitwear and restrained dresses are designed less as seasonal decoration than as a working uniform. The result is quiet but never passive. A beautifully weighted cashmere coat has authority. A sharply cut blazer makes movement feel deliberate. A hand-knit carries the presence of the person who made it. This is fashion for a traveler who would rather pack five exceptional pieces than fifteen forgettable ones.
Jet Set LatAM note: Hearst’s version of luxury is especially useful for travel: choose pieces that layer, repeat and gather memory. The goal is not a different outfit for every photograph, but a coherent wardrobe that becomes more personal with every journey.

Manos del Uruguay and the value of handwork

Since the label’s first year, Gabriela Hearst has partnered with Manos del Uruguay, the nonprofit cooperative network that supports rural women artisans. The relationship gives the house’s knitwear a direct connection to Uruguayan skill, place and economic opportunity. Handwork is not presented as nostalgia; it becomes part of a modern system where design, longevity and community reinforce one another. The brand’s sustainability timeline also documents the use of deadstock materials, compostable packaging and circular approaches to production. For Spring–Summer 2026, the house reported that 97 percent of runway wovens came from previous-season deadstock, with deadstock representing 83 percent of total production. These details matter because “sustainable luxury” can otherwise become an aesthetic rather than a measurable practice.

The coat

Look for architectural shoulders, noble fibers and a silhouette strong enough to anchor an entire travel wardrobe.

The knit

Uruguayan handwork brings texture and humanity to pieces designed for years rather than a single season.

The bag

Limited-production handbags favor sculptural form and utility over obvious logos—polished, tactile and discreet.

How to shop—and what to notice

Start with wardrobe architecture: outerwear, tailoring and knitwear that can move between climates. Study fiber composition, construction and care instructions before price or trend. Current collections include cashmere tailoring, aloe linen, recycled wool and embroidered botanical pieces, while the house’s bags offer a compact route into the aesthetic. For a destination-led introduction to the country, pair this story with our Bahia Vik José Ignacio guide. Then revisit the Jet Set LatAM resort-chic packing guide to build a lighter coastal counterpart to Hearst’s structured pieces.

The Jet Set LatAM styling perspective

For Montevideo, begin with fluid trousers, a fine knit and a softly tailored coat in camel, ivory or deep bordeaux. Add polished leather flats for daytime and a sculptural bag for evening. In José Ignacio, loosen the formula: an aloe-linen shirt, long skirt and woven texture feel refined without competing with the coast. On the ranch, practicality becomes the elegance—boots, denim, warm knitwear and a coat that can handle wind. Keep the palette narrow and the textures rich. One immaculate jacket can work over a dress, trousers or denim. A hand-knit should be folded rather than hung, while leather and suede travel best inside breathable dust bags. The smartest edit is always the one you can wear repeatedly.

Translate honest luxury with Luxe Jetter

Create a destination wardrobe inspired by Uruguay’s natural palette, then refine every layer for the climate, itinerary and mood of the trip. Open Luxe JetterIf the experience does not appear, launch Luxe Jetter here.

Luxury with a memory

Gabriela Hearst’s most persuasive idea is not that fashion must become austere to become responsible. It is that beauty gains power when it is made with purpose. Her Uruguay is present in the discipline of the materials, the dignity of handwork and the expectation that a cherished object should last. For the Jet Set LatAM traveler, it is an invitation to buy less, choose better and let every piece accompany a longer story.

title: Johanna Ortiz in Cali: The Art of Tropical Elegance
dek: Inside Johanna Ortiz’s Cali atelier: tropical elegance, Colombian handwork, what to notice, how to shop and how Luxe Jetter turns the house’s joyful language into a destination wardrobe.
body:
Fashion Strolls · Colombia

Johanna Ortiz in Cali

Inside the Colombian house where tropical exuberance, feminine movement and generations of handwork become a modern language of luxury.

Cali enters through the senses: the glossy green of palms after rain, salsa spilling from an open doorway, the warmth that softens the edges of an afternoon. It is easy to understand why Johanna Ortiz chose to build her fashion house here. Her clothes do not merely borrow the tropics as decoration; they translate the city’s rhythm into sweeping skirts, sculptural ruffles, placed prints and embroidery that seems to move before the wearer does.

Founded in Cali in 2003, the house began with resort and swimwear and grew into a global lifestyle brand spanning ready-to-wear, accessories, swim and home. Yet its emotional and productive center remains Colombia. For the Jet Set LatAM traveler, that rootedness is precisely the point: Ortiz offers a glamorous way to wear a destination without reducing it to a postcard.

A fashion house with Cali at its center

Ortiz returned to Colombia after studying fashion design in the United States and furthering her education in New York and Paris. Instead of relocating the business to a traditional fashion capital, she developed an atelier in her hometown. The decision shaped everything that followed. The brand’s official atelier notes that more than 90 percent of production is made in-house in Cali by a team of over 460 people, with women forming the majority of the workforce. This vertically integrated model allows exuberance to be precise. A dramatic silhouette is balanced by controlled construction; a botanical print is placed to frame the body; raffia, beads and embroidery add dimension without losing lightness. The result is festive but never careless—clothes designed for movement, conversation and entrances remembered long after dinner.
Jet Set LatAM note: Look beyond the headline ruffle. The most compelling Johanna Ortiz pieces reveal their luxury in engineered print placement, hand-finished texture and the way volume changes as you walk.

Craft, community and La Escuela

The house links its growth to social inclusion and the preservation of artisanal knowledge. Escuela Johanna Ortiz, established in 2016, provides couture-level sewing and embroidery training, psychosocial support and practical assistance to vulnerable women. The official program reports that hundreds of people have participated and that many graduates have joined the company. Alongside its Cali atelier, the brand works with Indigenous communities and artisanal associations on techniques and materials including iraca palm from Sandoná, paja tetera weaving, glass-beaded mochilas and hand-carved wood. These collaborations are most meaningful when understood as relationships with identifiable traditions—not as a vague “handmade” flourish. The house’s Original Piece label is intended to honor provenance and the community behind an object.

Movement

Ruffles, bias cuts and fluid layers create silhouettes that come alive in a warm breeze or on a dance floor.

Handwork

Raffia embroidery, beadwork and woven fibers turn accessories and garments into tactile keepsakes.

Tropical restraint

Botanical references and saturated color feel most modern when grounded with clean sandals, natural texture and confident simplicity.

What to notice—and how to shop

Begin with the dresses, but do not stop there. A printed skirt or sculptural top often carries the same expressive force while working harder in a travel wardrobe. Handwoven accessories add Colombian craft to neutral tailoring, and swim pieces make a natural bridge between city and coast. Examine product notes for materials, artisan techniques and preorder timing; limited production and hand-finishing can mean longer lead times. The official site lists boutiques in Cali, Bogotá and Cartagena, as well as international online shopping. If Cartagena is part of the itinerary, pair this story with our guide to designer boutiques and fashion-forward neighborhood shopping for the kind of slow, observant browsing that makes a piece feel connected to place. Confirm current store hours directly before visiting, especially around holidays and local events.

The Jet Set LatAM styling perspective

Let one Ortiz gesture lead. For a warm-city lunch, try a printed midi skirt with a crisp white shirt, flat leather sandals and a woven bag. At sunset, choose a fluid dress with sculptural earrings and little else. For cooler destinations, layer a ruffled blouse beneath an ivory suit or pair a botanical skirt with a fine knit and polished boots. The goal is not costume; it is equilibrium—volume with restraint, color with clarity, romance with enough structure to travel beautifully. Pack the most detailed pieces inside out in a breathable garment bag, cushion dimensional embroidery with tissue and keep woven accessories away from water, perfume and harsh chemicals. A compact steamer is useful, but always follow the care label before applying heat.
Style the journey

Build the destination wardrobe with Luxe Jetter

Turn the mood of Cali—or your next Latin American escape—into a wearable packing plan. Explore destination-led looks, refine the palette and save the pieces that make the whole trip feel considered. Open Luxe Jetter If the experience does not appear, launch Luxe Jetter here.

A house that wears its origin proudly

Johanna Ortiz has made Cali visible not by flattening it into a tropical fantasy, but by building a serious fashion ecosystem around local talent, technical skill and feminine possibility. The clothes are joyful because they are exacting; sensual because they understand movement; worldly because their point of view is unmistakably Colombian. For the traveler who wants fashion to hold the memory of a place, that is the rarest kind of souvenir.

title: PatBO in Brazil: Hand-Embroidered Glamour from Uberlândia to the World
dek: Inside PatBO’s world of Brazilian hand embroidery: Patricia Bonaldi’s Uberlândia atelier, the women preserving its craft, what to notice, how to shop and how Luxe Jetter styles the look.
body:
Fashion Strolls · Brazil

PatBO’s Brazilian glamour is stitched by hand.

From an atelier in Uberlândia to resort wardrobes and international runways, Patricia Bonaldi turns embroidery, movement and unapologetic femininity into clothes made for arriving beautifully.

There is a particular kind of confidence in Brazilian evening light: warm, theatrical and never interested in disappearing quietly. PatBO dresses belong to that hour. They shimmer without becoming precious, move without losing structure, and carry the unmistakable evidence of hands at work.

For the Jet Set LatAM traveler, PatBO is more than a label to know. It is a way to understand how Brazilian fashion translates place into texture—how Minas Gerais craftsmanship can meet São Paulo polish, beachside ease and the drama of an evening entrance.

From Uberlândia, a fashion language of her own

Patricia Bonaldi grew up in Uberlândia, Minas Gerais, where her mother taught her to sew. According to the brand’s own history, she began with one-of-a-kind evening gowns before building PatBO into a house spanning ready-to-wear and swim. The through line has remained remarkably clear: precise fit, exuberant color, hand embroidery and silhouettes designed to feel glamorous without becoming stiff.

The official PatBO story places craftsmanship at the center of the house. Artisans in Uberlândia bring Bonaldi’s designs to life stitch by stitch, connecting modern resort dressing with skills that cannot be rushed or convincingly imitated by a machine.

Why it matters: PatBO’s clothes do not use craft as surface decoration. Handwork is the structure of the brand’s identity—and part of every purchase supports its free community training initiative.

The atelier, the school and the women behind the embroidery

In 2015, Bonaldi founded Costurando Sonhos in her hometown. The free program teaches sewing, embroidery, hand-beading and garment construction. PatBO reports that hundreds of women have completed its courses, with graduates going on to open businesses, teach others or work as artisans.

That context changes how you see the clothes. A beaded bodice is not simply ornate; it represents time, training and a local vocabulary of making. The most compelling PatBO pieces hold that labor visibly. You notice dimensional flowers, dense beadwork, crochet and fringe that react to every step.

What to notice in a PatBO collection

Hand embroidery

Look closely at floral appliqué, beadwork and embellished surfaces. These are statement pieces, but the workmanship rewards an intimate view.

Movement

Fringe, fluid skirts and strategic cutouts are designed for motion—ideal for a coastal dinner, rooftop cocktails or a dance floor after dark.

Brazilian color

Botanical brights, sun-warmed neutrals and luminous evening tones make even a single piece feel like the center of a travel wardrobe.

The current PatBO edit ranges from beachwear to runway gowns, with crochet, poplin, chiffon, fringe and embroidery appearing across categories. Rather than packing multiple competing statements, choose one PatBO piece and let it set the mood for everything around it.

How to shop PatBO in Brazil

Begin with the brand’s official Brazil site for current collections and boutique information. PatBO says it operates its own Brazilian stores and is carried through a wider network of points of sale. Stock, opening hours and appointments can change, so confirm directly before making a special trip.

If São Paulo is part of your itinerary, treat the visit as an editorial afternoon: start with the polished fashion landscape of Jardins, pause for coffee, then compare PatBO’s maximal femininity with the city’s quieter tailoring and jewelry. Our guide to the best designer boutiques in São Paulo’s Jardins district is the natural companion.

The Jet Set LatAM styling perspective

PatBO works best when the rest of the look gives it room. For a tropical dinner, pair an embroidered midi dress with slim metallic sandals, sculptural earrings and a small woven bag. For a city evening, ground a fringe or beaded piece with a clean blazer and polished leather. Around the pool, choose one dramatic cover-up over a beautifully simple swimsuit.

The key is restraint around the statement: luminous skin, an intentional shoe, one piece of jewelry. Let movement and craftsmanship do the talking.

A final word

PatBO’s appeal is immediate—color, sparkle, movement—but its deeper beauty is slower. It lives in the hours of handwork, the women learning and preserving those skills, and the belief that glamour can carry a place’s creative memory. Pack one extraordinary piece and let it become part of your own travel story.

title: Sensi Studio in Ecuador: The Art of the Modern Panama Hat
dek: Meet Sensi Studio, the Ecuadorian fashion house transforming handwoven toquilla straw into modern Panama hats, sculptural bags and polished resort style.
body:
In Guayaquil, tropical light changes the logic of dressing. Shade becomes an accessory, natural fibers feel instinctively right, and a beautifully proportioned hat can transform a simple look into a complete point of view. Sensi Studio, founded by Ecuadorian designer Stephany Sensi, turns that relationship between climate, craft and style into modern Panama hats, woven bags and relaxed ready-to-wear.

The pieces carry the confidence of resort fashion without losing their origin. Toquilla straw is dyed, woven and shaped by hand; baskets and totes bring texture to city dressing; wide brims feel dramatic but never fussy. The result is Ecuadorian craft seen through a cosmopolitan lens.

From Guayaquil to the Andes

Sensi Studio’s headquarters are in Guayaquil, while its craft network reaches into Ecuador’s Andean region. The house says every product is manufactured in Ecuador and works closely with women artisans, providing fair remuneration while supporting the continuation of a millenary toquilla-straw weaving tradition.

This geography matters. Guayaquil brings coastal ease and an outward-looking fashion energy; the Andes bring the patient knowledge required to turn palm fiber into an object that is light, resilient and beautifully structured.

Stephany Sensi’s Fashion Education

Stephany Sensi studied fashion design at Istituto Marangoni in Milan and later completed a master’s degree in brand management there. She then worked with Tomas Maier in Miami from 2006 to 2010. That international training helps explain the brand’s balance: traditional materials are treated with the precision, color instinct and merchandising clarity of a global accessories house.

Launched in 2010 as a design and product laboratory, Sensi Studio began with genuine Panama hats, handwoven handbags and accessories. Ready-to-wear followed in 2014 with a focus on embroidered summer dresses.

The Pieces to Notice

  • El Campesino: a 100-percent toquilla-straw hat whose clean shape celebrates hand weaving and everyday versatility.
  • Lampshade brims: cone-like silhouettes with a small crown and widening brim—part hat, part architecture.
  • Wide-brim Cordovan shapes: polished enough for a city lunch, protective enough for tropical light.
  • Toquilla and sisal bags: baskets, buckets and totes that pair natural texture with leather, linen, fringe or sculptural handles.
  • High Summer 2026: the current collection mixes refined natural fibers with leather and elevated warm-weather detailing.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Edit

Let the hat set the proportion. Wear a wide lampshade brim with a slim column dress, flat sandals and a small woven bag. Pair El Campesino with high-waisted linen trousers and a silk scarf tied close to the neck. For the beach, a toquilla tote and oversized shirt feel more enduring than a themed resort look.

Keep the palette sun-washed—natural straw, cacao, ivory, clay—then add one unexpected color in the ribbon or bag. The craft should remain visible, so avoid over-accessorizing.

Made-to-order items generally require two to three weeks before shipping, so plan well ahead of travel. The brand lists a Guayaquil location at La Piazza Samborondón and recommends direct contact for current information.

A Hat with a Sense of Place

Sensi Studio makes the Panama hat feel not like a souvenir, but like modern design. Every brim carries the balance of hand and eye, Andes and coast, tradition and fashion. It is the kind of travel piece that protects, transforms and remembers where it came from.

title: Daniela Villegas: The Mexican Jeweler Turning Nature Into Modern Talismans
dek: Enter the vivid, nature-led world of Mexican jeweler Daniela Villegas, where beetles, butterflies and sea creatures become exquisitely crafted modern talismans.
body:
In Mexico City, beauty is rarely separated from symbolism. A carved doorway can feel like a portal; a garden can carry generations of memory; a flash of color can transform an ordinary corner into something almost ceremonial. It is the perfect imaginative starting point for the world of Daniela Villegas, the Mexican jeweler who turns the animal and botanical realms into intimate works of art.

Her pieces are not quiet in the conventional sense. Beetles glow with colored stones, chameleons curl around fingers, and manta rays seem ready to glide across the skin. Yet beneath the wit and exuberance is a thoughtful idea: jewelry can be a companion—a small guardian that carries memory, instinct and transformation wherever its wearer goes.

A Mexican Eye for Color, Nature and Meaning

Founded in 2008, the Daniela Villegas brand reflects its founder’s Mexican heritage through a sensibility that is joyful, surreal and deeply attuned to the natural world. The label’s official biography describes a talismanic universe shaped by metamorphosis, ancient myths, personal memory and the “spiritual intelligence of nature.” That poetic vocabulary gives her fine jewelry an emotional register far beyond ornament.

Villegas now lives in Los Angeles, where her pieces are handcrafted by master artisans. The cross-city perspective feels essential: Mexico’s warmth, imagination and symbolic richness meet California light and an almost cinematic sense of scale. The result is luxury with personality—precious, but never predictable.

The Creator’s Story: Wonder Made Wearable

Villegas approaches nature as both muse and message. According to the house, her designs bring creatures including beetles, butterflies, sharks, manta rays, chameleons and sloths into sculptural form. Each animal becomes a character with its own energy: an emblem of adaptability, protection, renewal or curiosity.

The material language is equally expressive. Eighteen-karat gold and precious or semi-precious stones are paired with unexpected organic elements such as beetles, porcupine quills, feathers, shells, pebbles and wood. The combinations can feel fantastical, but the craftsmanship keeps them exquisitely grounded. They are conversation pieces in the truest sense—objects that invite a closer look, then reveal another story.

The Pieces to Notice

  • Beetle jewels: perhaps the purest expression of Villegas’s world, where iridescence and transformation become richly detailed rings, earrings and objects of fascination.
  • Chameleons: playful, sculptural and beautifully suited to wrapping around a finger, they celebrate adaptability without losing their sense of humor.
  • Butterflies: familiar symbols of metamorphosis rendered with color, lightness and the polish of fine jewelry.
  • Ocean creatures: sharks and manta rays bring a sleek, slightly mysterious note to the collection—a reminder that the natural world can be elegant and untamed at once.
  • Organic-material designs: the most unexpected works mix traditional luxury materials with shells, wood, feathers or stones found in nature, creating pieces that feel collected rather than merely purchased.

How Jet Set LatAM Would Style It

The secret is to let one creature lead the look. Pair a sculptural ring with a cream linen suit and a silk camisole for a gallery afternoon in Mexico City. Give a colorful pendant room against a black column dress at dinner. For resort dressing, a manta-ray or beetle motif adds wit to a crisp white caftan, woven clutch and minimal leather sandals.

Villegas’s jewelry is especially compelling with pieces that carry their own tactile intelligence: handwoven textiles, fluid silks, softly tailored cotton and architectural accessories. The styling should feel collected across a life of travel, not matched in a single sitting.

How to Discover and Shop the Collection

For the clearest view of current work, begin with the official Daniela Villegas website, where the collections are presented inside the designer’s full visual universe. Because many pieces use unusual natural materials and intricate stonework, study scale, dimensions and care guidance closely before purchasing. For a significant piece, ask about materials, sizing, availability and aftercare directly through the brand’s official channels.

If this story has you dreaming of a design-led day, continue with our guide to São Paulo’s best designer boutiques in Jardins, another neighborhood where Latin American creativity becomes part of the walk.

A Talisman for the Journey

Daniela Villegas offers a persuasive answer to what modern luxury can be: technically accomplished, emotionally alive and unafraid of delight. Her creatures do more than decorate. They suggest that transformation is always close, that curiosity deserves to be worn proudly, and that the most memorable travel objects are the ones that keep revealing themselves long after the suitcase is unpacked.

body:
Top Spa & Wellness Destinations

ythos: Mexico | wellness | ancestral healing | luxury escapes

Mexico’s wellness culture is a living lineage—temazcales warmed by volcanic stone, herbal rituals passed down through Indigenous healers, and oceanfront sanctuaries where modern luxury meets ancient cosmology. This guide maps the country’s most transformative spa destinations, each paired with walking‑friendly micro‑itineraries so travelers can explore slowly, sensorially, and on foot.

🌿 Riviera Maya — Temazcal Rituals & Caribbean Calm

Why It’s Iconic

The Riviera Maya blends Maya cosmology, turquoise water, and jungle‑wrapped sanctuaries. Resorts here often integrate copal cleansing, sound healing, and cenote‑inspired hydrotherapy.

Top Wellness Retreats

  • Rosewood Mayakoba Sense Spa — Lagoon‑side treatment villas, Mayan herbal rituals, meditation labyrinth.
  • Nizuc Spa by ESPA — Mayan purification, hydrothermal circuit, oceanfront relaxation decks.
  • Palmaïa, The House of AïA — Plant‑based menus, daily rituals, shamanic ceremonies.

Walking Map: Playa del Carmen Wellness Loop

A 45–60 minute gentle loop ideal for grounding before or after treatments.

  • Start: 38th Street beach access (shaded palms, calm water).
  • Walk south along the shoreline to Calle 14 (boutique cafés + beach clubs).
  • Cut inland to 5th Avenue for fresh juice or coconut water.
  • Return north via Calle 38’s leafy pedestrian corridor.

🔥 Oaxaca — Ancestral Medicine & Mountain Energy

Why It’s Iconic

Oaxaca’s wellness traditions are rooted in Zapotec and Mixtec herbalism, copal smoke blessings, and steam‑bath temazcales guided by local healers.

Top Wellness Retreats

  • Hotel Escondido — Minimalist luxury on a wild Pacific beach; temazcal + ocean‑view massages.
  • Casa Silencio — Mezcal‑valley sanctuary with elemental rituals and sound‑bath ceremonies.
  • Hotel Azul Spa — Urban‑meets‑ancestral treatments using local herbs and clay.

Walking Map: Oaxaca City Healing Circuit

A 30–40 minute cultural‑wellness stroll.

  • Start: Templo de Santo Domingo (garden meditation).
  • Walk south along Macedonio Alcalá pedestrian street.
  • Pause at a local herbal apothecary for tinctures + teas.
  • End: Zócalo shaded benches for grounding and people‑watching.

🌊 Los Cabos — Desert Minimalism & Ocean Energy

Why It’s Iconic

Cabo’s wellness scene merges Baja desert stillness, Pacific power, and Japanese‑inspired minimalism. Treatments often use local salt, clay, and desert botanicals.

Top Wellness Retreats

  • Las Ventanas al Paraíso Spa — Four Elements rituals, desert‑rose massages, moonlit treatments.
  • One&Only Palmilla Spa — Baja botanicals, deep‑tissue ocean‑energy therapies.
  • Esperanza Auberge Spa — Cliffside cabanas, chakra balancing, desert‑salt scrubs.

Walking Map: San José del Cabo Art & Calm Route

A 60–75 minute slow‑paced loop.

  • Start: Plaza Mijares.
  • Wander the Art District’s galleries + courtyards.
  • Continue to the estuary viewpoint for bird‑watching.
  • Finish: Beachfront promenade for sunset grounding.

🌴 Puerto Vallarta — Jungle Wellness & Pacific Warmth

Why It’s Iconic

PV’s lush Sierra Madre backdrop creates a natural spa environment—river stones, jungle aromatics, cacao ceremonies, and open‑air treatment rooms.

Top Wellness Retreats

  • Xinalani Retreat — Yoga shalas above the ocean, holistic therapies, plant‑based menus.
  • Mousai Spa Imagine — Rooftop hydrotherapy, chromotherapy, jungle views.
  • Casa Velas Spa — Adults‑only calm, botanical facials, aromatherapy rituals.

Walking Map: Zona Romántica to Conchas Chinas

A 45–60 minute scenic coastal walk.

  • Start: Los Muertos Pier.
  • Walk south along the coastal path toward Conchas Chinas.
  • Stop at tide pools for grounding.
  • Return via quiet residential streets lined with bougainvillea.

🌺 Tulum — Jungle Rituals & Modern Spirituality

Why It’s Iconic

Tulum’s wellness identity blends Maya healing, sound baths, breathwork, and eco‑luxury design. Many spas are built around cenotes or jungle clearings.

Top Wellness Retreats

  • Yäan Healing Sanctuary — Energy work, herbal baths, Mayan deep‑tissue therapies.
  • Azulik Spa — Treehouse treatment rooms, clay rituals, sound healing.
  • Sanará Spa — Oceanfront yoga, detox therapies, plant‑based nourishment.

Walking Map: Tulum Beach Slow Path

A 30–50 minute shaded beach‑road walk.

  • Start: Nomade Tulum.
  • Walk north past boutiques + cafés.
  • Pause at beach access points for ocean dips.
  • End: Sanará for a post‑walk juice or treatment.

🌅 Final Takeaway

Mexico’s wellness landscape is a fusion of ancestral healing and luxury design, where temazcales meet hydrotherapy circuits and jungle rituals meet oceanfront sanctuaries. Each region offers its own rhythm—mountain mysticism, desert minimalism, Caribbean calm—and walking‑friendly micro‑routes help travelers slow down and absorb the energy of place.

title: International Connections in Colombia
dek: Do you need to make an international connection in Colombia? We did, so we started to look into that process. How would we get from the domestic to the international terminal? Would we be able to clear immigration in time for our connection? After finding so little information out there, we started to worry. As…
body:
Do you need to make an international connection in Colombia? We did, so we started to look into that process. How would we get from the domestic to the international terminal? Would we be able to clear immigration in time for our connection? After finding so little information out there, we started to worry.

As it turns out, our concerns were unfounded. On our Cartagena to Playa del Carmen flight connecting through Bogota, our experience was unexpectedly uneventful. For those with similar concerns, here are some tips and tricks for your journey:

  • Choose The Right Connection for You: We considered two options for our flight from Cartagena to Playa del Carmen: an Avianca flight connecting through Bogota and a Copa Airlines flight through Panama City. We chose the Avianca flight because it was less expensive and had a shorter, 2-hour layover. That 2-hour layover worked out in our case.
  • Our Anxieties: Flying through Bogota gave us a bit of anxiety. In Colombia, you must go through immigration at your port of exit. Since our Cartagena to Bogota leg was a domestic flight, that meant we had to clear immigration in Bogota. Would a 2-hour window leave us enough time to get through the airport, clear security again and get through immigration in time for our next flight?
  • How to Clear Immigration in Bogota: As it turns out, our anxieties were misplaced, at least for our specific situation We did have to walk from one end of the airport to the other, but lines for security and immigration were short, and the immigration checkpoint in Bogota has been fully automated. We got to our flight twenty minutes before boarding (in other words, about an hour and a half before flight departure). Here’s what to expect, as of February 2026:
  • Complete the Colombian Check Mig form online before your departure. We still haven’t figured out if the form is actually necessary, but why run the risk? The form is straightforward enough, with basic questions about your personal information and departure flight.
  • Arrive at the airport at least two hours before your first flight. Our flight left early in the morning (8:30 AM), so we arrived at 6:30. We checked our bags easily and breezed through the security lines. Keep in mind, there is a limit on the amount of liquids you can pack in your hand bags. The security officer in Cartagena did not seem to care about our liter bottle of water, but they were more strict in Bogota.
  • Once in Bogota, make your way from the domestic to the international terminal. It’s a long walk, and the signs are confusing. There are signs for “domestic connections” and signs for “connecting flights.” By process of elimination and asking a few agents, we figured out that we should follow the “connecting flight” signs. It would have been nice if there were signs saying “international connections,” but the airport authority only saw it fit to distinguish “domestic connections” from “connections”.
  • You will need to exit security to get to your international connection. Once you exit, walk past the baggage claim area and follow the (now conspicuous) signs to the international departures area. It’s on the second floor up a flight of escalators.
  • The security and immigration checkpoint is at the center of the international departures area. The signs are a little unclear, but they say “Gates A/B.” Scan your boarding to get through the gates, then join the queue for immigration check.
  • The immigration checkpoint in Bogota is fully electronic, and we got through it in a few minutes. We simply scanned our passport, confirmed our flight number and posed for a picture. The glass gates opened and presto, we were through.
  • Once you’re through immigration, you will need to clear security again. They are more strict about security protocols in Bogota, so don’t expect to get through with bottles of rum in your hand luggage.
  • What Else? Even though we made our connection just fine, we have read stories about long lines at immigration checkpoints when leaving Colombia. So make sure to leave plenty of additional time during peak travel periods. Even if you’re not travelling during a peak season, the trek from the domestic to the international terminal is very long. Make sure to leave yourself plenty of time to walk. Finally, if you’re one of those people who likes to have an even bigger buffer to get through immigration, you may want to choose a flight that connects in a different country. That way you can arrive to the airport even earlier than we did and control your own destiny.

Check back in tomorrow for our first day in Playa del Carmen.

title: Perfect Places to Avoid the Crowds: Dominica
dek: Dominica is the Caribbean’s best‑kept secret — a lush, volcanic island where waterfalls thunder through emerald forests, hot springs bubble beneath the canopy, and black‑sand beaches stretch into the horizon without a single sunbed in sight. body:
This post is not about a Latin American destination but it’s close.

Dominica is the Caribbean’s best‑kept secret — a lush, volcanic island where waterfalls thunder through emerald forests, hot springs bubble beneath the canopy, and black‑sand beaches stretch into the horizon without a single sunbed in sight. Known as the Nature Island, Dominica offers something rare in the Caribbean: a place where you can disappear into pure, unfiltered wilderness while still enjoying boutique luxury, soulful cuisine, and warm, understated hospitality.

If neighboring islands are polished and resort‑heavy, Dominica is the opposite — raw, cinematic, and blissfully uncrowded.

Quick Links

Plan and Book

Check Flights

Find affordable flights using Cheap-O-Air

Homes and Villas

Stay like a local at a VRBO villa.

Book Hotels

🎟️ Tours — Viator | 🚘 Transfers — Priority Pickups | 🌴 Experiences — Klook

🌿 The Vibe: Wild, Untouched, and Soul‑Stirring

Dominica is for travelers who crave nature, solitude, and authenticity. There are no mega‑resorts, no cruise‑ship chaos, no overdeveloped strips. Instead, you’ll find:

  • Rainforests that feel primeval
  • Rivers so clear they look unreal
  • Hot springs hidden in the jungle
  • Black‑sand beaches with dramatic surf
  • A culture rooted in resilience and community

It’s the Caribbean for people who want to feel something — not just see it.

🏖️ Beaches & Natural Wonders: Quiet, Dramatic, and Otherworldly

Champagne Reef

A surreal snorkeling spot where volcanic vents release warm bubbles, creating an underwater “champagne” effect.

Trafalgar Falls

Twin waterfalls crashing into a jungle amphitheater. Go early and you may have the pools entirely to yourself.

Emerald Pool

A rainforest grotto with jade‑green water and a soft waterfall — peaceful, mystical, and perfect for a refreshing dip.

Morne Trois Pitons National Park

A UNESCO World Heritage Site filled with boiling lakes, fumaroles, and cloud forests. It’s Dominica at its most cinematic.

Batibou Beach

A secluded, palm‑framed beach with golden sand and gentle waves. Often nearly empty.

Find Guided Experiences

🏨 Where to Stay: Boutique, Eco‑Luxury, and Immersed in Nature

Dominica’s accommodations blend sustainability with elevated comfort — ideal for travelers seeking privacy and atmosphere.

Secret Bay

Treehouse‑style villas perched above the sea, private plunge pools, and ultra‑personalized service. One of the Caribbean’s most exclusive eco‑luxury stays.

Jungle Bay

A wellness‑forward retreat with villas tucked into the forest, daily yoga, and access to world‑class hiking.

Rosalie Bay Eco Resort

A serene, oceanfront sanctuary where sea turtles nest and the river meets the sea.

Pagua Bay House

Chic, intimate, and perfect for travelers who want boutique style without the crowds.

🍽️ Where to Eat: Fresh, Local, and Flavor‑Driven

Dominica’s food scene is rooted in the land — think farm‑to‑table before it was a trend.

KoKoYa Restaurant at Secret Bay

Elevated Caribbean cuisine with hyper‑local ingredients and ocean views.

Zam Zam Café

A charming, plant‑forward spot with fresh juices, wraps, and vegan‑friendly dishes.

The Great Room at Fort Young Hotel

Refined island flavors with a modern twist, overlooking the sea.

Local Creole Stands

Try callaloo soup, grilled fish, bakes, and fresh tropical fruit — simple, soulful, and unforgettable.

🌋 What to Do: Adventure, Wellness, and Pure Nature

Boiling Lake Hike

One of the world’s largest boiling lakes — a challenging, bucket‑list trek through volcanic terrain.

Hot Springs Soaking

Wotten Waven is dotted with natural hot pools perfect for post‑hike relaxation.

River Tubing

Float through lush valleys on the Layou River — peaceful, scenic, and fun.

Whale Watching

Dominica is the only country where sperm whales live year‑round. Sightings are common and magical.

Canyoning

Rappel down waterfalls and swim through narrow gorges — Dominica’s most thrilling adventure.

🌤️ When to Go

  • December–April: Dry season, perfect weather, ideal for hiking and beach days.
  • May–June: Lush, quiet, and great value.
  • July–November: Rainier but incredibly green — ideal for wellness retreats and solitude.

🇺🇾 Travel Tips & FAQ for Dominica

🧭 Essential Travel Tips

💱 Currency & Money

  • Currency: Eastern Caribbean Dollar (XCD).
  • USD accepted: Widely accepted in hotels, restaurants, and tours.
  • ATMs: Available in Roseau and Portsmouth.
  • Credit cards: Accepted at most hotels and mid‑to‑high‑end restaurants.
  • Tipping: 10–15% is standard when not included.

🛂 Visa Requirements

  • Most travelers do not need a visa for stays up to 21–90 days, including visitors from:
    • United States
    • Canada
    • European Union
    • United Kingdom
  • Passport validity: Must be valid for the duration of your stay.
  • Extensions: Possible through local immigration offices.

💉 Health & Safety

  • Vaccines: No special vaccinations required.
  • Tap water: Safe to drink in most areas.
  • Safety: Very safe island with friendly locals and low crime.

📶 Connectivity

  • Wi‑Fi: Reliable in hotels; slower in remote areas.
  • SIM cards: Digicel and Flow offer tourist SIMs.
  • eSIM: Available for many carriers.

🚗 Transportation

  • Best way to get around: Rental car — Dominica is spread out and mountainous.
  • Driving: On the left side of the road.
  • Taxis: Available but can be pricey for long distances.
  • Ferries: Connect Dominica to Martinique and Guadeloupe.

🌤️ Weather

  • Tropical and humid year‑round.
  • Dry season: December–April.
  • Rainy season: June–November, with lush landscapes and fewer visitors.

❓ FAQ: Dominica

Is Dominica crowded?

Not at all. It’s one of the least‑visited Caribbean islands — perfect for travelers seeking space and solitude.

Is Dominica good for beaches?

Yes, but not in the typical Caribbean way. Expect dramatic black‑sand beaches, wild surf, and quiet coves.

Is Dominica expensive?

Moderate. Eco‑luxury stays can be high‑end, but food and activities are generally affordable.

Do I need to be fit to enjoy Dominica?

Not necessarily, but many of the island’s highlights involve hiking, climbing, or swimming.

Is Dominica good for families?

Yes — especially for nature‑loving families who enjoy waterfalls, rivers, and outdoor adventures.

Can I swim in the ocean?

Yes, but some beaches have strong currents. Calm spots like Mero Beach are ideal for swimming.

What’s the food like?

Fresh, local, and deeply flavorful — think Creole spices, seafood, tropical produce, and hearty soups.

Is Dominica worth visiting outside peak season?

Absolutely. The island is lush, quiet, and magical year‑round.
